item.title: [SCMP] How Taiwan’s new AI satellite system aims to speed up early warning against PLA moves
item.description:
Taiwan will acquire an AI-powered satellite imagery system capable of rapidly identifying People’s Liberation Army ships, aircraft and missile launchers, as it seeks to boost early-warning capabilities in the face of growing military pressure from Beijing.

The NT$46.55 million (US$1.45 million) system will use artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse satellite images covering 100 sq km (38.6 square miles) within minutes, potentially cutting the time and manpower needed to track changes in PLA deployments, according to the island’s defence ministry.

In a public procurement notice this week, the ministry’s Communication Development Office (CDO), a primary military intelligence unit, awarded the contract to ThinkTron, a Taiwan-Japan joint venture specialising in AI, geospatial information systems and monitoring technology.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan will acquire an AI-powered satellite imagery system capable of rapidly identifying People’s Liberation Army ships, aircraft and missile launchers, as it seeks to boost early-warning capabilities in the face of growing military pressure from Beijing.

The NT$46.55 million (US$1.45 million) system will use artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse satellite images covering 100 sq km (38.6 square miles) within minutes, potentially cutting the time and manpower needed to track changes in PLA deployments, according to the island’s defence ministry.

In a public procurement notice this week, the ministry’s Communication Development Office (CDO), a primary military intelligence unit, awarded the contract to ThinkTron, a Taiwan-Japan joint venture specialising in AI, geospatial information systems and monitoring technology.

The contract took effect on September 25, and the system is expected to be completed by the end of April.

Taiwan’s defence minister, Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, confirmed earlier this year that the island’s military planned to develop a prototype AI satellite imagery recognition system.

Ministry officials said the technology was intended to rapidly search for and identify enemy forces and activity at military bases and elsewhere near Taiwan, automatically compare new imagery with historical data and flag changes for intelligence analysts.

Sources familiar with the project said the aim was to improve strategic early warning and support combat-readiness decisions.

The system could analyse several 10km by 10km areas within minutes, identifying ships more than 10 metres (about 33 feet) long as well as smaller targets such as aircraft, missile launchers and radar vehicles, they said.

According to Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei, the project should not be confused with the acquisition of new reconnaissance satellites.

“The system’s main function is to use AI to help the CDO rapidly analyse imagery and information received from satellites,” he said.

The CDO did not itself operate the military-grade imagery satellites providing the data, Wang added. Rather, the AI would serve as an analytical layer processing imagery obtained from other sources.

That distinction also helps to explain the project’s relatively modest cost.

Wang said building an entire satellite reconnaissance architecture – from operating satellites to receiving their imagery – would require far greater investment.

The new system instead sits at the end of the intelligence pipeline, automatically screening large quantities of imagery that would otherwise require labour-intensive analysis.

Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, said the underlying technology was already mature and used by advanced militaries and remote-sensing organisations.

He explained that the significance for Taiwan lay in operationalising the technology and integrating it with the island’s existing intelligence capabilities.

“The PLA is already capable of installing AI systems directly on satellites to conduct preliminary analysis of imagery before the data is transmitted to the ground, allowing it to respond more quickly,” Lo said.

But the Taiwan project is different, he added, noting the analyses would be done on the ground at the CDO.

Lo said there would be no difficulty for the island to set up such an AI-powered system, noting that ThinkTron was jointly established by Taiwan’s Sinotech Engineering Consultants and Japanese geospatial specialist Kokusai Kogyo.

According to ThinkTron’s website, its existing “Tron Eyes” technology uses convolutional neural networks to analyse imagery for applications ranging from disaster prevention and infrastructure inspection to agriculture and transport.

Lo argued that AI could help address a growing intelligence challenge for Taiwan’s military: the sheer volume of information generated by frequent PLA operations around the island.

“Instead of requiring analysts to manually search large satellite images for ships, aircraft or mobile missile launchers, the system could automatically flag potential targets or changes for closer examination,” he said.

This would be particularly useful when monitoring large areas of sea, he added, with synthetic aperture radar, or SAR, detecting vessels at night and through cloud cover, while optical imagery could provide greater detail in clear daylight conditions.

By comparing successive images, AI could also help analysts track changes in the location and movement of military assets, Lo said.

“Potentially more important is the ability to combine what Taiwan’s intelligence apparatus ‘sees’ with what it ‘hears’.”

The Linkou-based CDO in northern Taiwan specialises in signals intelligence, intercepting and analysing electronic emissions and communications associated with the PLA.

Lo said AI-assisted imagery analysis could be cross-checked against such signals intelligence.

An unidentified vessel detected in satellite imagery, for example, could be compared with radar or radio emissions collected from the same area to help analysts determine whether it was associated with the PLA.

Such intelligence fusion could be particularly useful when military vessels operate among civilian shipping or switch off their Automatic Identification System transponders, making conventional tracking more difficult, according to analysts.

Wang said the system could help Taiwan more quickly assess PLA exercises, changes in tactics and force deployments.

“Most importantly, it could help Taiwan monitor PLA force movements and its broader strategic deployments, allowing the military to identify developments earlier and prepare appropriate responses,” he added.

The CDO is one of Taiwan’s most sensitive military intelligence organisations and has long specialised in collecting signals from mainland China.

Lo said the office’s strength in signals intelligence meant the new imagery system would complement rather than replace existing collection methods.

Intelligence generated by the system could also be compared with information obtained through cooperation with the United States and other partners, he noted, although details of such arrangements are rarely made public.

Wang said the project could lay the groundwork for wider use of AI within Taiwan’s military intelligence apparatus.

“I believe this system represents part of the technological foundation for further innovation by the Communication Development Office,” he added.

“In the future, we are likely to see additional and more comprehensive systems developed to analyse intelligence on the PLA.”

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

item.title: [SCMP] Modi under pressure as India’s youth protests rise to highest level in a decade
item.description:
Despite ⁠tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last ⁠week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away.

“Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus.

Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets.
item.content:encoded:
Despite ⁠tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last ⁠week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away.

“Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus.

Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets.

Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country’s 1 billion voters. But his government remains stable and the ‌next general election is not due until 2029.

The nation has suddenly found its voice

Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist

“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist who has played a leading part in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”

The government and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) declined comment.

Anti-establishment mood

The recent protests in the capital New Delhi and elsewhere were focused on demands that Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter roll revision that activists and opposition parties say favours the BJP and has helped it win several recent state elections.

The ruling BJP, the government and the Election Commission deny the accusations. The BJP says the party’s wins have come from Modi’s popularity and strong economic growth.

But the demonstrations are also reflecting something larger: growing anger at Modi for failing to deliver jobs to millions of unemployed youth in his 12 years in power despite the surge in headline economic growth.

Other issues have also fed into the anti-establishment mood, including leaks of ⁠question papers in key examinations for jobs and education, the high number of crimes against women and the rise of billionaire businessmen alleged to have close links to Modi.

Modi has a strongman image and his government has previously cracked down on pockets of dissent harshly, but that ‌has not fazed the youngsters on the streets.

“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who was part of massive protests in the capital last week.

Speaking after she clung to the windscreen wipers of a bus that police were using to detain protesters, Raturi said: “We don’t fear being detained or beaten up by the police. This generation enjoys it.”

Police have denied allegations that they beat up people at the ‌demonstrations, saying protesters were handled according to prescribed procedures.

The protests have been energised by the emergence of the first nationally resonant youth-led movement of the Modi era, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which grew from online ⁠satire into a nationwide campaign this June after India’s chief justice likened ⁠the unemployed to “cockroaches”.

India’s mainstream media is mostly pro-government, critics say, and has covered the protests sparingly. But thousands of protesters armed with mobile phones as well as independent news channels on YouTube have amplified the unrest and made internet stars of leaders like CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and firebrand left-wing activist Neha Bora.

Opposition parties that were subdued under Modi’s grip ‌on power have been re-energised, with Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi and tens of thousands of followers also on the streets.

The unrest has drawn comparisons with neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal, where youth-led protest movements brought down governments in recent years, although analysts caution that India’s political landscape and Modi’s popularity make such parallels imperfect.

Lack of jobs

Many of the youth protesters grew up during Modi’s rise ‌to power, ‌buoyed by promises of jobs, opportunity and cleaner governance.

A decade later, many say those aspirations remain unfulfilled and they say the Hindu nationalist government appears more focused on religious issues and divisive politics against minorities, especially Muslims.

The government has previously said the economy generated 168.3 million new ‌jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of any bias, saying his government works for all Indians.

Gauri Seth, a medical student based in Kolkata, became a voter in 2014, the same year the Modi government came to power.

When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.

Gauri Seth, a medical student

The 30-year-old said the Modi government promised “a ⁠lot, but has failed to deliver”.

“Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.”

When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs ⁠each year. Yet, despite India’s strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above 5 per cent, according to government data.

A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the severity of joblessness, especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9 per cent in 2025, according to the data.

Research by Azim Premji University’s State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40 per cent, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained ‌jobless.

In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for ‌national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class, after test papers were leaked.

Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study.

“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.

While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country’s biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi’s popularity.

Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome.

The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi’s partner tells murder trial she hid ex-in-laws’ financial reliance on her
item.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.
item.content:encoded:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.

After an acrimonious row over parenting in mid-2022, Choi allegedly told Tam for the first time that she had been supporting the Kwong family financially and urged him and his father to cut ties with them.

But Tam said he and Choi had kept up a friendly facade in front of her former in-laws while seeking to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) home registered in Kwong’s father’s name.

He acknowledged he had been “a bit sneaky”, but said this was unavoidable as the couple tried to recover what belonged to them gradually and through diplomatic means.

Asked whether he still viewed his former classmate in the same way after the dispute, Tam said: “I would say the friendship was no more.”

Kwong, 31, is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.

The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial began last month.

Prosecutors argued that the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the luxury flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.

They said Choi had registered her former father-in-law as the owner to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty but had never intended to give the property to her former in-laws.

The court heard that Choi had a heated argument with her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, at the Kadooria flat in June or July 2022, when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever.

Li allegedly told her son Alex to stay away from the child because she could infect him, prompting Choi to accuse her of favouring sons over daughters.

Kwong Kau allegedly joined the row, twice attempted to attack Choi, swore at her and called her a “birthing machine”.

The elder Kwong was subsequently barred from visiting the flat and seeing his two grandchildren, the court heard.

But the children were allegedly taken to see him and his girlfriend while Choi was attending a fashion event in France during the Chinese New Year holiday in 2023, much to her dismay.

Tam became friends with Alex Kwong in 2008, when they were studying at Concordia International School in Kowloon Tong, the court heard. Tam later continued his studies in Australia, while Kwong moved to Sear Rogers International School, where he met Choi, the court was told.

Tam appeared surprised when Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, suggested he had wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with his client when they were schoolmates.

“Definitely disagree,” the witness said.

Tam said he first met Choi in late 2013 or early 2014, during a brief holiday visit to Hong Kong to see Kwong, who was then married to her.

He said his relationship with Choi changed after Kwong “totally disappeared” one day in 2015. That year, Kwong began divorce proceedings and absconded from a trial over his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Tam and Choi began dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage, the court heard. Their daughter was born in September 2016 and their son three years later.

“After Abby and I were together, I knew through Abby that Kwong Kong-chi was fine with our relationship and sent us his blessing. I also know his relationship with Abby was something in the past,” Tam said.

He added that he and Choi would meet Kwong during leisure trips to mainland China. The three saw one another more often at family gatherings after Kwong returned to Hong Kong in 2022.

Asked whether they had remained close until Choi’s disappearance, Tam said it was reasonable for them to do so because of their children.

He said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023.

Li allegedly suggested that her former daughter-in-law had been abducted and that they should delay reporting her disappearance to police until the supposed kidnappers made their demands.

Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s stand-in driver at the time, allegedly evaded questions about her whereabouts and pretended to help by driving Tam around to look for her.

Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found at a rental flat in Lung Mei village, Tai Po, on February 24.

The trial also shed light on the Tam family’s wealth and financial dealings with Choi and her former in-laws.

Tam’s father, Tam Chak-kwan, founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian and received a share of the proceeds from its HK$1 billion sale to a Japanese company.

In 2019, the family moved into their current 4,000 square foot home on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong, which the elder Tam bought for HK$168 million.

He said he had given his previous home, a 1,800 square foot flat valued at HK$41 million at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, to Choi in 2018. But he had not expected his de facto daughter-in-law to live there, as he wanted to share a home with his grandchildren.

The court heard that the elder Tam gave Choi at least HK$200,000 a month to cover living expenses for her and his son. He also gave her more than HK$80 million in total to invest.

Chris Tam said Choi had made money investing in luxury watches, although he was unsure whether she had done so through her ex-husband.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, accused Alex Kwong of failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million her daughter had given him to invest. She also called him a “brute” and dismissed his claim that he had supported her financially as “a pack of lies”.

Choi also allegedly put money into the Kadooria flat and an egg waffle shop run by Anthony Kwong, but Chris Tam said both had proved poor investments.

The court also heard how Kwong Kau had helped settle a dispute over a HK$5 million gambling debt Chris Tam incurred in Macau in August 2021.

The younger Tam said he had refused to repay the loan because he knew the casino, run by SunCity Group, was about to close following the arrest of its founder and CEO, Alvin Chau Cheok-wa.

Tam’s father said he had approached Kwong Kau for help because he wanted to resolve the dispute.

He said he had transferred HK$5 million to Kwong Kau’s personal bank account in March 2022 and paid him a further HK$450,000 in gratuities for people with triad affiliations who had stopped debt collectors from harassing his family.

The elder Tam said Kwong Kau later asked him for a HK$400,000 loan, saying police had frozen his account. Tam agreed to lend him HK$250,000, which had yet to be repaid, the court heard.

He added that he had ignored Kwong’s request for help with legal fees after the former officer was remanded in custody in connection with the case.

The trial continues on Tuesday before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong touts distinct features to set it apart from London in global gold hub push
item.description:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.

Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect Asian liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.
item.content:encoded:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.

Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect Asian liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.

“We are confident achieving [this] because in the Asia time zone we see Hong Kong as uniquely positioned to do that,” he said.

In the wide-ranging interview, Hui also discussed the city’s efforts to promote the international use of the yuan, the development of China’s digital currency, the e-CNY, and next week’s Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong.

Asked whether the Saudi Central Bank’s recent departure from mBridge had dealt a blow to the project, Hui said it would press ahead. The China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform is seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system.

The Saudi Central Bank, a key participant, confirmed last month that it had left the project after completing what it described as a limited proof-of-concept trial in May last year.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Hong Kong is a founding member and co-developer of mBridge.

The city is also accelerating the development of its gold trading ecosystem as a key part of its first five-year plan, which runs to 2030. The initiative is intended to support the development of mainland China’s gold economy, which combines the world’s largest domestic gold production and consumption markets.

Hui said government ownership and backing, integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement and cooperation with Shanghai would distinguish Hong Kong’s offering. The cross-border cooperation would allow eligible gold stored in the city to be used to settle trades in both markets.

Asked about competition with Singapore as a regional gold trading hub, Hui said Hong Kong was focused on improving its own performance.

“What Hong Kong tries to do is always to compete against ourselves because fundamentally we have to focus on areas that are within our control,” he said.

He expressed confidence in Hong Kong’s competitive advantages.

“What sets a global commodities market from the other markets is that it is really a market that is not just about financials but also close to the real economy,” he said.

“It has to be about also storage, about logistics, and also, at the same time, about trading, of course. And also when it comes to disputes, there could also be some legal issues.

“So actually, it’s a whole value chain in terms of the potential composition of this industry association to be set up before the end of this year.”

Hui added that following a trial in July, the integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement service was due to launch officially in the first quarter of next year.

“The clearing system now in the UK is run by the London Bullion Market Association, which is an industry association,” he said. “But the clearing house in Hong Kong is owned and run by the government. So I think this government backing sets us apart in terms of credibility.

“Another thing that is different between Hong Kong and London in that context is the fact that our current system will not just do physical delivery but also money settlement.”

Hui said 11 banks were already taking part in the payment settlement arrangements and others had expressed strong interest in joining, adding that the city would discuss cooperation on delivery standards with the London association.

Hui, who chairs the board overseeing the clearing facility, said a representative of the Shanghai Bourse served as deputy chair. Under the cross-border delivery connect arrangement, physical gold stored in certified Hong Kong vaults can be used to settle contracts traded in the local market and on Shanghai’s international board.

“If there is gold that is going to satisfy both the settlement in the Hong Kong contract and the Shanghai contract, they can use the vaults in Hong Kong, catering for both the Hong Kong market and the Shanghai market to do that,” he said. “It is an area that is uniquely Hong Kong.”

He added that the government was aiming to increase Hong Kong’s gold storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, with half at the airport and the remainder expected to come from the private sector.

Some gold refineries have also been established in the city.

Asked how Hong Kong could help the mainland gain greater influence over gold pricing, Hui said this would come once the city had attracted enough market participants and built sufficient liquidity.

“I see pricing more as an outcome, in the sense that once we build up a sufficient liquidity, at the same time a quantum of gold here, so it will eventually come,” he said, stressing the importance of building a critical mass of market participants.

On products, Hui highlighted the relaunch of a US dollar-denominated gold futures contract and said details of a yuan-denominated contract would be announced before the end of this year.

With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Global Precious Metals Conference in April next year.

Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans.

“First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete plans” and “Hong Kong speed”.

Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

item.title: [SCMP] Is China’s Shenzhen ready to host Xi, Trump and Putin during Apec summit?
item.description:
In Shenzhen, drones are banned, shiny new hotels have opened their doors and taxi drivers are carrying devices that can translate nearly 150 languages.

Since President Xi Jinping announced last year that China’s southern tech hub would host Apec meetings in November, the city has done all it can to get ready under the watchful eyes of the local, provincial and national authorities.

While every Apec summit draws the world’s attention, this year’s edition is considered to be especially high-stakes as Xi, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all expected to attend. Last year, Putin did not join the summit in South Korea.
item.content:encoded:
In Shenzhen, drones are banned, shiny new hotels have opened their doors and taxi drivers are carrying devices that can translate nearly 150 languages.

Since President Xi Jinping announced last year that China’s southern tech hub would host Apec meetings in November, the city has done all it can to get ready under the watchful eyes of the local, provincial and national authorities.

While every Apec summit draws the world’s attention, this year’s edition is considered to be especially high-stakes as Xi, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all expected to attend. Last year, Putin did not join the summit in South Korea.

In the past few weeks alone, Guangdong’s provincial Communist Party chief Huang Kunming has inspected Shenzhen twice to make sure preparations are going as planned.

“Shenzhen must, on one hand, maintain focus on details to comprehensively plug any gaps, optimise and refine service guarantees, and go all out to ensure the conference is held safely, smoothly and successfully. On the other hand, it must take the hosting of the Apec meeting as a new starting point to accelerate the expansion of high-level opening up,” he said last week.

Compared with Shanghai and Beijing, which hosted Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summits in 2001 and 2014, respectively, Shenzhen is less internationally known. However, analysts say the city could benefit from the event in the long term.

When Xi made the announcement, he noted that Shenzhen had “transformed from a backward fishing village into a modern international metropolis in just a few decades”.

“Together with surrounding areas, it forms the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area, which can be considered a growth pole of the world economy,” he added.

This narrative emphasised Shenzhen’s alignment with the meeting’s agenda, said Zhang Jingjia, an economist at the Apec Study Centre at Nankai University. China has made “openness, innovation and cooperation” priorities for the summit, and Shenzhen was a living example of that, she said.

When Beijing and Shanghai held the meetings, they focused on diplomacy and international finance, said Han Yonghui, executive dean of the Guangdong Institute for International Strategies. But Shenzhen’s tech companies, manufacturing system, ports and border crossings could show how the digital economy can function in real-world scenarios, he added.

Hosting an inter-governmental meeting would test a city’s organisational abilities, Han said. It required proper venues, hotels, ports, railways, telecommunication networks and security, as well as diplomatic coordination, multilingual services, volunteers and community support, he added.

The city has made security its top priority. Since July, local police have imposed a strict no-fly zone covering the city centre and stepped up random checks of subway passengers.

A statement from the provincial public security bureau said at the time that hidden conflicts and risks should be detected, while street crimes – including thefts and robberies – needed to be “completely eradicated”.

“Ensuring Apec safety is a major political responsibility for police around the province,” the statement said. “We need to plan early … and act with a heavy fist.”

Special teams have also been equipped to patrol the region. Shenzhen police have formed a low-altitude drone unit to patrol more than 600 routes and reach any point in the city centre within three minutes, authorities said.

This week, the government also called for residents to take leave or work from home to reduce traffic during the summit.

The venue for the summit – the Shenzhen International Exchange Centre in Futian district – was built especially for the event. In July, it hosted the Apec Forestry Ministerial Meeting, which Zhang described as a “test run” for the leaders’ meetings.

Shenzhen previously hosted major exhibitions, including the China Hi-Tech Fair, the International Cultural Industry Fair and the China International Optoelectronic Exposition, which showed that the city had the capacity to host large-scale meetings, said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

According to the Shenzhen authorities, the city has focused on upgrading its airport, crossings and railway, including this week’s opening of the revamped Huanggang Port that connects the city to Hong Kong.

Language is also a concern. More bilingual signs have been erected in the airport and bus stops, while taxi drivers have been issued with translation devices able to handle 146 languages.

Downtown Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei – the world’s largest electronics marketplace – was offering language training sessions to vendors, and multilingual volunteers were stationed in community service centres across the city, a report on the local government website said in August.

According to media reports, parks, gyms and commercial centres have also been renovated. More than 1,500 training sessions were organised for officials, business owners, delivery riders, residents and volunteers on languages, diplomatic etiquette, business English and public service.

“In addition, Shenzhen’s tech enterprises and industrial achievements are themselves content that can be showcased to all parties during the meeting, which is a feature other cities are unlikely to have,” Zhang said.

Shenzhen could benefit from hosting this meeting, just like Beijing and Shanghai did, analysts said. After hosting Apec, Beijing’s suburban Huairou district developed a whole industry around international exhibitions and hosted several more global summits, Zhang added, while Shanghai saw greater development in tourism and commerce.

Shenzhen’s residents are mostly happy to see parks revamped and other infrastructure improved, but are also looking forward to the return of normality.

A local doctor said she and her colleagues were placed on call for the duration of the summit to handle potential emergencies, and all leave was prohibited. But she said she “welcomes and supports” the city hosting a meeting of such importance for the first time.

“For ordinary people, what’s most useful isn’t the buzz during the meetings, but the public services and environment that stay,” Zhang said.

She added that the new exhibition centre could host public events, while the summit would raise the city’s international profile and foster global cooperation – ultimately driving investment and job growth.

item.title: [SCMP] Shunned in the West, Ye hands Indonesia a rare mega-tour coup
item.description:
Taylor Swift and Lady Gaga each chose Singapore as their only Southeast Asian stop on recent world tours. Fellow American singer Olivia Rodrigo played Thailand and the Philippines, but likewise skipped Indonesia.

Next weekend, however, Jakarta is finally getting the big international headline act it has been craving – in the form of Ye.

The controversial American rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is set to play Indonesia’s capital next Saturday, marking the only Southeast Asian appearance on his current tour.
item.content:encoded:
Taylor Swift and Lady Gaga each chose Singapore as their only Southeast Asian stop on recent world tours. Fellow American singer Olivia Rodrigo played Thailand and the Philippines, but likewise skipped Indonesia.

Next weekend, however, Jakarta is finally getting the big international headline act it has been craving – in the form of Ye.

The controversial American rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is set to play Indonesia’s capital next Saturday, marking the only Southeast Asian appearance on his current tour.

The promoter, Raw Vision Collective, expects 15,000 international visitors to attend. In the first 24 hours of ticket sales going live, foreign buyers from 73 countries made up 52.8 per cent of purchases, according to marketing and communications lead Karen Tjahja.

“For the first time in Indonesia’s concert history, international attendees are expected to exceed more than 5 to 9 per cent of concertgoers,” Tjahja told This Week in Asia.

But the choice of Ye, who has faced travel restrictions and had concerts cancelled over his controversial remarks, has prompted questions about whether he is the right act to put Indonesia back on the international music map.

Capital gains

Raw Vision Collective says it invited Ye “less as competition” with neighbouring countries and “more as an opportunity to strengthen Southeast Asia’s live-entertainment ecosystem”.

It points to a large domestic audience, a vibrant creative scene and Jakarta’s Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, which can hold about 77,000 concertgoers.

Officials have thrown their weight behind the performance. At a press conference held by Raw Vision Collective last month, Indonesia’s Tourism Minister Widiyanti Putri Wardhana noted the potential for concerts by major overseas acts to generate benefits across various economic sectors, from accommodation and transport to food.

Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung also pledged the city’s full support for the concert, calling it an opportunity to showcase Indonesia’s capital to the world.

“We believe Jakarta can build on its own strengths,” Tjahja said, adding that successful productions elsewhere in the region had helped “establish Southeast Asia as a stronger destination for global tours”.

“We hope that with the success of this concert, this will just be the beginning of Indonesia positively being back on the global stage.”

Singapore serves as an example. The city state “has shown how major concerts can attract regional visitors and drive tourism”, Tjahja said.

Yet Singapore’s success has often come at the expense of its neighbours. Swift played six nights in the city state and nowhere else in the region in 2024. A year later, Lady Gaga also played four exclusive nights.

Permits and piety

Musicians who know the scene well say paperwork is part of Indonesia’s problem.

Herry Sutresna, also known by his stage name Morgue Vanguard and the founder of Indonesian hip-hop group Homicide, told This Week in Asia that Indonesia could attract foreign talent but was a harder sell than Singapore or Australia, partly because of its famously unwieldy bureaucracy.

“It’s not really about convincing the artists themselves, but rather the difficulty of organising concerts locally regarding permits, costs and all the other red tape involved,” he said.

Still, plenty of foreign performers have played Indonesia in the past. Hikmawan “Indra” Saefullah, who played guitar in the Indonesian indie band Alone at Last from 2002 to 2013, listed Deep Purple, Mick Jagger, Sepultura, Metallica and Green Day, as well as multi-day live music events such as the Java Jazz Festival and Hammersonic.

Lady Gaga was meant to play Jakarta in 2012, with all 52,000 tickets already sold for a concert when several organisations, including the Islamic Defenders Front, objected to the singer’s dance moves and outfits, calling her “a devil worshipper”.

Police subsequently refused to issue an event permit, saying they could not guarantee safety, and the show was ultimately scrapped.

Sutresna said such mass protest campaigns were relatively rare, however, pointing instead to routine logistical and bureaucratic issues as the cause of most event disruptions in Indonesia.

Purely business?

Ye is “a special case” because of his past controversies, according to Saefullah.

The rapper has been widely condemned in recent years for making antisemitic remarks that cost him major sponsorships and performance opportunities.

Last year, he released a song titled “Heil Hitler”, which several streaming platforms banned, after previously expressing admiration for the Nazi dictator in interviews, publicly denying the existence of the Holocaust and saying he identified as a Nazi himself.

Planned Ye concerts in Poland, France, Switzerland and India have been cancelled this year, with venues variously citing security and legal concerns. He was also slated to headline a festival in Britain this summer before the entire event was aborted after he was barred from entering the country.

In January, he took out a full-page advertisement in The Wall Street Journal, explicitly apologising to black and Jewish people, opening up about a previously undiagnosed brain injury and detailing his treatment for bipolar disorder.

Saefullah said Ye had a strong fan base in Indonesia, where rap had long been popular in “inspiring the growth of the hip-hop subculture within the local music scene” – but he still saw opportunism in Ye’s Jakarta booking.

“Regarding him performing only in Jakarta, I see it as a purely business-driven decision,” he said. “Raw Vision Collective capitalised on the situation Ye and his team were facing, with tour dates being cancelled elsewhere.”

Tjahja said the promoter understood “the concerns surrounding Ye’s past public statements” but was “not in a position to comment on an artist’s personal views or ideology”. This Week in Asia has asked Ye’s management for comment.

Yohanes Sulaiman, a lecturer in international relations at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said Ye’s past remarks were unlikely to be much of an issue in Indonesia, given its tense relationship with Israel, with which it has no formal diplomatic ties.

A number of Indonesian public figures had made antisemitic remarks over the years without consequence, he added.

“In Indonesia, he will probably have a lot of cheerleaders,” Sutresna said. “Unless he suddenly swings in another direction, like supporting [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu … That would be a different story.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s shoppers love Chinese e-commerce. Its factories pay the price
item.description:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.
item.content:encoded:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.

“Most items are much cheaper than in the Malaysian market. It’s hard to compare because they come directly from factories or warehouses in China,” said Esha, who works for a competing e-commerce site.

Delivery takes at least two weeks, far longer than many of the app’s local rivals. But that delay has had the opposite effect to the one you might expect.

“With the long wait, it makes more sense to buy almost every week, so the wait feels shorter when parcels keep arriving every week,” Esha said, adding that she still used local platforms for urgent orders.

Many Malaysians are now doing the same. Since the app’s launch in the country last December, social media has been awash with delighted shoppers showing off their hauls, from smartphones to sofas, rolls of toilet paper and even bags of cement.

But surging demand for goods shipped direct from China through the likes of Pinduoduo often comes at the expense of local retailers and manufacturers that struggle to match their Chinese rivals’ deep discounts.

Meanwhile, the millions of parcels flooding into Malaysia and the waste they create are testing the limits of the country’s ability to collect and dispose of it all.

Disappearing margins

Pinduoduo is far from the only e-commerce platform active in Malaysia. Small local businesses, especially in physical retail and manufacturing, have already seen their margins shrink amid intense competition from earlier entrants like Lazada and Shopee.

Still, the app’s arrival has prompted an outcry from local businesses, who complain that direct shipments from far larger competitors in China have unfairly priced them out of their own market.

Shipping direct from China is the strategy that has powered Pinduoduo’s growth since its founding in 2015, giving more established e-commerce players such as Taobao and JD.com a run for their money. Lazada and Taobao are subsidiaries of Alibaba Group, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

Pinduoduo built its empire on a simple premise: allow consumers to pool their purchases into bulk orders directly with factories and wholesalers to get better deals.

“The influx of low-priced products from foreign e-commerce platforms is putting tremendous pressure on Malaysian retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers, particularly micro and small businesses,” said Chin Chee Seong, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, an umbrella body for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Chin said operational costs had shot up by 80 per cent or more this year, citing an SME Association survey in April that found 76 per cent of respondents reported being hit hard by rising fuel and energy costs, with 45 per cent bracing themselves for a cash-flow crunch over the next six months.

“Malaysian SMEs are being squeezed from both sides – rising operating costs and increasingly aggressive price competition. Many simply cannot afford to keep reducing their prices,” he said.

A widespread slump in SME activity would be disastrous for the economy. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 97 per cent of all registered businesses in Malaysia and employ around 8 million people, roughly half the entire workforce.

“As local shops and businesses lose sales or cease operations, they will reduce hiring and reduce demand for supporting services such as banking, advertising, accounting and other business services,” said Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, a Malaysian think tank.

“Closed shops result in commercial and retail outlet vacancies, and the landlords may be forced to reduce rents to attract fewer available tenants, reducing property income.”

Retailers of imported consumer goods, from fashion to general merchandise, are likely to be the most immediate and visible casualties. Yet economists warn that the greater danger is that posed to Malaysia’s all-important manufacturing sector.

The rapid shift to buying electronics, apparel, footwear, cosmetics and furniture from overseas sellers could cause local factories to permanently lose their share of the domestic market, said economist Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University.

“The distinction matters because retail displacement can be transitional as traders pivot to services or niche products, whereas manufacturing capacity, once lost, is far harder to rebuild,” he said.

Trashy dilemma

E-commerce began taking root in Malaysia in the mid-2010s, but demand truly exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when strict movement restrictions forced millions of people to do their shopping online between 2020 and 2022.

That habit has become even more deeply ingrained in the years since. An estimated 900 million parcels were delivered across Malaysia in 2025, according to the latest available government data, a multifold increase from the 52 million a decade earlier.

The appeal for e-commerce players is clear. A February note from equity and market analysts at Kenanga Research forecast that the value of e-commerce merchandise in Malaysia would reach 1.5 trillion ringgit in 2027, up from 1.2 trillion ringgit in 2024 (US$268.9 billion).

But this penchant for hyper-consumption could overwhelm the country’s capacity to deal with the vast amounts of rubbish generated.

Malaysia’s 135 landfills are already close to capacity, handling an average of 39,000 tonnes of solid waste daily, according to government figures from last year. Any increase in e-commerce shipments will almost certainly add to the growing trash pile.

The government has also pointed to a low recycling rate of 37.9 per cent of recoverable materials and poor waste separation practices at household and local council levels.

“The growth of online shopping, driven partly by competitive prices and convenience, has increased the volume of packaging waste,” said Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the non-profit Environmental Protection Society Malaysia.

“Although some online platforms, retailers and manufacturers have begun reducing packaging and switching to more recyclable materials, such as paper filling instead of polystyrene, these efforts may not be sufficient to keep pace with rising consumption.”

A raft of government policies has been introduced in an attempt to modernise solid waste management, broaden the use of sustainable plastics and materials, encourage recycling and reduce waste generation.

But grand plans meant little if the problem was not addressed at the source, said Jeremiah, adding that efforts to reduce unnecessary packaging by a handful of platforms, retailers and manufacturers needed to be extended across the entire supply chain.

“At the same time, consumers should make more informed purchasing decisions and practice proper waste separation and recycling,” he added.

Fair play

The overseas e-commerce blitz is not all bad news for Malaysia, however. For some, losing business in one area opens up opportunities in another.

“We had a 40 per cent drop in demand over the past few months for small parcel deliveries because a lot of people can just get their items delivered straight to their homes,” said a local courier operator who asked not to be named.

“But demand has gone up for shipments of bigger items like furniture and kitchenware and even machinery for factories and construction.”

An early investment in warehouse space in Guangzhou, China’s outbound shipping hub, made all the difference for them in securing a steady stream of clients, the operator said, adding: “A lot of our customers nowadays buy direct from factories in China, so having our own warehouse there makes it easy to arrange shipments for them.”

Even entrepreneurs worried about the fallout from direct-to-consumer sales from overseas enjoy the savings as shoppers.

“You must also look at the other side [of the coin]. The consumer is very happy. I’m very happy that I can buy my socks for just 12 ringgit,” said the SME Association’s Chin.

What local businesses wanted was not to stop Pinduoduo and other foreign e-commerce giants selling in Malaysia, he said, but a level playing field.

Under Malaysian law, a 10 per cent sales tax on low-value goods took effect in 2024 to cover imported items worth 500 ringgit or less. But trade groups say many direct overseas shipments slip through untaxed, giving foreign sellers an edge.

Local industries have also warned that directly shipped items such as electronics and toys are not subject to Malaysian safety regulations and may endanger consumers.

“Malaysian businesses should not be disadvantaged simply because they pay local taxes, employ Malaysian workers and comply with our laws and regulations,” Chin said. “We must protect consumer interests without sacrificing Malaysian businesses, jobs and our domestic manufacturing ecosystem.”

When unveiling next year’s budget on October 9, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would introduce an e-commerce bill at the next parliamentary sitting to close legislative and enforcement loopholes and protect local businesses from unfair competition.

But the government must do more than just draft a new law, said Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

“Malaysian entrepreneurs are not asking for government handouts. They are not asking for competition to be shut down entirely. They only want fairness, so that competition is fair,” he told parliament during the budget debate.

“[Foreign e-commerce sites] need to establish a local presence. Work with local businesses, open offices and hire workers in this country … I am proposing a middle ground, not shutting them down entirely.”

item.title: [SCMP] Japan taps foreign tech to plug defence gaps as China’s power grows. Will it pay off?
item.description:
Japan is increasingly turning to foreign companies to accelerate its military modernisation, drawing on overseas technology, expertise and production capacity to plug defence gaps that could prove critical in a potential regional conflict involving China.

The push has gathered momentum over the past week, with Tokyo confirming a contract for Ukrainian interceptor drones and a multinational fighter consortium preparing to expand its design operations in Japan.

French defence giant Thales is also reportedly planning what could become Japan’s first foreign-run military maintenance facility, initially serving the Maritime Self-Defence Force.
item.content:encoded:
Japan is increasingly turning to foreign companies to accelerate its military modernisation, drawing on overseas technology, expertise and production capacity to plug defence gaps that could prove critical in a potential regional conflict involving China.

The push has gathered momentum over the past week, with Tokyo confirming a contract for Ukrainian interceptor drones and a multinational fighter consortium preparing to expand its design operations in Japan.

French defence giant Thales is also reportedly planning what could become Japan’s first foreign-run military maintenance facility, initially serving the Maritime Self-Defence Force.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi confirmed last Friday that Japan had signed a contract to acquire interceptor drones from Ukrainian start-up SkyFall.

The company’s combat-tested P1-SUN family is designed to intercept unmanned aerial systems, including reconnaissance and attack drones, but Tokyo has not disclosed which model it ordered.

The acquisition follows Japan’s fast-track mass-procurement contract for the Terra B1 interceptor from Japanese company Terra Drone, which has also invested in two Ukrainian drone manufacturers to tap into their military technology and combat experience.

Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics and a former Japanese defence ministry official, described Tokyo’s approach as a “two-phase” strategy of acquiring foreign systems to address urgent capability gaps while simultaneously developing domestic alternatives over the longer term.

Some overlap between the two was acceptable to avoid capability gaps during the transition.

He identified weaknesses in one-way attack drones and AI-enabled operational support systems, saying Japanese manufacturers had technical expertise but lacked know-how gained from “real-world battlefield experience”.

Beyond drones, Edgewing, a joint venture of Japanese, British and Italian defence companies, plans to open a design and development centre in Japan next year for a next-generation fighter programme.

According to Japanese news service Nikkei, the Aichi prefecture facility could eventually employ around 1,000 people.

Taken together, these developments point to a broader shift in Japan’s approach to military modernisation.

Tokyo has long acquired foreign-made weapon systems, mainly from the United States, but in recent years it has also sought partners elsewhere for advanced technology, joint development, production and maintenance.

Tokyo has acknowledged the limits of domestic industry.

Its 2026 defence white paper highlights pressures on the country’s defence-industrial base, including limited production volumes and companies withdrawing from the sector.

It advocates international research and development, licensed production and advanced foreign technology, while Japan’s Defence Buildup Programme calls for shorter development timelines to field urgently needed equipment faster.

Underpinning this shift is Tokyo’s stark assessment of regional security, with the white paper labelling Beijing’s growing military power and activities as Tokyo’s “greatest strategic challenge”.

Experts say closer cooperation with foreign defence companies could help Japan gain combat-tested technologies more quickly, share the costs and expertise required to develop advanced weapons, and expand its production and maintenance capabilities – potentially strengthening its ability to counter the People’s Liberation Army.

In a study released in July, Celine Pajon, head of Japan and Indo-Pacific research at the French Institute of International Relations, argued that foreign partnerships could ease Japan’s rising development costs, production constraints and dependence on US technology.

Her study linked a stronger domestic defence industry to Japan’s “strategic autonomy” and identified European countries as promising partners for joint development and technology-sharing.

Defence expert Yoshihiro Inaba, the Japan correspondent for the Naval News website, highlighted gaps in uncrewed weapons, low-cost missiles and AI capable of “processing vast amounts of information”.

Companies such as Anduril, Palantir and General Atomics were among those supporting Japan’s efforts to address those shortfalls.

In its fiscal 2027 defence budget request, Tokyo proposed developing and acquiring low-cost stand-off missiles.

Inaba argued that importing such weapons could help Japan fast-track its long-range strike capabilities while developing domestic alternatives, without requiring major changes to Self-Defence Forces equipment.

He pointed to China’s growing “quantitative advantage” over Japan, including its fleet of “highly capable but expensive surface combatants”.

Japan could therefore improve its ability to counter these vessels by combining its existing domestically produced missiles with “a larger inventory of lower-cost cruise missiles”, supported by the surveillance and command-and-control systems needed to identify and target them, he said.

Still, even if larger stocks of inexpensive weapons helped Japan to counter Chinese warships, sustaining their use throughout a prolonged conflict would pose a separate challenge.

Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, cautioned that the bigger test was whether Tokyo could “produce, maintain and replace” military equipment on the scale needed during a prolonged conflict.

She noted that China’s much larger defence-industrial base gave it a capacity for expansion that Japan “cannot readily match”. While foreign partnerships could help address specific shortcomings, they would not eliminate the fundamental imbalance between the two countries.

Matsuoka also warned that Japan’s military preparations could reinforce Beijing’s perception that Tokyo and its partners were “preparing for confrontation”, deepening mutual mistrust.

Beyond these geopolitical risks, Japan would still face major industrial challenges. Foreign partnerships could accelerate technology transfers, Matsuoka said, but producing weapons “reliably at scale” required skilled workers, qualified suppliers and secure access to components and materials.

Reliance on foreign export approvals, software support and critical components could leave Japan vulnerable during a conflict with China, Matsuoka warned.

Japan could also struggle to sustain operations if it acquired systems it “cannot repair, modify or replenish independently”.

Ogi also cautioned that foreign defence companies’ growing presence in Japan did not necessarily reflect Tokyo’s military requirements. Such moves were “primarily motivated by the commercial interests of foreign companies”, he argued, as they anticipated further increases in Japanese defence spending.

For Japan, the challenge will be turning foreign technology and expertise into military capabilities quickly enough to address some of China’s advantages, while ensuring those systems can be maintained, produced and replenished if a longer conflict disrupts overseas supply chains.

“Foreign cooperation does not eliminate dependence; it redistributes it,” Matsuoka said.

item.title: [SCMP] India’s proposed social media ban for under-18s wins parents’ backing
item.description:
Digangana Mukherjee, a mother of a six-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, has banned television at her home in the Indian city of Mysore because she does not want her children to become addicted to watching content on screen.

A year ago, when her son’s school started using a smart classroom board that streamed online content, she and her husband decided to enrol him in a school where teachers used chalk on a slate board, and the pace of lessons was slower.

Now, she is happy that the Indian government is reportedly planning to prevent children below 18 years from opening social media accounts under a new law, in line with a Supreme Court ruling that such accounts signed up by minors should be considered void.
item.content:encoded:
Digangana Mukherjee, a mother of a six-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, has banned television at her home in the Indian city of Mysore because she does not want her children to become addicted to watching content on screen.

A year ago, when her son’s school started using a smart classroom board that streamed online content, she and her husband decided to enrol him in a school where teachers used chalk on a slate board, and the pace of lessons was slower.

Now, she is happy that the Indian government is reportedly planning to prevent children below 18 years from opening social media accounts under a new law, in line with a Supreme Court ruling that such accounts signed up by minors should be considered void.

“I approve of it as a parent. My son is 10 and knows how to browse YouTube. It is already becoming scary for me. I don’t know what content is visible to him,” Mukherjee said.

While parents may welcome India’s proposed safeguards, enforcement could prove complicated in one of the world’s largest online markets.

Legal experts warn that policing underage accounts and preventing users from getting around restrictions and privacy rights would be the main stumbling blocks, while a blanket ban would deprive young people of valuable educational resources.

Other countries in the Asia-Pacific region have enacted such laws, with Australia setting the ball rolling last December when it banned social media access for children under 16 under its Online Safety Amendment Act.

Mukherjee, who runs a library at her home filled with old books and conducts storytelling sessions for children, said she could distinguish between those who have unrestricted access to online screens and those with limited exposure.

“I see a lot of children come in and out of my space. There is a stark difference between these children. The attention span is much less for those who have abundant access to screens. They are restless and are not able to sit still for long,” she said.

Children with unlimited screen access have many entertainment options, and they are not keen on books, according to Mukherjee.

“If there were fewer screens, people would read more books. Growing up, we had Sunday afternoons only to watch TV. The rest of the time, when I was really bored, I had to pick up a book,” she said.

Many social media users younger than 18 in India do not face online curbs.

Last month, India’s solicitor general Tushar Mehta concurred with the position of the Supreme Court, in response to a petition by the “Just Rights For Children Alliance” NGO, that social media accounts opened by minors should be voided. He said the federal government should step in to make such a ban mandatory.

Australia deactivated 4.7 million social media accounts opened by those below 16 in the first month of its ban. India’s Goa state has been considering an Australia-like social media ban for children, amid growing concerns over the impact of excessive use on their mental health.

Lawyers, however, warn that the proposed regulation to curb access for children in India is bound to face legal challenges.

“I understand the Supreme Court’s request to bring in safeguards and the government’s stance to bring in stronger regulation to combat the risks posed. What remains to be seen is the extent and severity of restrictions that ultimately take form,” said Ashima Chalia, founder and senior partner at Bengaluru-based Ayaam Legal.

The mother of a two-year-old baby said that she wished for such a legal curb to protect children from online risks such as sexual exploitation, cyberbullying and harmful content.

“As a parent, I would also wish to baby-proof the whole world against anything that may harm my kid,” Chalia said.

“No doubt there is a need for stricter legislation or rules, but the Indian government has a herculean task of balancing children’s access to education and beneficial digital resources,” she said.

These rules would have to address a user’s rights regarding personal information collection and storage as well as age-verification processes, she added.

While Chalia conceded that Indian regulators would face challenges from children in India lying about their age when opening social media accounts, she added: “An uphill battle surely, but absolutely attainable.”

Striking a balance

Ambareen Ali Shah, a New Delhi-based mother of a 14½-year-old boy, said she worried about how easy access to social media would affect children’s time management as they had to do online and offline school assignments.

“Once you have access to – say Instagram – the content is so interesting that it causes distraction,” she said.

Shah recalled that when she was a young girl, the only screen she had access to was the television, restricted to a few hours of viewing.

“We need to curb the time a child spends navigating the internet. On the other hand, social media is making kids smarter because they get access to a lot of information,” she said.

Amitraj Kaushal, a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India, said that there was a strong case for a statutory framework protecting children from risks associated with social media use.

Citing the need to limit their exposure to age-inappropriate material, Kaushal said: “Legislation can provide clarity by placing the primary compliance responsibility on platforms rather than criminalising children or their parents.”

Australia’s experience could be useful for India as its law requires social media platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent those below 16 years old from opening accounts, while children and parents are not penalised for non-compliance, according to Kaushal.

Debasree Basu, an adviser at G.M. International School in Mumbai, said, however, that a sweeping social media ban would be counter-productive.

“Restrictions do not work. We have already exposed today’s generation to so many things that to ban them now will only make them more rebellious,” she said.

“The message should be that we want to protect you, so please help us to do that. Then their whole attitude will change.”

item.title: [SCMP] A US scholar’s take on how shifts in US-China relations are felt in a Tsinghua classroom
item.description:
China and America are talking again. There are leaders’ meetings, phone calls and a new channel for discussing artificial intelligence. Officials are cautiously trying to keep the relationship from veering into crisis.

And yet some of the hardest questions remain untouched.

Neither side is giving much ground on advanced chips, export controls remain a battlefield and neither Washington nor Beijing appears ready to slow its race to develop increasingly powerful AI.
item.content:encoded:
China and America are talking again. There are leaders’ meetings, phone calls and a new channel for discussing artificial intelligence. Officials are cautiously trying to keep the relationship from veering into crisis.

And yet some of the hardest questions remain untouched.

Neither side is giving much ground on advanced chips, export controls remain a battlefield and neither Washington nor Beijing appears ready to slow its race to develop increasingly powerful AI.

So what, exactly, does it mean to “talk” when the two countries are still competing over the technologies that will shape the next decade?

It is a question Denis Simon is confronting in the classroom.

A veteran US-China technology and higher-education strategist and former executive vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, Simon is now teaching at Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University.

The residential college and its Schwarzman Scholars programme were founded by Blackstone chief executive Stephen Schwarzman with the aim of bringing together future leaders from around the world.

The programme, which celebrated its 10th anniversary last year, is described by some observers as one of the crown jewels in the bilateral relationship.

Simon’s course focuses on China’s science and technology policy and innovation strategy, but the country’s relationship with the US will not stay in the background.

He was teaching the second seminar of the course in Beijing when US President Donald Trump went to China in May, and the third when Trump’s Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, went to Washington last month.

“That’s a kind of very interesting coincidence of time that gives the course a booster shot,” he said in an interview from Beijing. “The students are aware of both meetings. They’re much more informed about what’s going on.”

His students are studying a relationship that has become deeply contradictory: Washington and Beijing are rebuilding channels of communication even as they narrow the space for technological and scientific links.

The summits have not resolved that, but they have changed the atmosphere in the classroom.

“These leadership meetings really created a much more positive environment,” Simon said.

Before May, when the two sides were not talking, things were “topsy-turvy”, he said, adding that neither the Beijing visit nor the Washington trip was “a resounding big deal”. But what registered was simpler: the fact that the two leaders were talking and had met twice within six months.

However, Simon said the “biggest change” was that some students “have become seemingly somewhat more cautious about revealing where they actually stand”.

For example, an argument about export controls can sound like an argument about America, while a criticism of Chinese technology policy can become a political declaration. Even defending academic exchanges may raise questions about political loyalties.

“They have become much better at distinguishing what they think from what they believe they ought to say in terms of political correctness,” he said.

“That distinction matters enormously in a classroom. A good seminar depends upon intellectual risk-taking.”

Over the past three years, the discussions have, in several respects, become more sophisticated even as students have become a bit more restrained.

That is partly because while 40 per cent of students are American and 20 per cent Chinese, the others come from all over the world and are asking why they should have to choose between the two superpowers.

“They are not merely referees,” Simon said. “They have their own interests.”

He said they wanted American technology and capital, and they wanted Chinese markets, manufacturing capacity, infrastructure and technology.

But they did not necessarily see technological alignment with either Washington or Beijing as inevitable, or desirable.

In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international

Denis Simon, Schwarzman College

“In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international,” Simon said.

Their presence has also pushed Simon to modify the course, including replacing older readings with newer ones that reflect what has happened since the leaders’ meetings.

He no longer sees the technology relationship as a straightforward story of engagement followed by competition. Technology, economics, national security, industrial policy, scientific research and geopolitics have become too deeply entangled.

The old idea of separating economic and security issues has largely disappeared. But Simon is equally wary of the opposite assumption: that everything involving China and technology should now be treated as a security issue.

His students study semiconductors, export controls, AI, data governance, supply-chain resilience and industrial subsidies and are also asked some fundamental questions: where should the two countries compete, where should they put guardrails in place and where should they deliberately remain connected?

Simon uses a red-yellow-green framework to assess the security situation, with red – covering areas where national security is at stake – being relatively straightforward.

The same applies to low-risk green areas, including basic science and ordinary educational exchanges, but Simon added that yellow was the “really difficult category”, which meant proceeding with “conditions, transparency, safeguards or limits”.

His concern is that Washington increasingly has a tendency to turn yellow into red.

“Once that happens, the burden of proof shifts,” Simon said. “Instead of asking, ‘Why should this be restricted?’ we begin asking, ‘Can anyone prove that it is completely safe?’”

That, he added, was not a sustainable basis for technology policy.

The same tension is visible in the emerging AI channel between Washington and Beijing. Simon argued there was value in the new mechanisms for communication, but warned “communication” and “governance” were not the same thing.

A hotline can provide a way to communicate after an accident or during a crisis, while dialogue can make contact habitual, but neither of these things settles questions such as who gets access to advanced chips, how frontier AI should be developed or what happens when the two sides disagree about the rules.

He added: “Great-power relationships often advance in very small increments. The existence of a channel may look insignificant until the day you desperately need the channel.”

The question is whether those channels become durable institutions or remain dependent on the political mood of the moment.

Simon said that concern extended to the academic sphere, with universities are being increasingly being forced to “price geopolitical risk” into their calculations given the cost of being caught up in a political controversy.

His recent experience at Duke University in the US sharpened these concerns where a China science and technology graduate seminar he had taught for several years was dropped even though funding was available.

“What it told me is that the issue is no longer simply whether there is money to teach a course,” Simon said. “The institution is also asking: what is the reputational and political risk of teaching it?
