“If American universities stop teaching about China’s innovation system because the China issue has become politically difficult, we will create an extraordinary paradox: we will become less capable of competing with a country precisely because we have become less willing to study it.”

Inside Schwarzman College, that question takes on another dimension. Students are watching China’s transformation from the “factory of the world” into an innovation power in electric vehicles, batteries, robotics, clean energy and AI.

To many observers, this change appears sudden, but Simon, who has followed China’s development for 40 years, sees something different.

“It really is part of a gestation period over time over the last 30-plus years in which China has steadily moved to make itself into an innovation-driven nation. So when people seem to be shocked, it’s that they haven’t been following this for 40 years, like I have.”

For Chinese students, he said, this was not simply a story of national technological achievement but the economy where they had to find jobs.

Many had assumed the factory era was behind them and that innovation was the next place to stand, but robotics and AI have complicated that assumption.

They may be headed back into the factory, but not the one their parents left.

Meanwhile, international students are confronting a different reality: China’s technological rise will shape the competitive environment in which they build their own careers.

The question, Simon said, was no longer simply whether China could innovate, but “how China’s innovation trajectory will alter international S&T [science and technology] affairs, including the once dominant role of the US”.

He said that ultimately that was what he wanted his students to understand, saying they should not expect a return to the US-China relationship of the 1990s or 2000s, while technological competition could not be wished away.

The objective, instead, was to build enough “connective tissue” around the new relationship that competition remained competition without becoming continuous conflict.

That is the wager behind institutions like Schwarzman College, NYU Shanghai and Duke Kunshan: not that they can eliminate strategic competition, but that they can continue putting people who might disagree in the same room, and teach them how to keep talking when agreement is no longer possible.

“Cooperation does not have to mean agreement, technological sharing, or slowing down,” he said. “Cooperation can mean simply agreeing on what happens when we disagree.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims for share of HK$350 billion yacht industry as travel scheme launches
item.description:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.

Under the scheme, mainland vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to sail in Hong Kong waters.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the global yacht market was expected to reach HK$350 billion by 2032 and that Hong Kong could capture a slice of the market.

He noted that there were about 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong and the government planned to roll out more measures to boost the yacht economy.

“The outline of the national 15th five-year plan clearly calls for developing leisure consumption such as cruises and yachts, and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan also stated that we will actively develop it,” he said.

“Our vision for the yacht economy also reflects the global trend.”

Wong said they are also pushing to build four new yacht clubs at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom, which would provide more than 1,100 berths.

The new yacht clubs would also have four “very attractive” clubhouses to improve and complete the infrastructure and ecosystem of the city’s yacht economy, he added.

Wong also revealed that three of the five registered vessels were from Shenzhen, one was from Zhuhai and one from Guangzhou’s Nansha.

The five vessels all moored at facilities in Discovery Bay provided by Lantau Yacht Club, which organised the launch ceremony.

Transport minister Chan also said the Marine Department would coordinate with local training institutions to offer online courses for overseas captains, with the aim of turning the city into a hub for superyachts.

Chan said the five yachts had varied itineraries, including sea tours and visits to urban areas, and that many of their passengers had booked hotels for stays of three to four days, reflecting “a new model of high-end tourism consumption”.

Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat said on Thursday that 23 individuals or groups had registered under the new travel scheme as of this week.

Max Teng, secretary general of the Shenzhen Boating Industry Association, was one of the five mainland yacht owners arriving on the first day.

He said he came to Hong Kong specifically for an “ice-breaking journey to witness the historic moment”, and would stay only one night in the city.

Teng was cautious, however, about his willingness to return. “Just the cost this time, not counting fuel, we already spent up to HK$40,000,” he said.

Entry and exit clearance fees were 14,500 yuan, he said, which included a processing fee of 2,000 yuan per trip, port berthing fee of 2,000 yuan per hour and customs declaration fee of 1,000 yuan per vessel.

He praised the smooth application through the official system, although he said some technical details still needed work.

“There are some things that don’t quite match, for example, the shore power interfaces,” he said.

“Freedom of navigation is the most important thing for mainland yacht owners.

“Many mainland businessmen buy boats and register companies in Hong Kong for its international endorsement and tax incentives.”

Teng said that he saw the scheme boosting Hong Kong’s yacht trading and benefiting nearby cities such as Shenzhen.

Another Shenzhen yacht owner, surnamed Sheng, said he had come to Hong Kong with several friends for a three-day free and easy trip, and planned to shop in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui.

“Shenzhen is very close to Hong Kong. Now that the government has made the process more automated and standardised, the more convenient it becomes, the more willing we are to come,” he said.

“If this scheme had come into effect before National Day, we might have stayed a couple more days – during holidays the roads are congested, but the sea is not.”

Sheng added that he would be more interested in sailing his yacht to Victoria Harbour to watch the fireworks during holidays.

Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, welcomed the “long-anticipated” scheme, saying the club had prepared for more mainland yachts coming to Hong Kong since 2019.

“We have special rates for our berths, and we purposely reserve space for people who come in on a transient basis, so we can accommodate yachts, unlike other yacht clubs that usually sell all that space to long-term owners,” he said.

Apart from berthing, the club also offers both long- and short-term service package discounts, including hotel accommodation and golf sessions, which are more cost-effective than a long-term membership.

Mak also noted that 10 mainland yachts had registered for the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show early next month and would start arriving from next week. They represented the largest number in years, up from just two or three previously.

David Norton, commodore of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, said one boat from Zhuhai was set to spend the night at its Causeway Bay headquarters on Friday.

Acknowledging that the club was quite full and could only offer berthing and hospitality on a case-by-case basis, Norton stressed the demand was real.

“There is a big demand in mainland China for participation in water sports, 60 per cent of entries in Hong Kong Race Week at the beginning of the year came from the mainland,” he said, adding he was excited to see if the scheme could bring more mainland entries to water sports events in Hong Kong.

Five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung will provide 115 berths, in addition to those at private yacht clubs.

There are also seven kiosks supplying water to vessels and eight designated bunkering areas, according to the Water Supplies Department and the Marine Department.

While saying the five anchorage areas were well located, Norton noted “there is a lack of facilities” around the areas.

“It’s very hard to get water and find someone to dump some trash or empty the tanks from the toilet,” he said.

He also added that tourists needed an easy way ashore: “They need a landing station, or maybe a water taxi service that will get them on and off the boat. So that’s what’s missing.”

Lawmaker Roy Chu Lap-wai described the registration of five yachts on the first day as “encouraging”.

“In the initial stage, I believe the five yachts that come here will go back and spread the word about how convenient and good Hong Kong is, if everything goes smoothly,” he told a radio programme.

Chu said Hong Kong had many distinctive islands for visiting yachts to explore. He hoped tourists would go island-hopping during the day, then dine and shop in urban areas at night.

“The government also held many successful big events regularly, and they could get more involved in different aspects, so these relatively high-end, big-spending yacht tourists can really spend more money in Hong Kong and contribute to our economy,” he said.

Chu said the city could also develop a “one-day tour” and other services, such as chauffeur-driven cars with professional guides, adding that the Tourism Board could do more to promote these offerings and increase the economic benefits.

item.title: [SCMP] Haze-hit Singapore parents call for Hong Kong-style school air con
item.description:
Salon manager Alice Pang says her 10-year-old daughter has likened the visibility inside her classroom in Singapore to Malaysia’s Genting Highlands, but while the mountain resort is often shrouded in fog caused by water particles, her child’s active imagination may have been triggered by worsening haze plaguing the city state.

Pang told This Week in Asia that her daughter, whose classroom did not have air conditioning, was already suffering from bad sinus, and the haze had made her eyes water.

While Pang would prefer her Primary 4 daughter to stay home as the pollutant standards index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some parts of the city state, the child is in the middle of exams.
item.content:encoded:
Salon manager Alice Pang says her 10-year-old daughter has likened the visibility inside her classroom in Singapore to Malaysia’s Genting Highlands, but while the mountain resort is often shrouded in fog caused by water particles, her child’s active imagination may have been triggered by worsening haze plaguing the city state.

Pang told This Week in Asia that her daughter, whose classroom did not have air conditioning, was already suffering from bad sinus, and the haze had made her eyes water.

While Pang would prefer her Primary 4 daughter to stay home as the pollutant standards index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some parts of the city state, the child is in the middle of exams.

Pang is among several parents who are increasingly worried about the open-air classroom environments in Singapore amid the transboundary haze fuelled by fires across Indonesia, particularly in Sumatra and Kalimantan.

“They have an air purifier in the classroom, but she says it isn’t working. It’s also too hot for the students. I think the government needs to step up and take action,” Pang said.

She argued that schools should roll out air-conditioning in classrooms to complement the air purifiers. Currently, her daughter’s school has air-conditioning only in certain facilities such as the music room.

On Wednesday afternoon, the PSI one-hour reading hit a high of 288 in the west of Singapore. The same day, Singapore began distributing N95 masks to vulnerable Singaporeans, including children aged between seven and 16, and providing air-conditioned rooms in shelters in community clubs and some residents’ committee centres.

On Saturday, Education Minister Desmond Lee said in a social media post that lessons and national examinations had continued in enclosed venues with air purifiers, and that his ministry might consider school closures if the next-day forecasts entered the hazardous range with a 24-hour PSI exceeding 300.

Across the 1km causeway in Malaysia, schools in several states have been shut until at least Friday. Under federal guidelines, educational institutions must close when the Air Pollutant Index (API) exceeds 180, or remains above 150 for three consecutive days. Both levels fall within the “unhealthy” range.

General practitioner Lawrence Ng said that common conditions triggered by haze included ⁠upper respiratory infections, bronchitis, ⁠conjunctivitis, allergic rhinitis, known as hay fever, and⁠ asthma.

“Children have smaller airways which are more susceptible to airway narrowing from pollutants,” Ng said.

Asked if implementing air-conditioning in classrooms was being considered to tackle the haze, Singapore’s Ministry of Education directed This Week in Asia to its haze management measures.

These include avoiding physical activities if the PSI is between 200 and 300, placing students in an enclosed indoor space with air purifiers and having those who are unwell temporarily placed in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier before they are brought to get medical attention.

Opposition MP Kenneth Tiong, who reiterated his call to provide air-conditioning in classrooms this week, told This Week in Asia he was not advocating for the air-conditioning to be on at all times but to have the option when needed.

In March, he advocated in parliament for air-conditioning in classrooms to help students and teachers handle the heat.

“The recent haze makes it more urgent. It has been very difficult for the kids: many are coughing, and I can see the toll it is taking on their health,” said Tiong, who is a Workers’ Party MP for the Aljunied constituency.

He noted that the National Environment Agency’s guideline said a purifier might not work as intended unless the doors and windows were closed, and that a closed, crowded room could build up heat.

“MOE’s haze plan says students who are unwell ‘will be temporarily accommodated in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier’. I believe a child should not have to fall ill first,” Tiong argued.

In March, then senior minister of state David Neo said Singapore had been careful not to rush into air conditioning, as the technology was not as energy efficient and instead relied on passive cooling solutions, such as cool paint, more breathable uniforms and school buildings designed for maximum natural ventilation.

Neo stressed there was a need to balance other considerations, such as long-term heat resilience, acclimatisation, energy consumption and impact on the environment.

Tiong told This Week in Asia that while sustainability was very important, air-conditioning in every classroom could be an insurance. “It has to be in place before the haze or the next heatwave arrives. Switched on only when needed, it uses far less power than air-conditioning left on all day,” he said.

He noted that in Hong Kong, the government had moved to air-conditioned classrooms for all public sector schools since 2017 for a more comfortable teaching and learning environment in hot weather.

A recurrent air-conditioning grant was provided from 2018 for Hong Kong schools to cover related daily expenses, including electricity charges and maintenance.

A mother of a six-year-old who previously lived in Hong Kong said she was shocked to learn that her child’s Primary 1 classroom in Singapore would not be air-conditioned.

Currently, her child’s kindergarten class is air-conditioned and has an air purifier, but she expressed concern about whether it had been serviced.

“I’m not asking them to have the air conditioning turned on every day,” she said, speaking on condition of anonymity. She questioned if some people underestimated the haze, given “this haze situation has been there for 20 years”.

Flynn Lee, a 50-year-old stay-at-home Singaporean mother of three children aged 11 to 16, however, said she trusted the government’s current measures. Only her daughter in Secondary 1 has air conditioning in her classroom.

“Air con is good to have, but I guess not all schools can afford it. It’s also not cheap to maintain, and this situation is not forever, so I guess we just have to get through this period,” Lee said, noting that her children’s schools had stopped all outdoor recess playing, moved co-curricular activities and physical education lessons indoors and reminded children to drink more water.

“It’s not really a fair statement to request for air con just because of the haze situation, which probably will last like weeks to a month and to have schools suddenly have to request to put up air conditioning.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s central bank insists it is independent. Investors want proof
item.description:
Indonesia has spent months trying to persuade investors that its economy is on the right course. A weakening rupiah, mounting budgetary pressures and a series of contentious policy decisions have made that task harder.

Doubts about the management of Southeast Asia’s largest economy have now coalesced around its central bank, whose independence has come under intense scrutiny recently as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to steer economic policy.

The appointment of Destry Damayanti – initially as acting governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) in late July before her formal appointment last month – was meant to reassure markets. But analysts say that confidence will only return if economic policymaking becomes more credible and decisions affecting the country’s financial health become more transparent.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia has spent months trying to persuade investors that its economy is on the right course. A weakening rupiah, mounting budgetary pressures and a series of contentious policy decisions have made that task harder.

Doubts about the management of Southeast Asia’s largest economy have now coalesced around its central bank, whose independence has come under intense scrutiny recently as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to steer economic policy.

The appointment of Destry Damayanti – initially as acting governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) in late July before her formal appointment last month – was meant to reassure markets. But analysts say that confidence will only return if economic policymaking becomes more credible and decisions affecting the country’s financial health become more transparent.

In an interview with Reuters on Monday, Destry insisted the central bank had “full autonomy” to set interest rates while maintaining “synergy” with the government.

“When we’re about to make a policy decision – whether to raise or lower interest rates or to ⁠use other incentives – we have full authority to make that decision,” she said.

Her assurances follow a turbulent few months for Indonesia’s economy. The rupiah hit record lows this year, with major credit rating agencies Moody’s and Fitch cutting their outlooks on the country’s sovereign rating from stable to negative.

Conflict in the Middle East has only compounded the challenges. Despite the soaring cost of oil globally, Jakarta has held subsidised fuel prices steady. State institutions have since had their budgets cut to pay for energy imports and Prabowo’s flagship welfare programmes.

On Friday, fears of foreign capital flight were further stoked after index compiler MSCI said in a statement that Indonesia no longer merited emerging-market status, citing “significant concerns” about market dysfunction, “including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement”.

The US firm said it was now proposing a downgrade to “standalone” status – worse than previously flagged – which would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by passive investment funds managing billions of US dollars. Indonesian stocks, already the world’s worst performers this year, plunged 11 per cent to multi-year lows on Friday in response – the steepest one-day drop since 1998.

Other developments that have unsettled markets in recent months include a new policy to centralise commodity exports, the abrupt dismissal of former finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and his replacement by Suahasil Nazara, and the appointment of Prabowo’s nephew, Thomas Djiwandono, as a deputy governor of the central bank.

In June, parliament passed a revision to the financial sector law that now requires Bank Indonesia to support economic growth and job creation, in addition to its duties managing money supply, keeping inflation under control, issuing and circulating legal tender, regulating national payment systems and acting as a lender of last resort.

Asked how much the government was involved in monetary policy, Destry said officials had been invited to attend part of the bank’s monthly policy review, adding that she herself had attended meetings with Prabowo.

“In Indonesia, the president is the head of government and the head of state. BI is under the state of Indonesia, so automatically, if the president wants to know about developments, I think it’s normal,” she told Reuters.

The central bank held its benchmark rate at 5.75 per cent at its latest policy meeting in September, after raising it by a cumulative 100 basis points between May and June to stabilise and support the rupiah, which was trading at a near-record low of 18,070 per US dollar as of Friday afternoon.

Proof over promises

Economists who spoke to This Week in Asia agreed that the new governor’s message was welcome, but said investors would need to see Bank Indonesia demonstrate its independence.

“The governor’s reassurance is a constructive and necessary signal, but it is unlikely to restore investor confidence on its own,” said Josua Pardede, chief economist at Permata Bank.

“Restoring confidence requires a broader and sustained improvement in Indonesia’s economic policy credibility, not merely reassurance from the central bank.”

While Bank Indonesia “remains legally independent”, Pardede said the unexpected resignation of its previous governor and changes to its responsibilities had stoked speculation that its “institutional independence has weakened”.

Destry’s predecessor, Perry Warjiyo, resigned in July citing personal reasons.

Yusuf Rendy Manilet, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, called for government-central bank synergy to rest on “clear data”, saying that the bank should, for example, consult the government’s employment figures before setting the benchmark interest rate.

“When that happens, I think BI can be interpreted as still being relatively independent in implementing its policies,” he said.

Yusuf also wanted the bank to explain its purchases of government bonds. According to Reuters, Bank Indonesia bought nearly 300 trillion rupiah (US$16.7 billion) of them between January and September 30 to support economic growth.

“BI must convince investors that its bond purchasing policy has strong justification as a monetary policy and not because it is an extension of the government,” he said.

Deniey Purwanto, a senior researcher at the Institute for Development of Economics and Finance in Jakarta, said the central bank would be fully autonomous only when it could set rates “without considering its impact on government debt costs”.

Downgrade danger

Indonesia ran a deficit of 1.24 per cent of gross domestic product in the first nine months of this year, with the full-year target of 2.85 per cent coming in just under the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent.

Analysts like Pardede say government spending is outpacing tax revenue, citing investor concerns that include the expansion of state spending commitments despite a “relatively narrow tax base”, rising energy subsidies, repeated changes among senior economic officials and “uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions”.

MSCI’s Friday announcement about Indonesia’s market downgrade surprised officials, coming a month ahead of a scheduled review. In January, the index provider had warned about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information. It suggested a possible downgrade to frontier-market status at the time.

Standalone status is reserved for markets that do not meet even this criteria. Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg.

Uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions

Josua Pardede, Permata Bank economist

Meanwhile, higher oil prices could weigh further on both the rupiah and Indonesia’s finances. International benchmark Brent crude has been stubbornly trading above US$100 in recent days following fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, threatening oil supplies and raising fears of a widening Middle East conflict.

Yusuf expects little relief for Indonesia’s currency in the near term, forecasting that the rupiah will remain “quite volatile” against the US dollar through to the end of the year.

Pardede’s prescription for Indonesia’s US$1.3 trillion economy was directed at the government rather than the central bank.

“The government should prioritise disciplined budget execution, transparent public investment governance, regulatory certainty and policies that attract private capital rather than relying excessively on the state to drive growth,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China-led team hits 83% success rate anticipating earthquakes in ‘seismo-ripples’ study
item.description:
A China-led international team has reported a new pre-earthquake phenomenon that has shown strong predictive potential for major earthquakes since 2022 with minimal failures.

The anomalous seismic, magnetic and ionospheric resonance signals they observed – termed “seismo-ripples” by the researchers – are ringlike disturbance patterns triggered before earthquakes happen.

Their findings challenge the long-standing scientific belief that these events are unpredictable, opening up a promising new path to earthquake prediction.
item.content:encoded:
A China-led international team has reported a new pre-earthquake phenomenon that has shown strong predictive potential for major earthquakes since 2022 with minimal failures.

The anomalous seismic, magnetic and ionospheric resonance signals they observed – termed “seismo-ripples” by the researchers – are ringlike disturbance patterns triggered before earthquakes happen.

Their findings challenge the long-standing scientific belief that these events are unpredictable, opening up a promising new path to earthquake prediction.

“Historically, earthquake prediction has been considered nearly infeasible,” said the team from institutes in mainland China and Taiwan, along with Brazil and Japan, in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal NPJ Natural Hazards on Sunday.

Using data collected from seismometers, magnetometers and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System receivers, the anomalous patterns were verified against 12 major earthquakes in China between 2022 and 2024.

“Since June 2022, prospective anomaly based on seismo-ripples has demonstrated a strong predictive capability for numerous earthquakes with a magnitude [greater than or equal to] six, with remarkably minimal to no failure,” the researchers wrote.

Of the 12 sites they proposed could be associated with future earthquakes, 83 per cent experienced a corresponding earthquake within three months of the seismo-ripple patterns emerging.

The average distance between predicted and actual epicentres was about 280km (174 miles) and the estimated magnitudes ran about 0.5 units larger than the final seismic readings.

“In essence, the core argument of our paper is that earthquakes are not inherently unpredictable,” said Chen Chieh-Hung, a lead author of the study and a professor at the Chengdu University of Technology.

Chen noted that prediction could mean different things to different people, with some expecting precision down to the exact minute or accuracy within a margin of a few kilometres, which he said would not be feasible at this stage.

“Nevertheless, we have opened a door. Earthquakes are not beyond the realm of prediction,” he said on Wednesday. “There is a possibility that they can be predicted. The next step is for the scientific community to work on refining this precision.”

Asia is one of the world’s most seismically active regions, with China experiencing roughly a third of all continental earthquakes despite having only about 7 per cent of the global land area.

Estimating long-term seismic probabilities – such as Japan’s assessment of a high probability for a major earthquake along the Nankai Trough in the next three decades – is an accepted scientific approach.

However, for decades, short-term earthquake prediction has been elusive and controversial.

According to the United States Geological Survey, a true earthquake prediction must specify three parameters: the date and time, the location and the magnitude of the incoming event.

This differs from earthquake forecasting, which calculates the probability of an earthquake occurring within a given area and time window.

Chen said the scientific consensus that earthquakes could not be predicted stemmed in part from papers published in the top journals Nature and Science in the 1990s. From then on, he said, this belief “effectively became an established rule”.

“Within the scientific community, the prevailing view is that earthquakes are unpredictable, and most researchers prefer not to wade into such controversial waters,” he added.

Chen pointed to other milestones once thought impossible, such as accurate weather forecasting and aircraft breaking the sound barrier.

“A more accurate way to frame it would be to say that we have yet to discover a sound, rationally valid or scientifically grounded method for predicting the occurrence of earthquakes,” he said.

Chen said that if the bar for prediction were set extremely high, then it would indeed be impossible. Instead, he argued that scientific efforts should focus on shifting from long-term forecasts to short-to-medium-term predictions.

Researchers from around the world have sought to identify earthquake precursors or signals occurring before seismic events that could be used for more reliable forecasting or even predictions.

In their paper, the China-led team explored a phenomenon of ringlike disturbances called seismo-circles or seismo-ripples that appear to propagate outwards from future earthquake epicentres.

“What’s particularly interesting about this phenomenon is that, initially, we did not know whether it was real or false,” Chen said.

To verify their findings, the team investigated past earthquake cases. They found that separate ripple-like anomalies had formed for two earthquakes that struck China within a day of each other in 2021.

Chen said this revelation gave the team the confidence to pursue the research further, and over the following two years they documented the anomalous occurrences and submitted formal reports.

In April 2022, after detecting anomalous ripple patterns in southwestern China, the researchers submitted a formal document to the China Earthquake Networks Centre – the country’s official body for earthquake monitoring and prediction evaluation – declaring a possible magnitude 6.3 event within two months.

On June 1, 2022, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck China’s southwestern Sichuan province, occurring 399km from the team’s predicted epicentre.

They then launched an effort between 2022 and 2024 to challenge the idea that earthquakes were inherently unpredictable, routinely monitoring seismo-ripples and submitting formal reports to authorities.

The team said its investigation highlighted a correlation between seismo-ripples and forthcoming seismic events, allowing for “reliable estimation of earthquake magnitude, location and timing”.

They noted there were still challenges to address, including ambiguous ripple signals that complicated exact estimates and the need for deeper understanding of the physics behind these anomalies.

In addition, seismo-ripple detection remains limited by instrument density and spatial network coverage.

To improve precision, an upgraded ground-based observation system is under construction in China. Looking ahead, the team plans to incorporate satellite data and artificial intelligence to enhance monitoring capabilities.

While their study focused on China’s North-South Seismic Belt, the researchers said the seismo-ripple phenomenon held potential for global application.

Chen said the main goal of their paper was not to claim that earthquakes could already be predicted but rather that they were not inherently unpredictable.

“At this stage, we are already able to distinguish between signals that are likely related to earthquakes and those that are not – a distinction we could not make previously,” he said.

“The next challenge is to improve precision, particularly regarding the location and timing of seismic events.”

Chen acknowledged that there was a long way to go before earthquake prediction would become a fully functional reality. But he said his team was committed to the task and invited other scientists to put their seismo-ripples model to the test.

item.title: [SCMP] The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
item.description:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.

“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

Arora’s experience, together with broader economic data, illustrates the challenge facing countries seeking to diversify their supply chains: shifting production out of China does not necessarily mean reducing reliance on Chinese industry. A recent report by investment bank Morgan Stanley examined this pattern, arguing the country had strengthened its role in global supply chains despite trade tensions.

“China has continued to deepen its presence in global supply chains by capturing value-added content in global imports and increasing exports to [emerging markets],” the bank’s analysts, including chief Asia economist Chetan Ahya and chief China economist Robin Xing, wrote in the note, published earlier this month.

The world’s second-largest economy was “well-positioned” to deepen that presence, the analysts argued, citing its focus on high-growth sectors, integrated supply chains, a financial system aligned with strategic goals and a large pool of skilled workers.

The upstream advantage

The challenge facing the likes of India and Vietnam is whether they can develop the industrial expertise and networks required to make more inputs at home. But a closer look at the data suggests that as manufacturing expands in these economies, Chinese supplies remain essential.

These developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China

Morgan Stanley analysts

“While India has made significant headway in electronics manufacturing, it still imports a large part of its intermediate and capital goods from China,” the Morgan Stanley analysts wrote, noting that 52 per cent of India’s imported Chinese content went into domestic investments.

Looking beyond where products are finally assembled, they tracked “value-added content” – the value contributed by a country through the goods and services used along the chain. A product assembled in Vietnam, for instance, may still contain Chinese parts or rely on Chinese machinery.

Using this measure, the analysts found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports rose from 12.6 per cent in 2017 to 14.3 per cent in 2024. The report also found that Chinese inputs are playing a growing role in Asian economies often touted as manufacturing rivals.

In Vietnam, 55 per cent of imported Chinese content is channelled towards exports, according to the analysts. “We also find that Chinese value-added content has not just increased in the rest of Asia’s exports to the US, but also to non-US markets as well,” they wrote.

“Overall, these developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China.”

Arora’s experience illustrates how difficult mainland China’s manufacturing ecosystem is to replace. Taiwan’s higher-end products, he said, were less suited to the low-cost goods his Indian customers needed while Vietnam offered fewer options.

“Only China has that ecosystem,” he said.

Nevertheless, Arora said he believed India was making headway. He cited the expansion of home-grown electronics giant Dixon Technologies into television and phone assembly, as well as the growing ability of Indian firms to design and develop circuit boards and prototypes that once required trips to Shenzhen. Despite the progress, however, local manufacturers continue to rely on China’s extensive network of component suppliers.

Arora estimated that China had gained 20 to 25 years of electronics manufacturing experience, compared with India’s push that gathered pace only around 2015. He argued India could reach the current capabilities of the world’s second-largest economy within five to seven years, although he expected China to have moved further ahead by then.

New Delhi is also pushing to develop more of its inputs at home. The government’s Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, launched in 2025 and expanded to 400 billion rupees (US$4.2 billion) in the 2026-27 budget, supports local production of parts and partially assembled products. By August, 106 projects had been approved and 38 plants had begun production, according to the Indian government.

But the government also acknowledged that India remained dependent on imports for critical components, including printed circuit boards, camera and display modules, connectors and capacitors.

Vietnam is pursuing a similar goal of strengthening its domestic supplier base. A revised industrial policy that took effect in September 2025 provides support for technology transfer, training and certification, as well as programmes intended to help local companies supply multinational manufacturers.

The limits of Western decoupling

For the United States and Europe, where the decoupling narrative has arguably been most pronounced, efforts to reduce dependence on China have transformed where products are sourced and how they reach their destinations. But the Morgan Stanley analysts found that lower direct imports from the world’s factory do not necessarily translate into less Chinese content in those goods.

They estimated that the US and EU together accounted for about 80 per cent of the increase in global reliance on Chinese value-added content. While China’s share of direct US imports plunged from 22 per cent in 2017 to about 8 per cent currently, the share of Chinese value-added content in US imports has remained broadly stable in recent years, standing at 15.4 per cent in 2024.

The analysts found that more US sectors had increased their reliance on China than reduced it, with only five of 13 manufacturing sectors recording a material decline in the share of Chinese value-added content in their imports since 2016.

“The US is still importing just as much value-added content from China, just not directly,” they wrote.

The report identified extensive re-routing of goods. About 25 per cent of Chinese content in US imports now reached the country indirectly through third economies, up 10 percentage points from 2017, according to the analysts. Nearly half of this indirect value passed through just three economies: Mexico, Taiwan and Vietnam, with the latter standing out for a much higher share of Chinese content in its exports to the US.

The analysts said the greater use of indirect channels, particularly from 2022 onwards, was “unique to US-China trade” and consistent with production moving to other countries to serve the American market while continuing to rely on Chinese inputs.

“We do not observe a similar shift towards indirect channels in imports of the rest of the world outside the US, nor for EU imports,” they said, estimating that the share of Chinese value-added content in Europe’s imports had edged up from 6.9 per cent in 2017 to 8.3 per cent in 2024.

Why China’s manufacturing machine endures

The stubborn persistence of Chinese inputs in overseas supply chains reflects the country’s unrivalled strength across a wide range of industries.

The Morgan Stanley report found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports increased in 10 of 13 manufacturing sectors over the past decade, with gains in both lower-value-added industries such as textiles, leather and footwear and more technologically advanced sectors.

In 2024, for instance, China accounted for 33 per cent of the value-added content in global imports of electrical and optical equipment, 24 per cent in machinery and equipment and 10 per cent in transport equipment.

“These patterns are consistent with China retaining higher-value production processes even as final assembly moves elsewhere, while China continues to supply the equipment and inputs needed by new manufacturing hubs,” the analysts said.

Meanwhile, China’s exports surged 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, customs data showed on Wednesday. The momentum – driven by strong global tech demand and a pre-holiday shipping rush ahead of the “golden week” break – logged a monthly high for its trade surplus in 2026 and put the country on course for another record gap this year.

A separate report from Goldman Sachs last week examined China’s rising proportion of global exports. According to the bank’s analysis, that share increased from 4 per cent in 2000 to 15 per cent in 2025, outpacing the peaks previously reached by Germany in the 1970s and Japan in the 1980s.

“Our benchmarking exercise implies that robust real export growth [in China] can continue over the next few years,” the bank’s analysts said. “The runway is therefore clear for now – but eventually will depend on stronger economic growth in importing economies.”

The Morgan Stanley report also highlighted emerging technologies as a potential source of further growth. “China is increasingly playing a critical role in global supply chains, not just in low-cost component supplies but also in high-end capital goods as well,” the analysts wrote.

“Our China team also believes China’s advantage in global manufacturing will be strengthened as it enters a new phase of industrial development in the form of ‘Industry 5.0’”, they added, referring to manufacturing enabled by artificial intelligence and robotics.

An earlier report by Morgan Stanley released in May argued humanoids and other robotics technologies could help China consolidate its dominance over global manufacturing, building on its decade-long expansion in electric vehicle manufacturing.

The bank’s analysts projected that China’s share of global exports would reach 16.5 per cent by 2030, up from about 15 per cent at the time of the report.

For countries pushing to become alternative manufacturing hubs, the findings suggest they would also need to develop the suppliers, expertise and networks that China has spent decades building. “Diversification is achievable, but decoupling will be challenging,” the analysts argued.

item.title: [SCMP] Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
item.description:
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.

The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.

The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.
item.content:encoded:
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.

The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.

The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.

Whatever one’s view of Venezuelan politics, that act made a mockery of an institution founded on Alfred Nobel’s will: that the prize go to the person who has done the most for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and for the promotion of peace congresses. A Nobel Prize cannot be re-gifted like a souvenir. As the organisers made clear, “a medal can change owners, but the title of a Nobel Peace Prize laureate cannot”.

In choosing Pillay this year, the Nobel Committee cited “her efforts to promote peace and international law” and her work showing that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide can and must be prosecuted.

It said: “The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”

2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time. This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. Learn more about the 2026 #NobelPeacePrize: https://t.co/JMjpp1jPKc #NobelPeacePrize #NobelPrize

— The Nobel Prize (@NobelPrize) October 9, 2026

Honouring Pillay is therefore not only about her biography; it is about upholding a principle.

In the West, it is the refutation of Thrasymachus’ contention in Plato’s Republic. In response to Thrasymachus’ declaration that “justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger”, Socrates answers that this cannot be justice at all. As Socrates puts it: “No physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient.”

In the East, the same contest is wangdao vs badao: the kingly way vs the hegemonic way. According to Mencius, he who uses force under the pretence of humaneness is a hegemon while he who uses his virtue to practice humaneness is a true king. The message is clear: a king dispenses benevolence with virtue; a hegemon appropriates benevolence by force.

Confucius also rejected rule by force: a ruler must govern by virtue and humaneness, holding the mandate of heaven by moral rectitude, not coercion. His great antagonist, Han Feizi, China’s Machiavelli, argued the opposite: man is selfish, order comes only from shi (positional power), fa (the law as an instrument of the state) and shu (techniques of reward and fear).

For Han, the first principle of political theory was the reality of human nature. This was the legalist doctrine favoured by China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, who unified the country in 221BC. I place Pillay firmly in the Socratic-Confucian lineage – might may prevail but that does not make it right, and even the strongest state is bound by law.

The third reason is more immediate, and it concerns Trump. His petulance at not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize – last year and, again, this year – would be comical if it were not consequential. Earlier this month, he argued that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize for having settled “eight wars”.

What is consequential is how American power has been deployed against the very institutions that Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), helped to build.

In February last year, Trump issued an executive order announcing sanctions on 13 ICC officials. On October 9 this year – hours after Pillay’s prize was awarded – the US Treasury added the ICC itself to its sanctions list, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying: “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”

For China, this moment carries a particular lesson. As a major power, China will be judged not only by its growth but by its rectitude.

Pillay’s career suggests what that choice requires. Her most controversial work was as the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on ‌the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year that Israel was failing to prevent and actively committing genocide.

The commission found that four of five acts defined under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention had been committed, and that Israel’s President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide. Israel dismissed the report as a “libellous rant” and “scandalous”.

Pillay, who in 1967 became the first woman to establish a law practice in South Africa’s then Natal province, who in 1973 won a case for Robben Island prisoners including Nelson Mandela to have access to lawyers, and who served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda that investigated the 1994 genocide, in which about 800,000 people were killed, knows that the law is fragile.

The world needed to understand that the alternative is the situation Thrasymachus and Han described. The 2026 prize is a reminder that we can still choose the normative path.

item.title: [SCMP] Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
item.description:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?
item.content:encoded:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?

The summit was necessary. Leader-level meetings are the only guardrail we really have in US-China relations right now. It is very important that these meetings happen.

I’m probably more positive on this than other people because I do think that leader-level meetings in US-China relations are always difficult to put together. And the fact that Trump has done this twice with Xi – once in Beijing and once in Washington – may help regularise such high-level meetings, which we absolutely need to keep the relationship on track right now since we don’t have much else.

I’m not surprised by the negative coverage. The US-China summits are always held to a higher bar when it comes to outcomes of the meeting.

There have been expectations built up over many decades that US-China summits are always a big deal when they happen because they’re very hard to mount, and then they always have to have these long lists of outcomes.

We need to try to normalise these meetings between the US and Chinese leaders if possible. If you have to have a long list of accomplishments all the time, it’s going to be very hard to hold these meetings.

Some argue that the prospect of multiple face-to-face summits this year has put constraints on both sides, especially when it comes to sensitive issues. How could the two sides avoid a repeat of disruptions to bilateral relations, such as the balloon incident in 2023 and the fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022?

What you’re getting at here is exactly the issue of whether we can have constructive strategic stability.

In the US, I believe that constructive strategic stability – to the extent that people who agreed to that were really understanding what the Chinese side was talking about – is really about avoiding these worst-case scenarios. Avoiding conflict, avoiding a crisis that leads potentially to a conflict, et cetera.

The key is for both sides to understand what those issues are that could lead us there. And I do think we have been making progress in this administration on those issues.

President Trump is not new to this. He did this before for four years, and it ended quite badly under Covid-19. But I think whenever I’ve heard him speak about that time, it seems to me that he has thought about it and understands what the dynamic was that led things to get so out of hand and doesn’t want to see that happen again.

I think others in the administration also understand this. I think [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent and [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio definitely understand that this is what they’re trying to accomplish.

You put that strategic stability on top of all of these areas of difference that we have, and it does make it quite difficult to manage. But I do think with those high-level cabinet officials understanding what the boundaries are, there are additional touch points.

Marco Rubio and [Chinese Foreign Minister] Wang Yi have been speaking more than previously. Scott Bessent has a lot of things on his plate, so it may not be as easy for him to engage regularly with his counterpart, but he has been managing to meet [Chinese Vice-Premier] He Lifeng frequently. And you’ve got a number of economic and trade officials under him and under [US Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer who are plugged in together and talking.

I don’t think the crisis will come in the economic sphere. We can work through those questions and not have a crisis. We’ve really been doing this for quite a long time now.

The crises will come in the security area, most likely, and in a way those are harder because the security bureaucracies in both countries aren’t very connected to one another and don’t really have regular dialogue mechanisms.

We’ve always been talking about having some kind of military-to-military mechanisms for communication hotlines. There’s been a little bit of that in this administration and it’s got a bit improved, but it seems always very unstable. So, I think that’s the potential area that has to be guarded against.

President Trump does know where [Beijing’s] red lines are on Taiwan. That has been a learning curve probably for him. But he has a pretty firm view on that issue now, and I feel like Beijing has been reassured that he understands what the mainland’s position is.

It seems to me that the tension over Taiwan has abated, but the one question that Beijing keeps bringing up concerns Taiwan arms sales. I’m hopeful that the US side can find a way to manage that effectively. We’ve managed it in the past and should be able to do it again. And I think Trump will focus on it and try to take care that it gets done in a way that doesn’t cause a crisis.

How do you view the role of this summit in potentially helping address difficulties and challenges ahead in the US-China relationship?

I see US-China bilateral ties as being in a state of fragile stability.

During the summit in Beijing in May and since then, many Chinese colleagues have been excited about the notion that we’ve been able to put a name on the relationship, so we have a framework within which we can know what we’re working towards, which is a constructive relationship of strategic stability.

Looking at this summit, it’s important that they could meet and normalise that, but it’s also important that we be able to see them meeting in the future. We don’t have those kinds of mechanisms set up yet.

In addition to the leader-level meetings, what would be important to maintain this constructive stability is the institutionalisation of the relationship, which we’ve lost over the last 10 years. We need to start building that back to maintain stability.

The summit in September was the start of an institutionalisation of things that were agreed upon in May in Beijing.

For example, the Board of Trade, which was announced in May but really didn’t do much between May and now because of the summits, was actually pressured to meet, set up working groups and talk to one another. There are groups of people under Jamieson Greer and under [Greer’s Chinese counterpart] Li Chenggang who are meeting and talking through these things. You need a lot more connectivity among professionals if you’re going to have stabilisation of this relationship in any way.

The other area maybe that will move forward is AI, which was also announced in May. Scott Bessent announced that there would be an AI dialogue, and maybe that will meet in Shenzhen.

So, we can start to see the institutionalisation of these things. It’s still not nearly enough between the US and China.

I hope we’ll remember how hard it is to get mechanisms restarted because institutionalisation is a big job and it doesn’t happen overnight.

Trump gave Xi a very high-level reception, breaking some traditional protocols, and that triggered a lot of questioning and even criticism in the US. How do you view that?

Trump wants to appear welcoming and hospitable but also strong, so there was a jet flyover during the military review. A lot of this is just Trump’s personal way of thinking about how he wants to stage events. It doesn’t have as much to do with diplomatic protocol.

There were previous occasions when a president went to meet someone at Joint Base Andrews, so it does have some diplomatic precedent.

But I would hesitate to attach a lot of significance to the protocol.

Think of all of the things that they did that are highly unusual for a presidential visit. Walking out to look at the presidential helicopter, going over to see the construction of the White House ballroom. All these things are very much a signature of Trump’s way of handling the visit. I think a lot of people just don’t understand this.

That’s the main criticism: it’s very, very long on symbolism, pageantry, pomp and circumstance, and short on outcomes. This may signal a change in US-China summitry.

We used to try to, in diplomacy, trade diplomatic protocol issues and ceremonial issues, which were very high on the Chinese agenda for a visit, for concerns on the US side, for substantive outcomes.

But it’s no longer the case that we can expect that the Chinese are going to make concessions for only protocolary and ceremonial kinds of considerations. I think that is a change in the relationship that we’re seeing.

Both sides offer high levels of protocol and neither side really gets any trade for that. Maybe we can dispense with the ceremony of a state visit in the future and focus more on substantive issues at regular leader meetings.

Do you think that this summit has laid a proper foundation for Trump and Xi to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in November and Group of 20 (G20) in December? The Chinese side has called 2026 a “big year” for bilateral relations, with the two countries’ leaders having the chance to meet face to face four times. But what about next year? How could the US and China keep up this head-of-state diplomacy?

They will have to make a big effort. This is why I think it is positive that President Trump seems to really value his meetings with President Xi and really wants to continue to communicate with him directly either via face-to-face meetings or other ways.

I hope we’ll take advantage of that because that hasn’t always been the case with US leaders in the past. That is an important advantage that Trump offers in this very difficult time in US-China relations. He’s open to talking to President Xi anytime, I think.

I would like to see if they could connect more on the phone.

Next year they are probably not going to travel as much as they did this year. And that’s another reason the relationship has to be institutionalised in the way that we’ve been talking about. There’s such a thin layer of professional expertise in the government that is plugged in to the other side, and that is probably not going to change too much over the next couple years.

The other thing we have to worry about is that if we institutionalise the relationship under this administration, what’s going to happen in the next administration? I hope the next administration would keep whatever institutionalisation has been started and build on that, not just try to always do their own thing. That’s not going to be a good way for us to proceed with the relationship.

There has been discussion that the Apec gathering in November could open scheduling windows for a US-Russia, China-US-Russia or Trump-Kim Jong-un summit. How do you view the likelihood of these potential bilateral or multilateral meetings taking place?

It definitely raises possibilities for dramatic diplomacy that could certainly appeal to President Trump.

President Trump has already invited [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to come to Miami for the G20 summit, and it’s likely that he’ll attend. It’s creating some ripple effects in Europe because they may or may not be too pleased that he’s coming, but I think that will all be worked out.

President Trump still sees himself as a broker of peace, and so he wants to create these opportunities for dramatic things to happen and big changes in some of the problem areas that we see. Certainly the Russia-Ukraine war is one of them, but North Korea is another one.

We know that he wants to meet again with [North Korean leader] Kim Jong-un, and that has not happened yet. If that could happen in Shenzhen during Apec – several people have mentioned this as a possibility, or that Trump could do it on his way to China – those would be dramatic opportunities.

We were talking earlier about the calendar for next year, and then Trump is getting towards the end of his term. It seems like he might want to do something in this area.

It might make it more attractive for Trump to actually go to Shenzhen and for Xi to come to Miami if there is an opportunity for progress on Ukraine or the North Korea nuclear issue.

It’s very hard to see the preparation going far enough between now and November or December to make dramatic successes out of such a meeting, however. Usually, such things take a lot more preparation, so I would be sceptical on that score. But I have heard a lot of people talking about such possibilities, so perhaps they will materialise.

You mentioned the AI dialogue. The US and China appear to be taking different approaches to developing this technology. There is also debate within the US over whether the development of advanced models should be slowed. Given these international and domestic differences, how do you view the prospects for the bilateral AI dialogue?

I do think it’s going to be extremely difficult.

I participated in US-China discussions on mechanisms to report cyber incidents. The AI dialogue is not exactly the same as that, but in the area that the US is concerned about, I think it’s quite similar and also just as difficult, if not more so.

The US and China have different concerns, and it’s very hard for the two of them to talk to each other because they’re just coming from completely different vantage points.

The Chinese government – and Chinese interlocutors that I’ve talked to reflect this – seems to be quite confident in its ability to control its AI operators and make sure that things that it doesn’t want to have happen in the AI sphere will not happen. Is it overconfident? I am concerned they are not really thinking about the possibilities of loss of control on the Chinese side with AI.

They’re mostly worried about what’s happening on the US side and the possibilities of loss of control, the fact that the US government doesn’t control these private companies, that the companies themselves are reporting a lot of things that are somewhat hair-raising and fear-inducing. The US government seems to be thinking that China is going to have the same concerns it has, whereas it really doesn’t.

And also, the two systems don’t match up in terms of reporting, transparency and other things that you would need to talk about if you were going to try to share best practices or discuss a strategy for keeping incidents from getting out of control.

Trump said that the line for AI safety in the US is the Department of Justice, in other words, the legal system, and that is just not the way the Chinese are going to operate in terms of AI safety.

It’s going to be very hard from an institutional and bureaucratic set-up perspective, this security-to-security bureaucracy mistrust. The Chinese system is just not given to being transparent about these things. Chinese media have focused on various US AI operators who are trying to do the right thing by self-reporting accidents that have happened.

In the Chinese system, these things would not be publicly reported. China has been criticising the US AI labs and taking advantage of this moment to make itself look like a more responsible actor, when I’m not sure that is fully justified.

It’s also very hard to understand how the US and Chinese governments would put together delegations that would look at all similar and have the same kind of expertise. So, I find it a little bit head-scratching as to how this is going to go ahead.

It’s important to get some of these people in the room together and have regular discussions. Maybe they can build up a little bit of personal familiarity that will help us at some point in the future when we hit a real problem. I think that would be an advantage.

Xi has invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China over the next five years. You travelled to China this year and last year to attend events on subnational cooperation between the two countries. What is your read on the state of bilateral local and people-to-people exchanges? Are they still constrained by factors such as visas and flights? There have been recurring calls to reopen the US consulate in Chengdu and the Chinese consulate in Houston. How possible do you think that would be?

This area is still a source of difficulty, even though the two governments have pledged to make improvements.

I noticed that they did mention the number of flights. Certainly, they talked about students. But the question is how to make this happen. There’s still extreme suspicion in local-level, people-to-people exchanges, mostly coming from, to be honest, local-level politicians. There are some organised groups that are also pushing against people-to-people exchange between the US and China.

I don’t see much change in this. I don’t know, if the US midterm elections in November see a huge shift in the Congress, what might happen there. Most of the local anti-China legislation is coming from Republican states, so it depends a little bit on domestic politics.

I don’t know if the Democrats will focus on this as an issue, but in general Democrats have been much more open about people-to-people travel back and forth. I don’t know if they can affect the atmosphere on this issue. It is something to watch.

Certainly, the downturn in Chinese students is noticeable. I work at Yale University, and we’ve got a number of Chinese students who were unable to come for the start of the semester because they didn’t get their visas in time.

Visas are still an issue on both sides. I know people who are having trouble getting visas to go to China, so it’s a two-way thing, and it’s very unfortunate. But it’s really hard to see where a push is going to come from in the US to fix this problem.

We should keep pressuring both sides to make improvements here. And again, the devil’s in the details. These two security bureaucracies have a deep, deep level of mistrust.

Treasury Secretary Bessent said China and the US had agreed to extend the trade truce for two months, until January 10 next year. Why only two months rather than a longer period? What could the two sides achieve during this time frame?

To me, it is a bit surprising that the extension of the Busan trade truce was so minimal. I think two months is about the minimum that they could have agreed.

What that says is they did not want the truce to end because neither side is prepared for what might happen or the consequences of ending that truce. But they couldn’t come up really with any agreement to extend it, so they’ve just basically rolled over the agreement from last year.

Both sides were probably hoping that they would be able to extend the truce and improve it, but apparently that didn’t happen. It’s probable that they didn’t have enough time to do that, because these kinds of negotiations take quite a bit of time and preparation. And you can’t just have a meeting on a Sunday in New York between top officials and expect to hammer these things out in that kind of time frame. So, my suspicion is that they did not manage to agree on any of the improvements in the rollover that they wanted, and they didn’t want to roll over the current truce, which is kind of minimal, for too much of an extended period of time because they still hope to get something better.

Probably the January time frame is not much time to do anything either. But at least if there is a meeting in November, then that gives another forcing function, and there’s also the G20 summit in Miami in December, that’s a lot of connectivity between now and January 10. So, there is a possibility of getting something done there, although it will be difficult.

And then we’ll hit January 10, and the truce will probably roll over one way or another. They won’t want to lose this truce, I don’t think, in January either.

The one factor that probably was pushing on the US side is the midterm elections coming up in early November. I think the US side wanted to get something that would get us past the midterm elections and give some comfortable margin after that to assess where things are going.

Observers in both countries argue that China is becoming more confident and increasingly sees itself as Washington’s equal, while perceptions of continuing US decline are growing globally. The narrative of “the East is rising and the West is declining” continues to surface in public discussions. What do you think about this? Before the September summit, some argued that China was in a stronger position at the negotiating table because of the war on Iran. If that is the case, how long could that last?

I do think China is more confident, reasonably so. And certainly, the US has been losing influence on the international stage for a period of time. In the wake of the war in Iran, that has accelerated, probably.

The question, really, is whether China is making gains from the losses that the US is inflicting on itself. I think China has made some gains, but it is not a slam dunk yet that China has made equal gains to the US’ losses. In other words, I don’t see that China is somehow displacing the US.

The interesting thing to watch is we’ve seen President Xi go to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan and the Brics summit in India, talking in many of his speeches about China being a responsible player, that China stands for a continuation of globalisation, openness and free trade, and I think what people see China doing in practice is somewhat different from that. Or at least they are sceptical that this is what China is standing for and what China is all about.

In fact, a lot of countries, especially in China’s neighbourhood, continue to have concerns about China and are actually threatened by China. And China hasn’t really done much to reassure those countries that they shouldn’t be afraid of China. I think this is the dilemma China has.

It wants to take advantage of this moment when the US is on the back foot, clearly, in Iran and elsewhere, and it has taken some advantage, but it has not managed to really convince people of what its ambitions and intentions are. I think that is going to continue to be a tough balancing act for China.

I hope China will start to show in its actions more what it’s actually thinking about for the long term, and I think that will be important in terms of the narrative too out there in the world.

The US is clearly in a transition period. Domestic politics are at a turning point, and we’re going to have to work through that. So, it’s going to be a period of time. Whether China can take advantage of our domestic transition is really a question for China’s own policy and diplomats to work out.

US allies such as Japan and the Philippines are strengthening their security ties, while tensions with Beijing continue to simmer in the South China Sea, the East China Sea and the waters east of Taiwan. Would this make it more challenging for Beijing and Washington to manage their bilateral relationship?

As for the South China Sea, some Chinese experts have said that Beijing’s goal is not to expel US influence from the region and that it could consider opening certain island infrastructure to US vessels to help ease tensions. Do you think this is realistic?

I don’t know about that specific proposal, but certainly China can’t be happy about what it’s seeing in terms of its immediate neighbours linking up in tighter coalitions for their security.

China hasn’t been doing much to reassure them that they shouldn’t be worried about China, and so that’s going to produce this natural kind of build-up of defence and military capability and trying to link with other countries in the region to strengthen their posture. It’s exactly what you would expect. And it can’t be something that China sees as a good development.

I have to say that it’s really hard for these countries to see in the future how China is going to not behave in a very kind of domineering way towards them. This is how things have been playing out in the region, which is why they seem to be so eager to have US engagement stay in the region.

I think that’s a big question mark right now, which is making people in the region even more worried about the future.
