And in Britain, the most familiar kind of Chinese food was the takeaway, which was extremely simplified – no bones, no shells, not so many vegetables, lots of fried foods. It was not designed for Chinese people to eat themselves. But this style of food really shaped perceptions of Chinese cuisine, both in Britain and in a similar way in the US.

The worst stereotype of Chinese food has been that it should be cheap. People will pay a lot of money for Japanese sushi, but while they may think Chinese food is tasty, they don’t necessarily see it as the kind of sophisticated, elite cuisine that you would pay serious money for.

Another misunderstanding is the idea that it’s unhealthy – again, because popular takeaway food involved a lot of fried food, few vegetables, few soups and so on. There is also a certain amount of Western prejudice against monosodium glutamate, which is perfectly normal in China, but Westerners don’t use it in home cooking or quality cooking, and so it’s very much stigmatised.

And then the other side of that coin is the idea that the Chinese eat a lot of weird, scary stuff like chicken feet and snakes.

The Chinese certainly do eat many ingredients that are seen as unusual or strange in the West, but this has always been seen through the lens of a notion that the Chinese eat such things because they were very poor and desperate, which is a terrible simplification, because obviously very rich Chinese people also like to eat duck tongues and goose feet.

There are other reasons Chinese people eat a lot of foods that Westerners reject. And they include this pleasure of texture, the pleasure of the sensation of food in the mouth, and also the Chinese idea of unusual and exotic food – the idea that since, for example, duck tongue is very small and there is only one of them in each duck, it’s a great privilege to have that particular part.

I think for Westerners it’s been a very strange picture because on the one hand, Chinese food has been hugely successful, everybody loves it. There’s no other foreign cuisine that’s been more popular globally than Chinese in a way, but it’s also been saddled with these rather negative prejudices that are very outdated.

As someone who is Chinese, you will know very well that these stereotypes are ridiculous. Because in China, yes, you do have cheap peasant food and street food, but you also have extremely extravagant, time-consuming gongfu food or banquet cooking, which is another aspect of Chinese food culture.

And then in terms of eating “weird” things, as I said, there are gastronomic reasons for this as well as economic reasons.

Finally in terms of health, I think no other culture is as insistent on the link between diet and health as the Chinese. In China, food has been seen as medicine for more than 2,000 years. And Chinese people talk about food and health all the time.

When I learned to cook Chinese food, I learned how to make vegetables taste delicious and how to eat food that is balanced and healthy as well as delicious. I think that is one of the most impressive things about Chinese cuisine.

What misconceptions do Chinese people have about Western food?

Just as Westerners can be very dismissive of Chinese food, Chinese people can be very dismissive of Western food.

All over China, people have told me that Western food is simple and boring, and a lot of people seem to think that it just consists of hamburgers and sandwiches.

And then recently there has been all this talk about “white people food”, which is just seen as completely uncouth and boring and depressing. And then there’s a very weird stereotype about British food – “dark cuisine”.

There’s an old-fashioned British dish from Cornwall called a stargazy pie and it’s a pie with fish heads poking up through the pastry. It’s a very obscure regional dish that I’ve never tried and most British people have never tried. But an English woman wrote a blog post about it that went viral in China, so it’s now almost certainly better known in China than it is at home.

I would say that a lot of Chinese people who have not had the chance to travel abroad make these huge generalisations about Western food that are just as silly as those some Westerners make about all Chinese food.

I’ve also found it very surprising that a lot of Chinese people have told me over the years that they think Western food is healthier because there’s this sort of tradition of scientific nutrition where you’re told how many calories and how much protein and that sort of thing.

But I find that very strange because it seems to me that people in China, certainly the older generation, have a knowledge of healthy eating that is incredibly deep and incredibly useful, whereas I think a lot of Westerners are actually quite confused about how to eat healthily.

There is also this idea that Chinese food can be quite oily and Western food is not. But again, I think that’s really strange because if you think about traditional Chinese food, it involves a lot of soups and steamed dishes and boiled dishes, and traditional Chinese home cooking does not use a lot of oil.

I think it’s quite sad to see that people in China are now making a lot of the same mistakes that we’ve already made in the West of cooking less and eating less fresh food. It is one of the unfortunate side effects of modernisation and industrialisation, isn’t it?

What do you think of Westernised Chinese food, such as the fast food restaurants popular in the US, like Panda Express?

You have to remember that Chinese food is not just the food of the country of China. It’s also the food of a huge Chinese diaspora.

So Chinese food is already part of global culture and it’s a presence in every city practically all over the world. Not only Chinese people living in the West want to eat Chinese food.

Chinese food doesn’t have to be one thing. I think people are always inventing and adapting and borrowing ideas from each other. For example, I recently wrote an article about Shanghainese Western food, which is a bit like Hong Kong-style Western food.

So in China you have versions of Western food that are completely separate from what Westerners actually want to eat. They are adapted to Chinese tastes, and I think in the West you also have Chinese food that’s not designed for Chinese people. It’s made for Westerners. I don’t have a problem with that. I think it’s fun to be inventive.

The only problem is when people start to judge Chinese food by Panda Express and think that it represents the cuisine of a very large and sophisticated gastronomic nation.

We just have to be a bit careful about judging it.

In many Chinese cities, the highly rated and expensive restaurants tend to be Japanese. This seems to be the case in other major cities around the world. Why is Japanese food more likely to be considered fine dining than Chinese food?

I think the status of food is always about money.

Japan got rich before China in the late 20th century, so its food acquired high status at a time when China was quite closed to the outside world and was not rich and did not have high status.

It’s the same within China with regional cuisines. For example, when there were many rich merchants from Anhui, Anhui food was considered one of the “eight major cuisines”. But when I was a student in Sichuan in the 1990s, all of the expensive restaurants were Cantonese because places like Hong Kong and Shenzhen got rich first.

What’s interesting now is that China is getting richer and more powerful, so I think the status of China and Chinese culture is rising. The problem at the moment is that we don’t have enough chefs in the UK. We have very tight immigration rules in Britain and it’s almost impossible these days for chefs to come here and work.

If we had more free movement of chefs, Chinese food here in Britain would become more ambitious and more expensive.

It’s even more important to find ways to communicate with each other, and it’s also incredibly important to try and understand each other

Fuchsia Dunlop

Do you face any challenges in defending Chinese food in the West?

The whole environment is becoming more complicated because of geopolitical tensions. Obviously the relationship between the West and China has become more complicated.

But I think in that context it’s even more important to find ways to communicate with each other, and it’s also incredibly important to try and understand each other.

So, for example, it’s fantastic that China is now more open to foreign tourists, because foreigners will go to China and actually see something of the country, meet people and have a real experience.

At the same time, the first encounters most foreigners have with Chinese culture often involve Chinese food, and it’s an area that’s not so politically contentious, a space where you can actually learn a lot about China and have a fantastic experience of China without being so complicated.

Have there been any obstacles to cultural exchange between China and Britain over the years? Could Chinese food serve as a bridge?

The real difference is that, as I’ve described, in the 1990s, when I started doing this work, the food was all Cantonese, now it’s very regional.

So we have restaurants in London that serve Sichuan food, as well as dishes from Chongqing, Hunan, and the northeast. We have some quite wonderful Shanghai supper clubs. Although we only see a small proportion of Chinese food because China is huge, already people can see that Chinese food is not one thing, that it’s very diverse.

And we now even have more northern food, so handmade noodles and breads, like Xian street food, that can just show different sides of Chinese food culture.

Some people say that if the Chinese ate less meat it would help slow down global warming. This is very controversial in China because meat is an integral part of Chinese cuisine. What are your views?

The truth is that we should all be eating less meat if we want to tackle climate change. The situation in China is that most people didn’t eat much meat until the 1990s. And now, with the reform and opening up that followed, everyone wants to eat more meat – more like the extravagant way we eat in the West.

So objectively it is a huge problem that you have over a billion people suddenly eating more meat. But I can understand the Chinese view that it’s really unfair.

Climate change is a global problem. It would be great if Chinese people were more aware of the role that eating meat plays in climate change, but people in the West also have to change their diets and eat less meat.

And I think traditional Chinese cuisine is a fantastic resource and inspiration for that. Because in traditional Chinese cuisine there are so many ways of using a little bit of meat to make vegetarian ingredients taste fantastic – like mapo tofu and dry-fried green beans.

There are all these dishes where you have a little bit of meat and lots of vegetables that are really delicious. We can learn a lot from traditional Chinese food about how to eat less meat.

But the main thing is that it is unfair for Westerners to put the whole burden on Chinese consumers without looking at their own behaviour.

How have Chinese eating habits changed over the decades? How much of the change is political?

The first thing is that so many young people don’t really cook. The older generation, when I lived in Chengdu, were really excellent cooks. Not only did they cook daily meals, they also made pickles, sausages and other preserves. You can really see how these skills are now being lost.

It’s also quite interesting to see how Chinese people are eating more industrialised and prepared food.

At the same time in Britain, there’s a book that came out two years ago about ultra-processed foods, looking at the harmful effects of eating too much processed food, and I see China making the same mistakes we’ve made, and it’s a real shame.

China has a fantastic food culture, which is a huge resource for how to eat healthily and deliciously.

So it’s sad to see that younger people are losing touch with that and I hope that as people in China become more health conscious, which they are, and as they become more aware of the environmental impact of how we eat, which I hope will become more widespread, then they will be able to see their own culture as an invaluable resource for eating more healthily and sustainably.

But I think it is more about economic changes. When I lived in Chengdu in the 1990s, there was very little manufactured food. There were no supermarkets and everyone went to fresh markets to buy vegetables and fish.

And now there’s a huge expansion of food production and factory farming in China. There’s mass production of meat and also of ready meals, as you mentioned, and even restaurants are serving food that’s pre-prepared.

It’s all driven by the same technology and economics as in the West, and also the whole sort of takeaway food system, the fact that you can order anything at home that you don’t have to cook.

Which dish do you think best represents Chinese cuisine?

If I had to choose one, I would probably choose mapo tofu.

The reason is that it’s a really good example of a recipe that uses a little bit of meat and very delicious fermented bean spices to give an amazing flavour to a plant food. For me, it’s a really good example of how Chinese food offers ways to eat healthily and sustainably but without sacrificing pleasure, because this dish is utterly delicious.

Do you have any ongoing projects?

At the moment I’m writing another cookbook, and it’s not just about one region. It’s more of a simple homestyle Chinese cookbook, a bit like my previous book Every Grain of Rice.

So it’s designed to give readers the tools of some traditional Chinese techniques to cook wonderful food at home, not always with Chinese ingredients, but to cook food that’s really delicious and quite healthy and exciting.

item.title: [SCMP] Macau’s opulent fine dining scene is using AI to tackle sustainability: how restaurants in Galaxy Macau, Sands China and Grand Lisboa are leading the green march forward
item.description:
In a city as vibrant and fast-paced as Macau, the hungry need not look far to find a fine dining institution worthy of a visit. The city’s leading restaurants are known for their high quality produce and innovative twists on classic cuisines.

Now, increasingly, attention is being paid to sustainability – no easy feat in a territory that, by necessity, imports most of its ingredients and where much hospitality is focused on clients expecting only the very best.

In one sense at least, local traditions provide a head start.
item.content:encoded:
In a city as vibrant and fast-paced as Macau, the hungry need not look far to find a fine dining institution worthy of a visit. The city’s leading restaurants are known for their high quality produce and innovative twists on classic cuisines.

Now, increasingly, attention is being paid to sustainability – no easy feat in a territory that, by necessity, imports most of its ingredients and where much hospitality is focused on clients expecting only the very best.

In one sense at least, local traditions provide a head start.

“Cantonese cuisine has always been curated based on sustainability. We fully utilise every part of the ingredient,” explains chef Tam Kwok-fung of the eponymous one-Michelin-starred establishment Chef Tam’s Seasons, located at Wynn Palace.

Keith Lei, senior vice-president of human resources and sustainability at MGM Macau, says adopting a traditional nose-to-tail approach has granted chefs a sense of culinary liberty. “[This] has challenged chefs to be more creative in their use of less common cuts of meat, leading to a resurgence of diverse cooking techniques and a broader appreciation for the entire animal, discovering new flavours and textures.”

While nose-to-tail and farm-to-table dining are popular trends, chef Tam explains how fish and poultry are prepared. Bones are put aside for flavoursome broths, while vegetables take centre stage or accent dishes as garnishes. “All of this puts our sustainable beliefs and theories into an actual dish,” he says.

Recognising the geographic limitations of a pure farm-to-table approach in Macau, Galaxy Macau’s sustainability and technical services facilities management team sees the success of this approach most in its seasonal menus.

Andre Lai, executive chef of Galaxy’s Andaz Kitchen at the Andaz Macau, sees identifying sustainable sources as the most important component of an all-round sustainable approach to fine dining, and balancing this with “maintaining the identity of our own cuisine”. “Local sourcing is the priority, but we must also look to sustainable initiatives in native cuisine countries,” he says.

Galaxy Macau introduced a Central Production Kitchen in 2021 in a bid to improve energy efficiency and further reduce waste. Feedback on portion sizes and unconsumed food has helped to facilitate menu adjustments and improve future planning. Brand-specific partnerships include a deal with Nespresso that allows for their single-use coffee capsules to be recycled.

Lai shares plans for an urban garden, currently in the development phase, to grow more items to encourage self-sufficiency. “In the future, once we have our urban garden, we aim to introduce our own produce at Andaz Kitchen and our own fermented beverages at Andaz Bar,” he adds.

Julien Tongourian, executive chef of Michelin three-star Robuchon au Dôme – situated atop SJM’s Grand Lisboa hotel – champions a zero-waste philosophy. In an interview with the Michelin Guide, Tongourian explained that the restaurant’s produce is never ordered in bulk, maximising freshness and reducing the risk of excess and waste.

“We never keep our fridge stocked with ingredients. Yes, it’s a challenge for our team to have to work from scratch with new ingredients that arrive every morning, but that’s also how we ensure we get the best flavours from our produce,” he said.

Melco Resorts, which counts City of Dreams, Altira Macau and Studio City among its portfolio in Macau, has been steadily growing its green credentials. Among its many reputable dining establishments are Jade Dragon and Alain Ducasse at Morpheus, both of which featured in last year’s 100 Top Tables guide. The philosophy of small batch ordering is echoed across Melco Group’s establishments and the group has announced a goal of zero waste by 2030, including food waste.

In 2019, Melco announced it would trial the use of dedicated Winnow AI technology, explaining this decision in its sustainability report: “Being the most advanced food waste measurement technology on the market, this initiative will allow us to maximise operational efficiency and data accuracy, with the ability to reduce food waste by up to 50 per cent by value.”

Wynn already uses Winnow technology across its outlets, including at Chef Tam’s Seasons. “[We are] applying computer vision-based monitoring technology powered by AI and machine learning to track and measure what food is being wasted. The system then delivers data-driven insights, enabling us and also other Wynn dining outlets to take an analytical approach to food production that enhances efficiency without compromising on quality,” says Tam.

Wynn Group has also installed a Nordaq water bottling plant, enabling high-quality filtered water to be produced locally and served in reusable glass bottles. Producing around 2,000 bottles per hour, Tam says this will save an estimated eight million plastic bottles every year.

Similarly, at MGM, the implementation of a zero-plastic programme has resulted in the elimination of an estimated 4.5 million pieces of single-use plastic.

Lei and Adam Mathis, culinary director at MGM, emphasise the importance of education in ensuring sustainable practices are adhered to throughout the organisation. They explain that e-learning on sustainability practices is offered to all new food and beverage employees in the organisation. MGM additionally relies on advanced technologies to minimise food waste, including a food digester, composter and food dehydrating machines.

Chef Alex Gaspar, executive director of culinary at Sands China, sees a truly sustainable approach as one that is “multifaceted, using sustainably sourced products, with a zero-waste mindset, to extract as much flavour as possible from the product, utilising as much of it as possible”.

Unable to rely solely on local agriculture, Gaspar places a strong emphasis on working with speciality producers around the region. Winnow AI has also informed Sands China’s approach to food waste, leading them to create live cooking stations instead of using chafing dishes, and portioning up food presented in buffets.

Gaspar urges the importance of sustainable approaches to fine dining without compromising on quality. The proof lies in dishes such as the artichoke risotto at The Londoner’s Churchill’s Table. “We use the artichoke in three different ways: braised, puréed and even using the skin, which is normally discarded – through a special technique we turn it into a crispy and delicious garnish for our risotto,” he says.

“As chefs, we must challenge ourselves to highlight our ingredients and pay respect to all the work that was involved in our dishes.”

item.title: [SCMP] Is Philippines geared for El Nino? Critics say water-planning has run dry
item.description:
As the Philippines braces for months of drought and shortages in key resources due to the current El Nino season, questions are mounting over whether it could have prepared better to deal with a crisis that has been predicted well in advance.

The government’s haphazard response to El Nino reflects its persistent track record of failing to do adequate disaster and infrastructure planning, according to climate and risk specialists.

El Nino is a weather phenomenon that causes changes in winds and rainfall and erratic weather around the world due to warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. The 2026-2027 El Nino event was declared in June by the World Meteorological Organization and is expected to peak in November and December.
item.content:encoded:
As the Philippines braces for months of drought and shortages in key resources due to the current El Nino season, questions are mounting over whether it could have prepared better to deal with a crisis that has been predicted well in advance.

The government’s haphazard response to El Nino reflects its persistent track record of failing to do adequate disaster and infrastructure planning, according to climate and risk specialists.

El Nino is a weather phenomenon that causes changes in winds and rainfall and erratic weather around the world due to warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. The 2026-2027 El Nino event was declared in June by the World Meteorological Organization and is expected to peak in November and December.

On Thursday, Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque told reporters that there was no need for residents to hoard bottled water and that supplies and prices of basic goods remained stable, following social media posts showing that Filipinos were buying water and other items in huge quantities at supermarkets.

“There is no need to panic, there is no need to hoard. We have enough to supply,” Roque said.

However, a suggestion on Wednesday by Rex Gatchalian, secretary of the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to buy buckets to collect rainwater and help prevent water shortages did little to assuage the public’s concerns.

The department said it would be distributing water treatment kits, with Gatchalian demonstrating that water filtered by one such kit was safe for drinking at a media briefing.

One social media user complained: “Telling citizens, many of whom are already struggling with rising living costs, to rely on buckets is a temporary band-aid.”

Analysts question Manila’s readiness to deal with a prolonged drought, amid reports that the government has cut Metro Manila’s water allocation in anticipation of El Nino peaking later this year.

Ven Paolo Valenzuela, a research fellow at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said the Philippines experienced one of its strongest El Nino events in 1997 and disaster planning had not improved almost 30 years later.

He said the problem was not the filtration technology, which he described as “very good” in helping communities hit by super typhoons and other natural disaster events. Rather, it was the absence of a broader plan to address an event with potentially far-reaching effects, he added.

“Thirty years later, you still haven’t solved these problems, still haven’t put [the infrastructure] in place.”

Patrick Manuel, country director of Waves for Water, a non-governmental organisation supplying the filtration kits to the government, said the devices alone could not address the challenges posed by El Nino.

His organisation first introduced the kits to remote communities whose access to clean drinking water was disrupted by the destruction caused by Typhoon Haiyan in 2013.

Manuel said addressing the impact of El Nino required a whole-of-society approach involving government agencies, local governments, the private sector, civil society organisations and communities to boost the country’s water infrastructure and promote responsible water use.

“Through our work with communities from all across the country, we’ve seen that there’s much more work to be done to provide Filipinos with the right tools and infrastructure to be able to have reliable access to clean and safe water,” Manuel said.

Pamela Cajilig, a Philippines-based disaster anthropologist and a fellow of the Atlantic Institute, said the government’s stopgap measures had fuelled distrust as they were seen as transferring responsibility for dealing with extreme weather to ordinary Filipinos.

While Filipinos should do their part, the government’s overemphasis on household measures without implementing a systematic national disaster plan appeared to show its preference for “romanticising resilience”, Cajilig said.

“There is also the practical question of how these filtration devices will work on a mass scale and for a prolonged period. A quick demo for the press does little to help us imagine actual scenarios,” she added.

Keith Paolo Landicho, a research associate of S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ humanitarian help and disaster relief programme, said Filipinos should be told how they would be protected by the state instead of being given another reminder on how to cope with the next disaster.

“Filipinos are tired of their resilience being celebrated while the systems that leave them exposed remain unfixed. Being told to collect rainwater in buckets is not a sustainable solution; it is a stopgap dressed up as preparedness,” Landicho said.

Compared with its neighbours, the Philippines appears to be lagging in preparation ahead of natural disasters, according to analysts.

Valenzuela cited Vietnam, which invested in infrastructure projects such as irrigation systems and sluice gates to regulate water flows from the Mekong River following the 2015–16 El Nino event.

Across the region, countries have been preparing for this season’s El Nino, such as Thailand’s enhancement of its climate databases and Indonesia’s establishment of a drought emergency mechanism in several districts, according to media reports.

The Philippine government’s move to limit Metro Manila’s water supply was a clear sign that it had planned poorly to deal with El Nino’s effects, Valenzuela said.

“We can’t even figure out how to put systems in place when it comes to decades of planning to prevent another major disaster that could happen in 10 or 20 years,” he added.

Landicho said, however, that the water supply situation in Metro Manila appeared to have improved compared with a few months ago, while the water levels in the nearby provinces of Bulacan and Pampanga had recovered from record lows in July.

Nonetheless, with the Philippine state weather bureau Pagasa having issued forecasts on El Nino as far back as March, the country was ill-prepared for “one of the most forecastable hazards”, Landicho added.

Cajilig said an El Nino-related disaster could ultimately have a devastating impact on the Philippines over the long term.

“Unlike rapid onset disasters in which we can immediately witness wide-scale loss of life, livelihood, and infrastructure, slow onset disasters like drought are less dramatic. Yet studies show that their economic impact can be greater across time – mostly because their effects go unaddressed and therefore linger,” she said.

Athea Penaloza, executive director of the Asia-Pacific Alliance for Disaster Management-Philippines, is concerned about a fall in food production and sustained price pressures faced by Filipinos as the agricultural sector could be the hardest hit if dry conditions were to persist, particularly in the first half of next year.

Calling on Manila to provide immediate support to agricultural communities, she said: “This is where the government needs to prepare more proactively. It is important to put concrete measures in place now to support farmers, protect agricultural production and minimise the impact on food security and the cost of living.”

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea’s cruise missile launches test regional defence as arms race intensifies
item.description:
North Korea’s apparent use of different launch methods to fire two types of cruise missiles from a tactical nuclear-capable submarine could complicate regional defence, while raising fresh questions about the operational readiness of its growing undersea arsenal, observers have said.

The North’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said on Thursday it had “test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles” off its eastern coast.

The tests “contributed to inspecting the regular mobilisation readiness of underwater combat systems and honing the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions”, KCNA said.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea’s apparent use of different launch methods to fire two types of cruise missiles from a tactical nuclear-capable submarine could complicate regional defence, while raising fresh questions about the operational readiness of its growing undersea arsenal, observers have said.

The North’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said on Thursday it had “test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles” off its eastern coast.

The tests “contributed to inspecting the regular mobilisation readiness of underwater combat systems and honing the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions”, KCNA said.

They also demonstrated “the high reliability, dependability and capabilities of the means of war deterrence”, it said, adding that the tests “had no negative impact whatsoever on the security of neighbouring countries”.

South Korea’s military did not publicly announce the launches, sparking speculation that it might have failed to detect them. The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said on Thursday, however, that it had tracked and monitored the launches throughout.

The JCS stressed that the military did not usually disclose North Korean cruise missile launches, limiting public announcements primarily to ballistic missile tests.

Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said the projectiles were believed to include the Pulhwasal-3-31 (Fire Arrow Type 3-31), a strategic cruise missile with a potential range of about 2,000km that could carry small nuclear warheads.

“Their low-altitude, evasive flight profiles could complicate and potentially overwhelm South Korea’s and the United States’ missile defence systems,” Yang said.

The report appeared on KCNA but was not carried by the ruling Workers’ Party’s official newspaper, Rodong Sinmun, which primarily targets a domestic audience.

In a brief report comprising just four sentences, KCNA withheld technical specifications, including the missiles’ flight duration and range, unlike previous reports that publicised test results in extensive detail.

The agency, however, released several photographs showing the submarine under way, missiles emerging from the water in bursts of flame and the projectiles in cruise flight.

Experts analysing the images identified the launch platform as the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a new 3,000-tonne-class submarine.

The launches marked the vessel’s first publicly reported operation since it was unveiled in September 2023, as well as the third known test of submarine-launched cruise missiles (SLCMs) since March 2023, analysts said.

Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said the missiles appeared to have been launched using both vertical launch systems and torpedo tubes.

“Wednesday’s launches indicate that these missiles are being prepared for operational deployment,” Shin said. “Further test launches of submarine-launched ballistic missiles [SLBMs] are also expected.”

Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said the simultaneous launch of two missile types with different diameters, lengths and launch methods from a submarine of the Hero Kim Kun Ok class was “unprecedented”.

North Korea appeared to be combining two launch methods – vertical launch systems and torpedo tubes – Hong said, pointing to two distinct launch profiles in the released photographs.

One showed a near-vertical ascent, while the other appeared to involve a launch at an angle of about 60 degrees to 70 degrees, accompanied by falling debris.

The combination of different missile types and launch methods would make it harder for adversaries to predict which missile might be fired from which launch tube, he said.

“By extending from land to the maritime domain its demonstrated ability to deploy multiple types of warheads, North Korea is seeking to increase uncertainty for potential adversaries and strengthen its deterrence,” Hong said.

The latest tests followed the first known SLCM test in March 2023, when North Korea launched cruise missiles from the ageing 8.24 Yongung (Hero) submarine.

The North described the latest launches not as development tests but as a “routine inspection of the mobilisation readiness” of its deployed forces, suggesting that it wanted to portray the weapons as approaching operational service.

Under a strategy combining lower-cost military assets with higher-end weapons, nuclear-powered submarines under construction would serve as more sophisticated platforms, while ageing but modified Romeo-class submarines could provide a larger number of relatively inexpensive assets, Hong said.

The Hero Kim Kun Ok appeared designed to be not merely an interim substitute until North Korea completed a nuclear-powered submarine programme, but also a tactical nuclear platform for coastal and near-seas operations that could remain in service even after nuclear-powered submarines became available, he said.

Hong, however, cautioned against overstating the submarine’s capabilities.

“Its operational capabilities remain unproven in several key areas, including submerged launches, extended-duration patrols and the deployment of SLBMs. Its current level of combat readiness is therefore best assessed as limited operational capability,” he said.

Thursday’s tests were the latest in a series of North Korean missile launches this month, amid an intensifying arms race with South Korea, which successfully conducted the first test launch of its domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle a week earlier.

Yang said the latest launches were part of Pyongyang’s efforts to showcase the diversity of its missile arsenal, including short-range ballistic missiles, hypersonic weapons and submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles.

“North Korea is signalling its ability to complicate or neutralise the South Korea-US missile defence network,” he said.

The tests come ahead of a planned Asia trip by US President Donald Trump, fuelling speculation about a possible resumption of diplomacy between Washington and Pyongyang.

Trump said on Monday that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during his coming trip to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

Asked whether he planned to meet Kim during the trip, Trump replied, “I may,” adding: “That’ll be exciting, won’t it? But I get along with him.”

The two leaders met three times during Trump’s first term: in Singapore in June 2018, in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019.

On Saturday, Trump told a campaign rally in Ohio that he “gets along great” with Kim, stressing the importance of maintaining good relations with leaders of nuclear-armed countries.

The latest launches could be intended in part to strengthen Pyongyang’s leverage ahead of a potential meeting, Yang said.

“The series of missile launches in October appears to be aimed at pressing Washington to recognise North Korea as a nuclear-armed state” ahead of a possible Trump-Kim meeting.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Nepal’s unending cycle of avalanches, floods and landslides
item.description:
Nepal has weathered three disasters in six weeks, including the deadly August flash flood, making this year one of the deadliest in a country where monsoon rains already frequently wreak havoc. Experts warn that climate change is only making matters worse.

The rock-ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border that opened the floodgates in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 killed more than 1,450 people, with nearly 6,000 others still missing. It was followed by a massive landslide after parts of a mountain collapsed into a river in the Mustang region in late September.

And on Sunday, another rock-ice avalanche flooded the Budhi Gandaki River – which joins the Trishuli downstream – in central Nepal’s Gorkha district, with concrete-like slush swallowing houses, bridges and trekking trails, though no casualties were reported.
item.content:encoded:
Nepal has weathered three disasters in six weeks, including the deadly August flash flood, making this year one of the deadliest in a country where monsoon rains already frequently wreak havoc. Experts warn that climate change is only making matters worse.

The rock-ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border that opened the floodgates in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 killed more than 1,450 people, with nearly 6,000 others still missing. It was followed by a massive landslide after parts of a mountain collapsed into a river in the Mustang region in late September.

And on Sunday, another rock-ice avalanche flooded the Budhi Gandaki River – which joins the Trishuli downstream – in central Nepal’s Gorkha district, with concrete-like slush swallowing houses, bridges and trekking trails, though no casualties were reported.

“To have two similar events, nearby and in one year, is unprecedented in Nepal,” said John Pomeroy, director of the Centre for Hydrology at Canada’s University of Saskatchewan, who has been following the events.

“While climate change did not directly trigger these catastrophes, the thawing of frozen ground, melt of glaciers, increased lubrication of frozen materials from rapid snowmelt and rainfall all destabilised the high mountains and created the preconditions that permitted these events to form.”

Nepal’s cycle of disasters – evoking scenes from Hollywood doomsday films – made global headlines this year, but the same places have experienced recurring floods and landslides over the years.

Before the August floods, the border area in Rasuwa was washed away in July 2025 after a superglacial lake burst, killing at least nine people. Chame in the north-central district of Manang experienced similar floods and landslides last month and in 2021, and such events have become cyclical in Mustang and Humla districts, both near the Tibetan border.

Sudan Bikash Maharjan, a geologist at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, said his team’s analysis showed that only 11 glacial lake flood outbursts (GLOFs) were recorded in the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins between 2010 and 2019. However, seven such incidents occurred in the 2020-2025 period, suggesting there will be more in the coming years.

“The patterns are different, but the cascading effects are making these disasters bigger,” he said. “Such events are increasing compared to before, and this could be an annual occurrence.”

Global warning

What is happening in Nepal is a warning to the world, as mountain rainfall occurs more frequently and intensely, according to climate scientists.

Pomeroy said disasters due to thawing frozen ground, rapid snowmelt and glacier melt were increasing in mountain regions worldwide.

He added that countries such as the United States, Switzerland and Canada were seeing related problems, prompting them to develop advanced early warning and hydrological forecasting systems, while GLOFs were occurring more frequently in Nepal, India, China, Central Asia and the Andean nations.

“It’s a problem that is spreading globally,” he said. “High mountain regions are often impoverished, poorly serviced by infrastructure, populated by indigenous peoples, bisected by international boundaries, sparsely gauged and monitored, and far away from decision-making centres. This makes them particularly vulnerable to disasters such as those that have befallen Nepal in recent months.”

Global events from the past five years alone make the case clear.

A massive flood in Chamoli in India’s Uttarakhand state, triggered by a rock-ice avalanche, killed more than 70 people in February 2021. Over 55 died two years later in “one of the most catastrophic GLOFs to hit the Himalayas” in India’s Sikkim state, while a glacier collapse flattened the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025.

In Argentina’s El Chalten village, scientists and officials are also watching Nepal’s disasters closely, knowing their mountainous region could face a similar catastrophe. An El Chalten official told The Guardian they were “preparing for the worst-case scenario”.

“The disasters we are experiencing in the Himalayas should be an important exercise in learning and warning,” Maharjan said. “We cannot exactly say when or where they might occur, but they will happen.”

Environment vs economy

Decades of fossil fuel use and human activities have driven greenhouse gas emissions, pushing global temperature to around 1.4 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. And countries like Nepal, with negligible emissions, are paying the price.

Losses from the August disaster exceed 408.28 billion rupees (US$2.66 billion). While the new government formed after last year’s youth uprising promised 7 per cent economic growth in the next five years, the World Bank projects growth will slow to 3.7 per cent next year.

Arpita Nepal, an economist and director of research and development at Kathmandu’s Samriddhi Foundation think tank, said disasters affected Nepal’s major growth sectors, including energy, tourism and agriculture, and could dent people’s confidence in reinvesting in disaster-prone areas in the long run, creating endemic poverty cycles in those places.

“Nepal’s public debt is 45.1 per cent of its GDP, and the current fiscal deficit level is 1.7 per cent of GDP – this implies that we do have fiscal space at the moment to invest in recovery and reconstruction,” she said.

“As the number of disasters climbs, our fiscal space to react will contract. However, post-2015 earthquake recovery shows that recovery from a natural disaster is possible and growth can pick up.”

But for that, analysts say Nepal should prioritise an ecologically friendly growth model and uphold environmental impact assessments for infrastructure projects, which critics say are largely ignored. The recent disasters have also put a spotlight on the country’s hydropower building spree – a dozen were destroyed in the August flood – largely built on mountainsides to harness electricity from rapid river currents.

Sanjaya Devkota, a geoscientist and civil engineer currently heading the Forum for Energy and Environment Development at the Institute of Himalayan Risk Reduction, said Nepal should rethink its development model.

He said planning should protect floodplains and natural drainages, establish setbacks based on local hazard assessments, and consider how roads, bridges, embankments, settlements and hydropower projects interacted.

“The policy contradiction is that we depend on rivers for energy, agriculture and livelihoods while sometimes allowing development that constricts their space or increases exposure along their banks,” Devkota said.

“We should be honest about whether Nepal has fully applied its own lessons. Producing a report after a disaster is useful, but learning becomes meaningful when it changes a road alignment, a construction approval, a warning procedure or a budget before the next event.”

While experts call for stronger mitigation measures and the government plans reconstruction, survivors in flood-ravaged Trishuli are left staring at the mounds of mud and debris where their homes once stood.

The heartbreak of losing loved ones has given way to fears of displacement and loss of livelihoods. Some are already considering going abroad for employment, a trend that has seen an exodus of young Nepalis, while others have little idea of what comes next.

“One really does not recover psychologically from natural disasters – it becomes a collective trauma that we carry,” Nepal said.

“Recovery requires demonstrable actions from the state to protect its citizens’ lives and property. [But] if we do not recover economically, then we will be brewing another revolution where citizens will keep looking for political actors who can deliver on their promises. This will make us more politically unstable in the long run.”

item.title: [SCMP] How a fuel crisis is threatening Bangladesh’s reform goals: ‘it hit our citizens hard’
item.description:
Faced with a fuel crisis beyond its control, Bangladesh’s government is spending the equivalent of hundreds of millions of US dollars each month to insulate its people from surging prices.

But as growth slows and inflation rises, the new government’s reform plans are being tested before it has had much time to clean up the country’s troubled financial institutions or retool its young, abundant – but underemployed – workforce for the AI era.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office on February 17, elected on promises of sweeping economic and social reforms to turn the country of 175 million people into a US$1 trillion economy within a decade.
item.content:encoded:
Faced with a fuel crisis beyond its control, Bangladesh’s government is spending the equivalent of hundreds of millions of US dollars each month to insulate its people from surging prices.

But as growth slows and inflation rises, the new government’s reform plans are being tested before it has had much time to clean up the country’s troubled financial institutions or retool its young, abundant – but underemployed – workforce for the AI era.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office on February 17, elected on promises of sweeping economic and social reforms to turn the country of 175 million people into a US$1 trillion economy within a decade.

An interim government had steered the nation through the treacherous months following former leader Sheikh Hasina’s downfall in 2024. She was ousted by a student-led revolt after what they called 15 years of repression, corruption and bad governance.

Her critics say those years saw cronies freely dip into state banks, stuffing them with bad loans and leaving the healthcare and education systems in tatters, all while filling the civil service with loyalists to her Awami League party rather than competent administrators.

But just 11 days after Rahman – a scion of a rival political clan to Hasina – was sworn in, the US and Israel attacked Iran, sending the price of oil and gas skyrocketing upwards.

In Bangladesh, which imported about 65 per cent of its energy needs last year, that has meant power cuts, long queues at petrol stations and rising costs for everything from transport to food.

“Energy is not just buying oil, gas or fertiliser,” Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, an adviser to Rahman, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the IMF–World Bank summit in Bangkok.

“It hit our citizens hard,” he said. “Our estimates are that from late February [to now] we have spent an estimated US$4.1 billion in additional costs.”

Some of the impact should have been cushioned by solar power, especially in a nation increasingly scorched by global warming.

But “the previous government didn’t build any sustainable energy security infrastructure”, Titumir said, part of a legacy of years of mismanagement and corruption.

The World Bank and Asian Development Bank have both provided hundreds of millions of US dollars in loans to help lighten the government’s energy cost burden.

The IMF, which has about US$1 trillion in loan capacity, has also dispersed nearly US$3.6 billion to Bangladesh since 2023 – a loan Rahman’s government is hoping to renegotiate this week in Bangkok.

But as the outside pressures build, the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday trimmed Bangladesh’s growth projection for 2027 to 3.2 per cent from 3.6 per cent this year, placing it behind Cambodia and climate-battered Nepal among developing Asian nations.

It also forecast inflation to nudge upwards to 10.9 per cent in 2027 from 8.7 per cent this year – although Bangladesh’s government said both projections had not fully taken into account the impact of its structural reforms of financial institutions, indebted businesses and a hollowed out welfare state.

“Unfortunately the people are suffering for the misdeeds of the previous regime,” Titumir said. “We have already brought five banks to be owned by the government … after fears there will be a bank run, that has now calmed. We want to bring discipline into the system [and] then provide finance for investment, finance for expansion.”

He said future growth would sprout from foreign investment into new manufacturing – including electronics and toys – infrastructure, solar power, deep-sea ports and new special economic zones, including the US$1.3 billion China-backed zone in Anwara, southern Bangladesh.

Bangladesh also has a young population, deep experience in manufacturing – including in its key garment industry – and a rich seam of cheap workers available to be tapped by firms looking to relocate from Southeast Asia, where costs are rising.

But questions remain over how Bangladesh will equip itself with the energy, skills and infrastructure needed to capitalise on the AI revolution that now undergirds much of global growth.

The IMF’s message in Bangkok this week pointed to a two-speed world economy: one weighed down by sky-high energy prices and another propelled by the trillions of dollars invested into AI and its spin-off industries, from data centres to semiconductors and printed circuit boards.

“Who is taking the biggest hit? Low-income countries. Especially those who are energy importers or left out from technology boom,” IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.

She hailed Asia as “the engine of global growth” but warned nations hit by the energy crisis to run a tight ship, despite the political temptations to roll out sweeping subsidies.

“First protect your buffers, protect your fiscal space,” she said, advising governments to give out “temporary and targeted support to the most vulnerable”.

Bangladesh, South Asia’s second-largest economy, is now at a turning point.

Rahman’s Bangladesh National Party government swept to power with a two-thirds majority in February’s election on a platform of reform, but it now faces a populace anxious for immediate change after the toxic Hasina era.

His family has traded power with Hasina’s clan for much of the South Asian nation’s short but turbulent history.

The 57-year-old returned from years in self-exile in London to successfully contest this year’s election, following a transition period overseen by an interim government, led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, which navigated the chaotic and violent aftermath of Hasina’s ousting by student protesters.

“We have delivered in the past,’’ added Titumir, the prime minister’s adviser on finance and planning, noting that Rahman’s “political approval” had handed his administration a clear mandate for reform.

Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia, served three terms as prime minister between 1991 and 2006. She was detained several times for her political activism during a decades-long power struggle with Hasina – the daughter of independence icon Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

Zia died last year. Her husband, the former army commander and war hero Ziaur Rahman, was assassinated in 1981 after leading the country for five years.

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to Guangdong, exploring the rich tapestry of Cantonese culinary traditions
item.description:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.
item.content:encoded:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.

From Guangdong’s northern coast, the traditional Chiu Chow or Chaoshan dish of poached saltwater chicken sees the meat steeped in a heavily seasoned salt brine or master stock, cooled and served at room temperature with a pounded garlic vinegar dip.

Hakka culinary heritage, founded in the hills of the province’s interior, takes an entirely different approach, wrapping the chicken tightly in paper and burying it completely in a pot of blazing hot, coarse sea salt.

Four distinct takes, four very different culinary approaches. Yet all of these dishes developed in the historic Guangdong province, an area roughly a third the size of France or Spain. Despite their common origin, should these different culinary traditions all be considered Cantonese?

Yes and no, says Silas Li, chef at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983. “I look at this almost like a family tree,” he says. “Technically, they represent distinct cultural traditions, but practically – and especially here in Hong Kong – they live under the same big roof.”

Historically, geography is a key determinant of a cuisine’s evolution. Li calls it the “true mother of recipe development”.

Shunde, sitting within the fertile Pearl River Delta surrounded by streams and fish ponds, supported a cuisine based on freshwater fish, mud carp, milk-yielding water buffalo, and tender river vegetables. For Li, this is the “cradle of classical Cantonese cooking”, the place where the region’s core standards for knife skills, slow-braising, seafood precision, and controlling the wok were established.

Elsewhere, along Guangdong’s Chaoshan coast, Chiu Chow communities had direct access to the ocean, inspiring a cuisine centred on deep-sea catches, saltwater poaching, and marine preserves, such as home-made fish sauces.

Hakka communities, however, were historically migratory and lived up in landlocked, rugged hills that offered no easy access to the coast or rivers. Consequently, they relied on calorie-dense pork, preserved salted vegetables and heavy salt-baking.

In Hong Kong, however, the different traditions have lived together for so long that the lines have naturally blurred.

“For me, Shun Tak is Cantonese core, while Chiu Chow and Hakka are sibling traditions that make our local food scene so much richer,” says Li, who draws inspiration for modern and classic dishes from all three culinary traditions at his restaurant in Happy Valley.

Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing from Puning in Chaoshan is behind Shanghai’s two-Michelin-starred Amazing Chinese Cuisine and Selection by Du.

Du says he prefers not to view the question of whether Chiu Chow is part of Cantonese cuisine as a “battle over belonging”. Instead, he casts a wider, more inclusive net, thinking of both traditions as integral parts of the cuisine of Lingnan, a geographical area below the Nanling mountains that encompasses Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Hong Kong, Macau and northern Vietnam, once occupied by the ancient Baiyue people.

“From the perspective of Chinese culinary culture, Lingnan cuisine has always been a rich and open system. Cantonese (Guangfu), Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines together form the essential components of Lingnan culinary culture,” he says.

Cantonese and Chiu Chow cooking both place great emphasis on seasonality, ingredient quality, natural flavours and a high level of craftsmanship. But for Du, the main defining feature of Chiu Chow cuisine is not a specific classic dish or set of dishes, but an obsessive pursuit of xian, or freshness/umami.

“This freshness is not just about flavour, but an overall respect for seasonality, origin, firepower, knife skills, and the state of the ingredients. People in Chaoshan often talk about ‘eating fresh’ (shi xian), which means savouring the best possible state of today, this season and this exact moment,” he says.

If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience

Silas Li, Hong Kong Cuisine 1983

Chef Huang Jinghui, better known as Chef Fei, was born and raised in Chaoshan. He runs a small empire of celebrated restaurants, all of which specialise in Cantonese and Chiu Chow dishes.

Chef Fei also highlights how porous boundaries between culinary traditions can be. “I see Chiu Chow cuisine and Cantonese cuisine as deeply interconnected culinary traditions, rather than two that need to be clearly separated,” he says.

He points to the considerable overlap in ingredients, techniques and culinary traditions – from delicacies such as abalone, sea cucumber and fish maw to Chiu Chow-style braised dishes, Cantonese barbecue and traditional slow-cooked soups, each with its own expression across the two cuisines.

However, he says that at the same time, Chiu Chow cuisine has its own distinctive regional character and culinary traditions.

“For me, rather than focusing too much on how Chiu Chow cuisine should be categorised, what matters more is the flavour, craftsmanship and traditions it represents, and the richness and diversity it brings to the dining experience,” he says.

While Du and Chef Fei are less fussy about a fluid, inclusive view of Cantonese cooking, Li at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 argues that maintaining distinct categories remains essential for the dining experience itself.

“If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience,” he says. “If we just call it generic Chinese food, it dilutes the respect these ancient subcultures deserve.”

While he finds diners from the communities whose cuisine he cooks to be his toughest critics, Li notes that the average local guest has become far more sophisticated.

“The modern Hong Kong diner – and even international guests – is way more educated now,” Li says. “They aren’t just looking for a vague ‘Chinese meal’; they want provenance, they ask about techniques, and they appreciate the subtle regional nuances.”

At Yan Garden in Beijing – a restaurant conceptualised by Chef Fei and led day-to-day by executive Chinese chef Peter Chen at the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen – Chen sees this curiosity playing out among broader audiences. He notes that around 10 to 15 per cent of guests are international, while the remainder are local Chinese consumers, with the dining experience itself serving as an educational bridge.

“Dishes such as our traditional marinated specialities, seafood preparations and seasonal Chiu Chow delicacies often spark conversations about the cuisine’s heritage and techniques,” Chen says.

Du observes a similar dynamic at Selection by Du in Shanghai. “Guests from Europe and the Americas tend to view us as ‘Chinese cuisine’, hoping to discover Chinese food through this meal,” he says. “Guests from Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau – owing to the deep Chiu Chow or Nanyang cultural roots in their home regions – more easily recognise the delicate nature and emphasis on original flavours in Chiu Chow cuisine.”

This evolving awareness reflects a broader transformation across Chinese gastronomy. Over the last 10 years, Du notes that diners’ knowledge has expanded rapidly, moving regional cooking into a dynamic new phase.

“More regional cuisines are establishing their own brand identities – Yunnan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Taizhou, Shunde and Zhejiang cuisines are all receiving increasing attention,” he says. “This does not mean Cantonese cuisine’s influence is waning, but rather that Chinese dining as a whole is becoming richer and more specialised.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
item.description:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.
item.content:encoded:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.

Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation.

South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator.

Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted.

“The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia.

The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.

A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government.

From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.

To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content.

Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.

“Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them.

South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy.

But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide.

Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures.

Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement.

“As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models.

In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown.

Brewing with bots

At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition.

What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business.

“It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers.

Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors.

He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots.

“The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings.

“With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.”

Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools.

“People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said.

That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot.

“That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.”

Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees.

Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important.

“My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.”

No juniors needed?

Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming.

And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade.

This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest.

At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year.

Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum.

“Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension.

The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29.

Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management.

“I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?”

Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University.

“When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said.

“But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.”

New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”.

Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way.

“Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.”

Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology.

“In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said.

“Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.”

AI-fuelled abuse

South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse.

The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024.

Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty.

Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.

In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial.

The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools.

Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.

“Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.”

Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI.

“Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”.

“We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.”

To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution.

“Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school.

Generation chatbot

Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper.

“In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said.

Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks.

“Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province.

While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song.

“It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot.

“I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.”

The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month.

“Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.”

The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic.

“Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.”

Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments.

“Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.”

This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] Emboldened by hybrid car deal, Europe coalesces around tougher China stance
item.description:
