The EU’s surprise deal with China on hybrid cars last week was supposed to ease the pressure on Beijing. Instead, Brussels is preparing to intensify its crackdown on Chinese trade practices, emboldened by the discovery that its threats are finally delivering results.

Now, those driving trade policy for the bloc believe they have landed on a two-track formula. Intensive dialogue is seen to have yielded results and will continue.

But so too will the European Union’s efforts to counter what they see as distortive policies in China. There is a clear sense that Beijing responded positively to a threat from the two biggest EU members, France and Germany, last week to quickly close the market to Chinese firms.
item.content:encoded:
The EU’s surprise deal with China on hybrid cars last week was supposed to ease the pressure on Beijing. Instead, Brussels is preparing to intensify its crackdown on Chinese trade practices, emboldened by the discovery that its threats are finally delivering results.

Now, those driving trade policy for the bloc believe they have landed on a two-track formula. Intensive dialogue is seen to have yielded results and will continue.

But so too will the European Union’s efforts to counter what they see as distortive policies in China. There is a clear sense that Beijing responded positively to a threat from the two biggest EU members, France and Germany, last week to quickly close the market to Chinese firms.

It represented a dramatic pivot from Berlin – by far China’s biggest trade partner in Europe – which has previously opposed assertive measures.

In meetings with businesses, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao was said to have been struck by the shift. He noted, sources said, the potential for a political backlash in Europe if Beijing did not check its exports in important sectors, which they believe helped pave the way for a deal.

“Why is China agreeing to something they’ve never agreed to before? We put that question to [EU Trade Commissioner] Maros Sefcovic and he said: ‘They start to realise that they are killing their customers’,” said a senior EU diplomat who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.

Buoyed by convincing China to accept an agreement that will limit its hybrid car exports to the EU at 350,000 a year – less than half the forecast volume for 2026 – Brussels is now revving the engines and ready to accelerate on a raft of unilateral actions.

“It goes hand in hand – in order to have a credible dialogue, we are seen to have instruments that allow us to take action when needed,” said a second diplomat.

A spate of safeguard investigations is expected soon in sectors ranging from pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery. They are likely to use tariffs and quotas to restrict Chinese access to industries in which they are dominant, much like the hybrid car arrangement, but are seen as a stopgap while officials come up with new tools.

Before Christmas, the union’s top brass want to present a series of new weapons that will help them reduce dependencies on China and compensate those hit by Beijing’s retaliation.

The cherry on top for Brussels would be a tool to close the EU market to Chinese companies should the government there take coercive actions in response. There are questions about whether such a complicated instrument could be ready by December, but a varied range of member states are now lining up behind the concept, first proposed in the Franco-German paper last week.

“We see on export moderation that China agrees to the fact that there is a problem, that something needs to be done in terms of rebalancing, and that is of course a conversation that we will continue,” said Tomas Baert, a trade adviser to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, at an event in Brussels on Wednesday.

“But that alone will not solve the structural imbalances. I think one sectoral solution is probably not enough to deal with the structural issue that we have, and that is where leaders tomorrow will actually take stock and see what more we need to do,” said Baert, referring to Thursday’s European Council summit, where the China policy will be discussed.

It would be a stretch to say that Europe is speaking with one voice on China, but in the run-up to Thursday’s meeting, there are notably fewer discordant notes in the choir.

“The French-German paper is helpful that it has shown the Chinese that we are quite united. I mean, if you bring together Germany on the one hand and France on the other, and it kind of I think gave also a boost of credibility to the EU,” another diplomat said.

Talks with China are continuing at working level, with the EU’s top trade enforcer Denis Redonnet travelling to China for talks on medical devices in the next weeks. Sefcovic will speak with counterpart Wang in January by videoconference before another meeting in March.

But the commission’s trade bureaucrats will continue developing sharper tools in the background, despite warnings from Beijing that it will retaliate against any deviation from the cooperative agenda.

“You always have to be ready for escalation, but we shouldn’t let ourselves be led by fear,” said a third senior diplomat, who added that capitals remained galvanised by the task of tackling what is described as the China Shock 2.0.

“I don’t think there are many member states on the table who see this hybrid deal and now it’s done. We’re chipping away and it’s not something you can do in one go. So more should follow,” they said.

At the heart of the energy is a fear that if Europe does not move yet to protect its industries from high quality yet cheaper Chinese competition, there will be nothing left to shield.

In Berlin, too, the success of the far-right party Alternative for Germany in recent state elections sparked fears that if mainstream parties do not do something about it, then populists will.

The urgency was made plain in China’s trade data for September, published on Wednesday, which showed that last month alone, China’s trade surplus with Germany rose by 201.7 per cent compared to September 2025. For France, the gap expanded by 251.8 per cent, while for the whole EU it was up 52.3 per cent.

“If current trends continue or accelerate, large parts of Europe’s industrial base are at risk and China’s supply chain dominance will continue to increase. That could undermine Europe’s prosperity, its social model and its ability to act geopolitically,” wrote Etienne Hora, a specialist in geoeconomics at Bertelsmann Stiftung, a German think tank.

In a sign that the EU’s 27 members are coalescing around a hardline China strategy, a draft statement for the European Council summit was updated on Wednesday to demand the commission “urgently enhance the EU toolbox with new instruments to better address these imbalances”.

The change was subtle, but significant by the careful standards of the EU – which remains reluctant to directly name China as it seeks to maintain some diplomatic decorum. It reflected, almost verbatim, oral conclusions communicated after the last summit in June, which were not made public.

The shift on China – also breakneck compared to the glacial pace at which Brussels ordinarily moves – even caught EU trading partners by surprise. Both parties to the deal insisted that the quotas on hybrid vehicles should apply to all other countries, otherwise they would breach World Trade Organization rules.

“China’s quota will not be lower than that of any other import source for the EU,” read a Chinese commerce ministry statement.

This appeared to be news, however, to Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bulat, who met Sefcovic in Brussels on Tuesday. Asked after the meeting by the South China Morning Post what sort of quota his country – a major automotive hub – has been allocated for hybrid car exports, Bulat claimed it would not apply because Ankara has a customs union with the EU.

“Therefore, it has nothing to do with the EU’s new deal with another country,” he said.

The European Commission did not immediately respond to a request to clarify whether Bulat was correct, but trade experts agreed that his remarks were likely wide of the mark – a sign, perhaps, that Brussels’ new trade policy is moving so quickly that even some of its closest partners are struggling to keep up.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea’s offender tracking under scrutiny after stabbing spree exposes ‘serious gaps’
item.description:
A stabbing rampage by a repeat violent offender wearing an electronic ankle monitor has raised questions about whether South Korea’s system can adequately supervise those deemed high-risk and prevent attacks before they happen.

The 59-year-old suspect told investigators he had become frustrated over what he perceived as mistreatment at a hospital, police said on Wednesday.

Three criminal profilers were helping investigators establish the motive for Tuesday’s attack at a shopping centre in Incheon, which left 10 people injured, including a woman in her 20s who remained in a coma.
item.content:encoded:
A stabbing rampage by a repeat violent offender wearing an electronic ankle monitor has raised questions about whether South Korea’s system can adequately supervise those deemed high-risk and prevent attacks before they happen.

The 59-year-old suspect told investigators he had become frustrated over what he perceived as mistreatment at a hospital, police said on Wednesday.

Three criminal profilers were helping investigators establish the motive for Tuesday’s attack at a shopping centre in Incheon, which left 10 people injured, including a woman in her 20s who remained in a coma.

“I did not target any specific person, and I chose people who looked weaker than me, but I had no intention to kill,” the suspect was quoted as saying during questioning at Namdong Police Station in Incheon.

He wielded knives tied to both hands as he moved between floors via an escalator before shoppers managed to subdue him by throwing chairs at him.

“He swung the knives at everyone he saw. People fled in panic. Most people were stabbed in their backs,” said an employee who was working on the shopping centre’s first floor.

Another witness said: “He went after anyone he encountered. He just kept swinging his knives without saying a word.”

Police said the suspect was carrying what appeared to be prescription psychiatric medication in his backpack but tested negative in a preliminary drug screening.

According to police, he had been receiving treatment for athlete’s foot at a local hospital but was dissatisfied that his symptoms had not improved.

In August, he began staging a one-man protest outside the hospital while holding a knife, prompting the facility to report him to police. He was subsequently indicted last month.

“I was unhappy because I was investigated by police after the hospital reported me,” he was quoted as telling investigators.

President Lee Jae Myung visited the Incheon Metropolitan Police Agency and called for effective measures to prevent similar incidents from recurring.

The justice ministry apologised and pledged a thorough investigation and a review of the country’s electronic monitoring system after the suspect was identified as a repeat violent offender wearing an electronic anklet.

“We will conduct a comprehensive review of the electronic monitoring framework and the system for supervising and guiding offenders, and promptly prepare measures to address any gaps,” the ministry said in a statement.

“We will focus all our capabilities on preventing similar incidents from recurring, placing the lives and safety of the public as our top priority.”

Safety shortcomings

Lee Dong-gyu, a professor in the department of disaster and emergency management at Dong-A University, said the attack had exposed serious shortcomings in the surveillance and management of dangerous offenders.

“This incident has laid bare the serious gaps in monitoring and controlling high-risk offenders,” he said.

At the centre of the system is an electronic ankle tag that certain high-risk offenders are required to wear under court orders.

The device continuously transmits location data through cellular networks to monitoring centres, allowing authorities to track an offender’s movements around the clock.

If the wearer enters a restricted area or leaves a designated zone, the system alerts monitoring authorities at the justice ministry.

However, Lee Dong-gyu said the ministry lacked sufficient personnel to monitor offenders’ movements and coordinate with police officers on the ground to intervene when necessary.

He also suggested that the government upgrade the electronic monitoring devices so they could detect changes in physiological signals, such as an elevated heart rate potentially associated with alcohol consumption, and alert authorities to possible risks.

The system’s limitations have been highlighted in previous cases.

In 2025, police remained unaware for six days that a convicted sex offender, Cho Doo-soon, had tampered with electronic monitoring equipment installed at his residence.

Cho repeatedly violated restrictions on leaving his home despite being under close supervision after his release in 2020.

He had served a 12-year prison sentence for raping an eight-year-old girl and inflicting injuries that required prolonged medical treatment.

“The government should have learned from the Cho Doo-soon case and bolstered its manpower and equipment to prevent similar incidents,” Lee Dong-gyu said.

Justice ministry statistics show that repeat sexual offences by people wearing electronic monitoring anklets continue to occur, averaging about two cases a month.

According to data the ministry submitted on Wednesday to Park Jie-won, a lawmaker from the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, 106 repeat sexual offences were committed by individuals under electronic monitoring between January 2022 and August 2026, an average of 1.9 cases a month.

During the same period, there were two repeat murder offences and two repeat robbery offences under electronic monitoring, the data showed.

Violations of court-imposed restrictions have also increased. The number of breaches of restrictions on leaving home rose by 26 per cent, from 759 in 2024 to 956 in 2025.

Between January 2022 and August 2026, authorities recorded 4,552 violations of restrictions on leaving offenders’ residences, equivalent to roughly two to three incidents a day.

The same period also saw 41 violations of no-contact orders protecting victims and 31 cases of tampering with electronic monitoring devices.

Analysts attribute the trend in part to a decline in field supervision personnel despite an increase in the number of offenders subject to electronic monitoring.

The number of people under electronic monitoring rose by 23 per cent, from 4,316 in 2022 to 5,301 in August this year.

By contrast, the number of staff directly responsible for supervising and managing these individuals in the field fell by 21 per cent, from 255 to 234.

As a result, the average caseload per supervisor increased from 17.1 offenders to 20.3.

Lee Do-sun, a professor of police science at Hannam University, said the government needed to urgently increase staffing for efforts to prevent repeat offending.

“There are manpower shortages both at the ministry tasked with monitoring dangerous repeat offenders and among police officers on the ground who should act quickly to bring offenders under control,” he said.

He called for an integrated system through which government agencies and police could share real-time information about high-risk offenders, citing the United Kingdom as a potential model.

“Electronic tags only reveal where the wearers are, but through these devices, you never know how dangerous they are or what their propensity for violence is,” he said.

South Korea also needed more specialists capable of assessing the risk of reoffending, including factors such as alcohol dependence, impaired impulse control, obsessive behaviour and other psychological problems, he said.

“With the current manpower, these tasks are almost impossible to carry out,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hegseth calls US$1.5 trillion defence budget ‘critical’ to counter China
item.description:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has called a nearly US$1.5 trillion defence budget request “absolutely critical”, warning that whoever falls behind in autonomy, robotics and AI will fall “even further behind” as Washington eyes China’s rapid military modernisation.

Speaking at a panel discussion during the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition on Wednesday, Hegseth said that Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate drone and autonomous warfare capabilities, is the “end state” of what the administration has focused on since “day one”.

Under the current US Department of Defence plan, announced by Hegseth on September 30 during his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Project Agincourt includes the creation of a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command by October 1, 2027, building on the Replicator initiative from the Joe Biden administration and the Drone Dominance Programme initiated in 2025.
item.content:encoded:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has called a nearly US$1.5 trillion defence budget request “absolutely critical”, warning that whoever falls behind in autonomy, robotics and AI will fall “even further behind” as Washington eyes China’s rapid military modernisation.

Speaking at a panel discussion during the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition on Wednesday, Hegseth said that Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate drone and autonomous warfare capabilities, is the “end state” of what the administration has focused on since “day one”.

Under the current US Department of Defence plan, announced by Hegseth on September 30 during his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Project Agincourt includes the creation of a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command by October 1, 2027, building on the Replicator initiative from the Joe Biden administration and the Drone Dominance Programme initiated in 2025.

Asked how significant the increase to nearly US$1.5 trillion in the defence budget is, Hegseth replied that it is “absolutely critical” and a “one-time generational investment” that gives Washington a chance to “fully rebuild” the military amid threats from adversaries.

“We’re in a different moment. We’ve got a near-peer adversary who’s building a military, the most historic military build-up potentially in world history,” said Hegseth, in a tacit reference to China’s recent military modernisation drive.

“That’s not hyperbole. That’s just objective truth. You add up the step changes in autonomy, in robotics, in space, AI, whoever’s ahead now is going to get much further ahead.

“Whoever’s behind now is going to fall even further behind. And so investments now are going to matter, and they’re going to ripple not just for years but for decades across our joint force.”

The rare panel discussion had Hegseth speaking alongside the civilian heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force – acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – as well as Derrick Anderson, assistant secretary of defence for special operations and low-intensity conflict.

The Pentagon has requested US$54.6 billion for the Defence Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG), established last year for coordinating, testing and integrating autonomous weapons across all military domains, for the financial year 2027 budget, an almost 24,000 per cent increase from US$225.9 million in the previous year.

According to the Department of Defence Fiscal Year 2027 Mandatory Budget Overview published in April, which explains the fiscal allocation of the Trump administration’s record-breaking US$1.5 trillion defence budget request, DAWG was allocated US$53.6 billion under the US$350 billion reconciliation package, leaving US$1 billion under the base request.

The budget included US$39.2 billion for a multi-year investment in autonomous systems procurement, domestic production capacity and advanced capabilities, and US$14.4 billion for counter-unmanned systems development and deployment.

The Trump administration has repeatedly used budget reconciliation to secure increases in defence spending. The process allows legislation to pass the Senate by a simple majority, bypassing the usual 60-vote threshold and reducing the need for Democratic support.

Hegseth defended the use of the process as a means to “supercharge” the architecture of Autonomous Warfare Command and “reestablish a deterrent to rebuild the military around the world” by acquiring “a million” drones.

China’s drone build-up has been one of the major drivers for the Trump administration to ramp up its autonomous systems acquisition. During the panel discussion, Meink referred to China as having “the largest weapons build-up probably in the history of the world,” resulting in Beijing “leveraging” over Washington, such as using low Earth orbit satellites to target US weapons systems.

“So the question is, what do we do about that? How do we degrade their systems? How do we make sure our systems are survivable no matter what domain we are in?” said Meink.

“And that’s what we’re working with entire joint forces to do. And the autonomous systems are going to be part of that.”

Under the 15th five-year plan released in March, covering the period from 2026 to 2030, China prioritised the People’s Liberation Army’s transition towards ‘intelligentised’ warfare, emphasising artificial intelligence, unmanned and autonomous systems, networked information infrastructure and emerging technologies.

A satellite imagery analysis also suggests that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stationed over 200 obsolete 1960s-era J-6 supersonic fighter jets – converted into attack and cruise-missile-like drones – across six airbases near the Taiwan Strait.

China is also known to be the world’s largest exporter of drones. According to a report by the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies, Chinese companies accounted for more than 80 per cent of global drone supplies.

Hegseth criticised the previous Biden administration for treating the world as “stagnant” and taking a “nap” on advanced military technologies such as hypersonics, space weaponisation and drones, even as adversaries like China were rapidly expanding their capabilities. He said the Trump administration was now working to regain its “competitive advantage”.

“Now we’re changing the cost paradigm for our adversaries on the battlefield, and they’re the ones having to understand how to deal defensively with our capabilities,” said Hegseth.

“The drones that this will require, all of those investments are part of reconciliation of that 350 [billion dollars] … The coming months will be critical, and it’s not hyperbolic to state whether or not we rebuild our military to meet the threats of the country will depend on funding the president’s vision for US$1.5 trillion, and our goal, come hell or high water.”

On the question of how he came up with the decision to establish a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command despite Congress’ call to reduce the number of general officers in the past 15 years, Hegseth said that it “completely meets the intent” as it requires sufficient authorities to “ensure we can drive change quickly”.

Hegseth said building up drone capabilities required more than training and cooperation with industry. It also meant getting the technology into the hands of frontline commanders, who could test it on the battlefield and learn how to “iterate it, change on it, innovate on it”.

item.title: [SCMP] Huang Qifan, China’s political tumbler, falls after a decade of close corruption calls
item.description:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.
item.content:encoded:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.

Bo and Sun were both members of the Politburo, the pinnacle of the party’s power, and their downfalls were two of the biggest political earthquakes the country has seen in recent decades. Yet Huang survived.

Huang, 74, was also very visible after he left public service in 2018. Rather than retreat to retired obscurity, Huang kept up a busy schedule of interviews and conferences across the country, firing hot takes on China’s economic issues.

So when news of the corruption investigation into Huang finally came on Tuesday, it was a surprise to many – not only because it involved one of China’s most celebrated economic technocrats, but also because it came so long after the political tremors around him appeared to have stopped.

“Subjecting someone like Huang, who had emerged from many previous rounds, to a formal corruption investigation, before the fifth plenum sends a very serious message to the whole party: corrupt officials should not harbour any illusions of escaping detection,” said a Beijing-based political scientist, who declined to be named due to sensitivity of the matter.

“There is no political ‘tumbler’ and no safe landing for corrupt officials in the anti-corruption fight.”

The fifth plenum is a party meeting scheduled for October 26-29 in Beijing at which the organisation’s inner circle will discuss and adopt a landmark document to “deepening party self-governance”.

The event is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, tightening internal political oversight, and eliminating organisational loopholes across the bureaucracy and state sectors.

While many anti-corruption investigations into retired senior officials go unnoticed and unannounced, Huang’s unusually heavy speaking schedule made his downfall difficult to hide from the public.

The South China Morning Post understands that Huang was originally scheduled to deliver a keynote speech in Beijing on October 25 and another in Hangzhou the next day.

Before Tuesday’s announcement, word got out that he would miss the Hangzhou event. An employee at AIA Group – the organiser of the October 25 speech in Beijing – said they had not been able to reach Huang or his secretary since Monday.

Huang’s reputation as a tumbler goes back to his relationship with Bo, the charismatic and swashbuckling Politburo member who ran Chongqing from 2007 to 2012.

As Bo rolled out his ideologically charged “singing red songs and smashing the dark forces” campaign, Huang was the administrative and economic brain behind the policies that became known as the “Chongqing model”.

The model combines state-led capitalism, aggressive public-welfare provision, and foreign direct investment with a populist revival of revolutionary Maoist culture and a heavy-handed public security crackdown.

Positioned as an alternative developmental path to China’s coastal, market-driven consensus, the model gained national and international attention as a potential blueprint for addressing rising wealth inequality, regional imbalances and social stratification.

The two men projected an image of an unshakeable governing duo. During the national parliamentary “two sessions” in Beijing in March 2010, Huang famously described his working relationship with Bo as “like a duck to water”. He was also a magnet for reporters at the annual meetings, readily answering questions about the economy and Chongqing.

That alliance faced a critical test in February 2012, when Bo’s estranged police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to the US consulate in Chengdu, triggering one of China’s biggest political scandals in decades.

Following the diplomatic stand-off, Bo was removed from the party’s leadership. He was later sentenced to life in prison on charges of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power.

The aftershocks hit many of Bo’s subordinates in Chongqing, as the municipality’s new leadership headed by caretaker party chief Zhang Dejiang, repeatedly pledged to “eradicate” Bo’s “toxic influence”. Despite the chaos, Huang remained in position.

In November 2012, Sun took over from Zhang, becoming Huang’s new partner and direct supervisor.

Like Bo before his fall, Sun was also seen as a political rising star. He relied on Huang to maintain the city’s administrative machinery and drive double-digit economic growth. Huang, it seemed, had weathered the Bo saga unaffected, and was among six regional officials to be part of President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States in 2015.

The political ground shook beneath Chongqing again in 2017, just months after Huang stepped down as the city’s mayor. Sun was rounded up in anti-corruption investigation during a trip to Beijing for a top-level meeting, and ultimately sentenced to life imprisonment on corruption charges.

The southwestern metropolis again pledged to clean up the negative influence of a disgraced party boss and again Huang appeared to sail through the controversy. Huang stayed on in his semi-retired role in the national legislature as vice-chairman of the National People’s Congress Financial and Economic Affairs Committee, finally stepping down in March 2018.

Even after his retirement, Huang, respected as a capable economic manager, remained an influential intellectual heavyweight. Affiliated with prestigious platforms including the China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, the China Finance 40 Forum and Fudan University, he had a towering media profile, offering perspectives on a wide range of economic issues.

In 2021, he warned that the business models of Chinese internet firms would no longer work in the coming decade, slamming them as “taking advantage of weaknesses in human nature to entice purchases”.

In 2022, Huang warned that China’s property market had reached a turning point, questioning whether the country could sustain its decades-long construction boom.

As recently as May this year, he described China’s record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 as “shocking”, urging Beijing to rebalance trade through a combination of gradual yuan appreciation, tariff cuts and improved benefits for workers.

He is known among various lecture organisers as exceptionally proactive and eager to take the podium, and is said to have told organisers that he is willing to talk on any issue.

He is also believed to be in good health for his age, with a fondness for steak and cigars.

His confidence was built on decades of economic policy experience.

Born in Zhuji in Zhejiang province in 1952, Huang rose through Shanghai’s industrial bureaucracy.

Entering the municipal party and government apparatus in 1983, he was deeply involved in the early development and opening of the Pudong New Area.

In October 2001, he was transferred to Chongqing as a vice-mayor, overseeing the city’s industrial policy, state-owned assets, taxation and financial sectors before becoming mayor in January 2010 – a post he held for nearly seven years.

Under his stewardship, Chongqing logged consecutive years of double-digit GDP growth, routinely outpacing the rest of the country.

Huang promoted the Chongqing-Xinjiang-Europe freight railway, and attracted Hewlett-Packard and Foxconn to build an electronics manufacturing hub in the city.

He also pioneered the municipal investment vehicle modelled on Singapore’s state fund Temasek and kept runaway property speculation in check through strict land-supply management and an expansive public rental housing programme.

Huang’s downfall follows a smaller earthquake in Chongqing. Since 2022, the anti-corruption drive has sped up, targeting more and more senior officials across the country.

Chongqing was hit hard, with seven other high-ranking provincial officials coming under investigation since then. The most senior of the seven was then-mayor Hu Henghua, who came under the microscope in March, triggering another shake-up across the administration.

The investigation into Huang comes less than two weeks before the party’s fifth plenum, which brings together the hundreds of full and alternate members of the Central Committee.

The Central Committee’s ranks have been thinned by the anti-corruption campaign, with 34 of its 205 full members under investigation or stripped of their status as deputies to the National People’s Congress.

The Beijing-based political scientist said Chongqing had been the epicentre of China’s most disruptive political tremors over the past two decades and the investigation of Huang nearly a decade after retirement showed Beijing’s resolve to clean up Chongqing’s factional legacy, allowing no perceived seniority to impede its continued organisational housecleaning.

Not all are that surprised by Huang’s fall.

His family’s commercial dealings cast a persistent shadow over his administration. In Chongqing, the extensive business footprint of his son was “an open secret” among political and business circles, according to sources familiar with the situation.

“Many in Chongqing’s government and financial circles know his son very well, as Huang Qifan is widely regarded as the ‘godfather’ of Chongqing’s state-driven financial vehicles, which can mobilise a lot of resources,” said a source who worked with Huang.

The source said the younger Huang quickly immersed himself in China’s capital market deals.

item.title: [SCMP] Cloudy outlook? How haze crisis is testing Singapore’s events economy
item.description:
When Daniela Cruz arrived in Singapore last week, hazy skies obscured the picture-perfect sights she had seen on social media, offering a different view of the city state from the one she had expected.

The 27-year-old bank associate had travelled from Australia for the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix, but the smoky weather dampened her experience. “The buildings we saw on social media were covered in haze, and it made conditions extremely hot and humid,” she said.

The haze blanketing Singapore’s skies over the three-day event raised fears of disruption. On Thursday, a day before racing began, motorsport governing body FIA said the conditions could potentially restrict entertainment acts and outdoor activities.
item.content:encoded:
When Daniela Cruz arrived in Singapore last week, hazy skies obscured the picture-perfect sights she had seen on social media, offering a different view of the city state from the one she had expected.

The 27-year-old bank associate had travelled from Australia for the Formula One Singapore Grand Prix, but the smoky weather dampened her experience. “The buildings we saw on social media were covered in haze, and it made conditions extremely hot and humid,” she said.

The haze blanketing Singapore’s skies over the three-day event raised fears of disruption. On Thursday, a day before racing began, motorsport governing body FIA said the conditions could potentially restrict entertainment acts and outdoor activities.

This was not the first time the marquee event had faced uncertainty due to haze. In 2015 and 2019, organisers introduced precautionary measures, including health advisories and the sale of N95 masks, while both editions of the night race proceeded without major disruption, as did last weekend’s event.

The poor weather did little to diminish the novelty of the night race, which drew a crowd of more than 300,000 this year.

But while Singapore managed to keep one of its flagship events running, the recurrence of haze could weaken the city state’s appeal as an international events hub, observers said. Smaller events have also faced cancellations as air quality deteriorated, with conditions showing little sign of improving.

The stakes are significant for a city that has invested heavily in attracting international visitors and major events.

From its debut in 2008 until 2024, the Singapore Grand Prix generated more than S$2.2 billion (US$1.72 billion) in incremental tourism receipts, with the figure for 2025 still being calculated, Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong said in February.

Singapore’s meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector is another important contributor to its visitor economy, with tourism receipts from the segment reaching S$2.3 billion last year, a 35 per cent increase from S$1.7 billion in 2024.

Dedicated sports fans were unlikely to be deterred from future editions of the Singapore Grand Prix, one of the most distinctive events on the F1 calendar, said Guy Llewellyn, an assistant professor at EHL Hospitality Business School.

“A single hazy weekend is unlikely to outweigh its unique atmosphere, entertainment line-up, and broader appeal as a destination,” he added.

But first-time and leisure travellers who viewed the event as part of a wider holiday experience could be discouraged from revisiting the night race and Singapore, Llewellyn said.

For Cruz, the smooth traffic flow and multitude of activities during the grand prix set a high bar for future races. But she gave the concerts, which featured American singer Lana Del Rey and Swedish pop star Zara Larsson, a miss to avoid having to walk long distances in the heat and haze.

“Regarding the haze, we can tolerate a level similar to the weekend’s, but a worse level would lead to us reconsidering visiting again.”

Foggy road ahead

In recent weeks, air quality in Singapore has deteriorated amid an increase in hotspots in neighbouring Indonesia and unfavourable weather, raising concerns over outdoor activities across the city state.

While the F1 race avoided disruption, some domestic events have been cancelled or suspended. The fate of coming activities remains uncertain as the government prepares contingency measures for worsening pollution.

Air quality in recent weeks has stayed primarily in the “unhealthy” range, with the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reading staying between 101 and 200. The city state recorded its highest reading this year of 192 on the opening day of the grand prix on Friday.

Singapore recorded its highest PM2.5 reading this year – which reflects the average concentration of fine particles in the air – on Wednesday, peaking at 288 in the western region.

As at 5pm on Wednesday, the PSI reading remained in the “unhealthy” range, rising to 175 in the west.

Some Singaporeans have chosen to stay indoors, with others donning masks outdoors.

Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Saturday said the government had contingency plans in place across different air quality levels, and would distribute masks to eligible Singaporeans, such as the elderly or those in lower-income brackets, when the PSI exceeded 200 – deemed to be in the “very unhealthy” range.

Several public sports centres shut their doors on Wednesday, and the city state’s health promotion agency, which organises workout sessions and nature walks, has cancelled all outdoor activities since Saturday.

A number of running events have been suspended in recent weeks, including a ticketed 5km run at Sentosa on Sunday.

In 2015, thick haze led to the cancellation of the first night of finals at the FINA World Cup. PSI levels entered the “hazardous” range of above 300 that year.

Organisers with events slated for October told This Week in Asia they were prepared to suspend activities if the situation worsened and would heed advisories and regulations set out by authorities.

The National Environment Agency advises the public to avoid prolonged strenuous outdoor physical activities if air quality is in the “very unhealthy” range, while those with lung conditions are asked to refrain from being outdoors altogether.

Singapore’s sports agency advises organisers to consider suspending or modifying outdoor activities, and review the risks of conducting events in air-conditioned settings, when air quality levels enter the “very unhealthy” range.

Decisions on cancelling or modifying the Garmin Run Marathon Series on October 25, which 6,000 had signed up for, would be made a day before the race, a spokesperson said.

Garmin Run Club has cancelled multiple practices due to the haze in recent weeks and advised runners to adjust their training plans depending on the day’s haze levels.

Local club JRT Volleyball Academy cancelled training sessions on Saturday after forecasts showed air quality could deteriorate into the “very unhealthy” range.

Coaches were tasked with monitoring air quality and readings before and during sessions, said director Jerry Teo.

Observers urged event organisers to prioritise safety over commercial viability.

According to Llewellyn, destinations that adapt and manage health risks effectively are better placed to protect their reputation in the long run.

“Contingency planning can no longer be treated as an occasional disruption. It needs to become part of standard event management,” he said.

Zilmiyah Kamble, senior lecturer in hospitality and tourism management at James Cook University Singapore, said while the haze created “considerable uncertainty” for outdoor events, the city state was likely to remain an “attractive choice” as organisers were also assessing “the destination’s broader capacity to manage health, safety and operational disruption”.

item.title: [SCMP] A fortune, a HK$72m flat and a family feud: inside the Abby Choi murder trial
item.description:
A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard.

The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”.
item.content:encoded:
A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard.

The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”.

Giving evidence for the prosecution, Cheung became emotional at times as she accused Choi’s former in-laws of living in luxury without contributing to the upbringing of the two children her daughter had with her ex-husband.

She wept in the witness box while watching footage of her daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat on February 21, 2023, the day she was last seen alive.

“My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her kindness to the wrong people. This family really bit the hand that fed them.”

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial after pleading not guilty to murdering her.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial.

The killing came to light after some of Choi’s dismembered remains were discovered in a 600 square foot flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village on February 24, 2023.

Inside, police found a hammer – the alleged murder weapon – a meat mincer, two cooking pots containing Choi’s remains, and multiple saws and knives.

The prosecution alleges that the killing stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his sons to help kill her so he could keep it.

Prosecutors have described the alleged murder as a carefully crafted plot in which each defendant played a role. It allegedly involved renting the village flat, driving Choi to the remote location on the pretext of collecting her daughter from school, and striking her with a hammer during the journey.

Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC suggested that money was the motive and highlighted the significant wealth gap between the two families.

Choi’s stepfather, Choi Cho-san, was described as a wealthy businessman who provided a monthly allowance of more than HK$1 million to support his wife, Cheung, Choi and the model’s two stepsisters in Hong Kong.

The court heard that Choi received a HK$41 million flat as a wedding gift from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, who also came from a wealthy family, although the couple never formally registered their marriage. She was also said to have received more than HK$300 million from the Tam family over the years.

The Kwong family, according to the prosecution, was far less affluent. Kwong Kau’s wife, Jenny Li Sui-heung, and their two sons were said to be unemployed, while he relied on an annual pension of HK$145,000 after retiring from the police force in 2006.

The court also heard that Kwong Kau had worked as a taxi driver, although his lawyer disputed this.

Cheung testified that her daughter had registered the Kadooria flat in Kwong Kau’s name to avoid HK$9 million in double stamp duty, with the understanding that he would hold it on trust for the two children she had with Alex Kwong.

But when Choi indicated in June 2022 that she wanted to sell the flat and move the children closer to their school in Tuen Mun, Kwong Kau allegedly attacked her and threatened to kill her and her entire family if she went ahead.

In a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, Choi complained that her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years. She also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in her former father-in-law’s name.

Cheung said she and her daughter had supported the Kwong family for years but received nothing in return.

She told the court that Alex Kwong had obtained more than HK$70 million from his ex-wife after saying he would invest the money in luxury watches. He also persuaded Choi to lend him her credit card to pay his living expenses in mainland China while he was evading justice over his involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case, Cheung said.

Anthony Kwong received HK$2 million from Choi to run an egg waffle shop in Sham Shui Po, according to Cheung. He became Choi’s stand-in chauffeur in early 2023 after he and his mother repeatedly urged her to give him a job, the witness added.

The court also heard that Choi gave Kwong Kau a monthly allowance of HK$20,000 and paid more than HK$200,000 towards his medical expenses when he was seriously ill.

During cross-examination, defence lawyers challenged Cheung’s account of their clients’ financial dependence on Choi.

Anthony Kwong’s lawyer, Trevor Beel, said his client had never received substantial financial support from Choi. He said the egg waffle shop had been set up at her request because her two children loved the snack.

Oliver Davies, representing Kwong Kau, described his client as a businessman with considerable savings who had contributed half of the Kadooria flat’s HK$60 million purchase price in 2019.

He challenged Cheung’s account of her husband’s wealth, arguing that Choi Cho-san was “constantly in debt” and could not have afforded to give her HK$1 million a month.

Davies also pointed to the limited assets Choi left behind, suggesting that she was not particularly wealthy either.

Cheung will face further cross-examination by Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, when the trial resumes on Monday.

item.title: [SCMP] After losing both legs, snowboarder Neil Tsui sets his sights on the Paralympics
item.description:
I was born in 1981, in Surrey, south of Vancouver, in Canada. I’m the youngest of four – three boys and one girl. My father is Chinese, originally from Shanghai. He left during the communist revolution and moved to Macau and then Hong Kong. My mother is Brazilian, originally from just outside São Paulo. They met in Brazil and immigrated to Canada in 1970. My upbringing was very outdoors. Everywhere you go, there are mountains and ocean. I got into snowboarding when I was about 13 years old. It’s my favourite thing to do.

I went to Earl Marriott Secondary School, and didn’t go to university, much to my parents’ frustration. I loved carpentry, was a petrolhead and enjoyed fixing cars with my brothers. Then, I worked in sales. I had a great life, friends, family. But as I approached 30, I felt that if I didn’t leave, I was never going to go. I went to visit my sister, who was living in Hong Kong, and just like everyone else, I fell in love with the city. So, I got a job working in business development and marketing for professional services.

From 2011, for three years, I lived in Mid-Levels and was a recruiter and really enjoyed it. I was then approached about a technology role within recruitment. It was a start-up, an American firm, and that was a great experience. The start-up was based in San Francisco, but we launched it in Asia. I later worked for another tech company, Phaidon. In 2019, my sister and her family left Hong Kong, and I felt ready for my next move.
item.content:encoded:
I was born in 1981, in Surrey, south of Vancouver, in Canada. I’m the youngest of four – three boys and one girl. My father is Chinese, originally from Shanghai. He left during the communist revolution and moved to Macau and then Hong Kong. My mother is Brazilian, originally from just outside São Paulo. They met in Brazil and immigrated to Canada in 1970. My upbringing was very outdoors. Everywhere you go, there are mountains and ocean. I got into snowboarding when I was about 13 years old. It’s my favourite thing to do.

I went to Earl Marriott Secondary School, and didn’t go to university, much to my parents’ frustration. I loved carpentry, was a petrolhead and enjoyed fixing cars with my brothers. Then, I worked in sales. I had a great life, friends, family. But as I approached 30, I felt that if I didn’t leave, I was never going to go. I went to visit my sister, who was living in Hong Kong, and just like everyone else, I fell in love with the city. So, I got a job working in business development and marketing for professional services.

From 2011, for three years, I lived in Mid-Levels and was a recruiter and really enjoyed it. I was then approached about a technology role within recruitment. It was a start-up, an American firm, and that was a great experience. The start-up was based in San Francisco, but we launched it in Asia. I later worked for another tech company, Phaidon. In 2019, my sister and her family left Hong Kong, and I felt ready for my next move.

I moved with the company to Singapore in September 2020. I’d met my (future) wife, Sarah, on a dating app in 2019. We finally met in person in May 2021 and an attraction was that she loved wakeboarding, like me. We got married in 2023. Six weeks after we arrived back from our honeymoon, I had an eczema spot on the back of my leg. My dermatologist gave me a cortisone jab but made me get a blood test as I had also been taking Olumiant, a strong drug for alopecia, for six months. I then went wakeboarding on Sentosa beach, where the water is filthy, and, in the evening, started getting chills. My fever got worse and I collapsed on the bathroom floor. We got a taxi to the hospital. My blood pressure was spiking and I passed out.

The following day, my wife told me I had developed sepsis and gone into septic shock. I had necrotising fasciitis, which is a flesh-eating disease. My whole body was shutting down. I was put into an induced coma, so that my body could fight to stay alive. My sister flew out from Amsterdam and my mother-in-law came from Britain. For three days, my wife just held my hand, staring at a heart monitor, not knowing if I was going to make it. Miraculously, after four days, I started turning around – my heart, my kidneys on dialysis, everything was starting to turn around. They woke me up 10 days later. My legs were covered in bandages. And all I could see were my feet, which had gone this kind of blue-purple colour. Three of my doctors came in and told me they had given me an inotrope drug – it’s what they give anyone who goes into serious septic shock. It redirects all the blood flow to your torso, to preserve your vital organs. As a result, your extremities – such as hands, feet, even your face, your nose – get cut off from adequate blood flow. So, they stood by the bed and explained all of this, and then said, “We’re going to give you a bilateral amputation. We’re going to amputate both your legs below the knee.”

All I could picture was my wife, who I’d been married to for six weeks, pushing me in a wheelchair. And then I thought about my dad. My parents started out as broke immigrants. And my dad’s outlook is: if you fall, it’s up to you to pick yourself up. In my head, it just clicked – “OK, you’re going to own this” – and I opened my eyes and looked at the doctors and said, “Can I still snowboard?” And they said yes. I was lucky to be alive.

I typed into Instagram: “Amputee Snowboarding”. And it came up with a Canadian athlete named Tyler Turner. He’s the first Canadian to win a gold medal for snowboarding, at the 2022 Beijing Paralympics. And he was the same as me – a double amputee below the knee. I wrote to him and then we talked for an hour and a half. He told me to harness the snowboarding as that would get me through my recovery. As a joke, he said they were always looking for double-amputee athletes for the Paralympic team. In my head, it clicked – getting on the team would be my North Star.

Four days later, I had the first leg amputated. (Tsui has undergone 17 surgeries in total.) A couple of months later, I got my first set of prosthetics. I felt so tall! I had an incredible physiotherapist, who worked with me on my core, and knew about my snowboarding goal. I just kept building up my strength and balance, and started playing tennis again and riding a bike. I met Tyler in the summer of 2024 and we went surfing together in Tofino, on Vancouver Island; it was an instant bond.

He asked me if I wanted to go to the Netherlands in November 2024, to get my classification for the Paralympics and, since I was living in Singapore, I hadn’t even been on a snowboard yet. I went to Trifecta Singapore, a sports facility with an indoor Snow Arena for practising snowboarding and skiing using hi-tech simulators. I couldn’t even balance. I was there for an hour and I couldn’t let go of the bar long enough. When I got home, I ripped my legs off and was on the floor, absolutely broken. Sarah encouraged me to go and meet Tyler and get the classification.

Two weeks later, I was in the Netherlands, at SnowWorld Landgraaf, an indoor ski resort. I strapped my snowboard on and we went up in the chairlift and Tyler filmed. As soon as I started going, it just clicked. I did a big carve right, a big carve left, and then I just ripped all the way to the bottom without falling. I was screaming and hooting. The video is quite ridiculous; I’m literally whooping the whole way. And I’m crying. I was so elated and, all the way down, I was saying, “We did it!” I was just thinking about Sarah and how this was for us – this is what had got us through a hellish year, to get to this moment. It was 366 days after my right leg was cut off. I did two runs and went to get my classification.

We now have a son, he’s nine months old, and we are moving back to Canada next year. Canadian Olympic snowboarder Mark Fawcett said I need to spend as much time on snow as I can. I’m still aiming for the Paralympics in 2030. We bought a house on Vancouver Island. By the time of the next Winter Paralympics, in 2030, in the French Alps, I’m going to be 49. Three years ago, I was getting my legs amputated and I’m now snowboarding with Mark, one of the godfathers of snowboarding.

I now do public speaking at corporations and at schools. I’m not trying to be some sort of inspirational person. I am just trying to be the old Neil, who just loves activity. But, obviously, I know there is a lesson in there. The irony is that it took me losing both of my legs to feel limitless. I won’t know until literally a month or two before the actual Games if I’m on the team. It’s a lofty goal and a total gamble, but you need to stay the course.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Will South China Sea’s code of conduct remain elusive as deadline looms?
item.description:
A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026.

More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.

Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace.
item.content:encoded:
A long-awaited code of conduct (COC) for the South China Sea risks becoming a toothless agreement, analysts have warned, as Beijing and Southeast Asian nations scramble to hammer out a deal by the end of 2026.

More than three decades since it was mooted, the proposed pact has remained gridlocked over how to balance competing territorial claims among China and four rival claimant states – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.

Maritime experts speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur this week agreed that the code was not meant to settle sovereignty disputes and were divided on whether it could keep the peace.

“If anything involves clarifying maritime rights, not only China but also the Philippines and Vietnam will not accept a binding COC,” Ding Duo, a researcher at China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Maritime Institute of Malaysia’s 9th South China Sea Conference on Tuesday.

Ding said the biggest obstacle was the COC’s scope, arguing that it should focus on maritime states managing their activities and preventing confrontations rather than settling territorial differences.

Claimant states held differing positions on which activities should be permitted or restricted under the agreement, including operations involving external powers, he added.

“Such differences should be settled within the COC platform,” he said, adding that disputes should not be resolved elsewhere.

Asean has repeatedly called for restraint and clear rules under the COC, which was first proposed in 1992, to manage disputes in the contested waterway.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China exchanged draft proposals in 2000 but failed to reach an agreement on such a code. Instead, they signed a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) in 2002.

Consultations on the code resumed in 2013, and negotiators began working on its draft text in 2018.

The code was intended to set operational rules for parties in the disputed waterway to ensure that incidents at sea would not escalate into conflict, said Sumathy Perumal, acting director of research and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia.

“I don’t think [the] COC will impact maritime rights or maritime claims,” Sumathy said.

However, continued confrontations in the South China Sea had complicated negotiations and made it harder for parties to reach consensus on the code, she noted.

“The incidents on the ground [are] probably delaying [negotiations], and a lot more details [need] to be agreed upon by those intending to sign the COC,” she said, explaining that a mutually accepted framework was important to help China and Asean preserve peace in the waterway.

Questions persisted over whether the claimant states would accept legally binding rules that could restrict their activities in the waters.

“The fact a COC has not been realised until today is reflective of the fact that nobody seems to really want it. If they had wanted it, they would have really made it happen,” said Nazery Khalid, a maritime security expert and senior fellow at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia.

He said claimant states were reluctant to surrender their freedom to pursue competing maritime claims because binding rules could restrict activities currently permitted under the 2002 declaration.

“With a legally binding Code of Conduct, there are certain things that you cannot do any more, which you can do under the DOC,” Nazery said.

Reality at sea

On the water, maritime tensions – between several Asean claimant states and China, and among the Southeast Asian neighbours – have continued to flare over fishing grounds, offshore energy resources and disputed maritime zones.

Disputes between Malaysia and the Philippines have persisted over their overlapping claims in the waters off Sabah.

In June 2024, the Philippines submitted a claim to the United Nations to extend its continental shelf 350 nautical miles from Palawan, prompting Malaysia to file an objection over Manila’s move.

Tensions grew after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr signed two maritime laws in November 2024 that Malaysia said infringed on its territory.

Malaysia also lodged two separate diplomatic protests in February and July ahead of Manila’s presentation of its continental shelf submission to a UN commission in July.

Malaysia and Vietnam also hold overlapping continental shelf claims in the South China Sea, despite having jointly submitted a claim to the UN in 2006.

In December 2019, Malaysia separately filed a submission to extend its continental shelf northwards into the waters around the Spratly Islands, prompting Vietnam to lodge its objections that the submission overlapped with its maritime entitlements.

Confrontations involving China have also been frequent across the region.

In January, a Chinese coastguard vessel entered Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) – the 200-nautical-mile band in which a coastal state holds special rights to marine resources – near the South Luconia Shoals off Sarawak on Borneo. The Royal Malaysian Navy’s offshore patrol vessel KD Kelantan had shadowed the Chinese ship since December 2025.

According to local media reports, Chinese vessels have maintained a near-continuous presence north and south of the shoals since 2014.

In October 2021, Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Chinese ambassador to protest the presence and activities of Chinese ships, including survey vessels, in Malaysia’s EEZ.

While Beijing did not respond to the protest then, it claims the shoals as part of its Nansha Islands – known internationally as the Spratlys – and maintains that its coastguard patrols in the area are lawful operations within waters under Chinese jurisdiction, even as it prefers dialogue with Putrajaya to manage differences.

Philippine and Chinese vessels have also clashed in the disputed waters, with tensions rising in recent weeks despite a 2024 provisional bilateral arrangement meant to calm waters around the Second Thomas Shoal.

Last week, Manila accused a Chinese coastguard vessel of firing a water cannon and carrying out dangerous manoeuvres to delay the medical evacuation of an ailing Philippine Navy sailor from its grounded warship at the shoal by nearly 10 hours.

Beijing countered that it had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after prior notification, accusing Philippine vessels of using the mission to cause “infringements and provocations”.

That stand-off followed an incident in September in which Manila accused Chinese warships and coastguard cutters of blocking a Philippine resupply run to the same outpost – the first reported interception there since the 2024 arrangement was reached.

Chinese coastguard spokesman Jiang Lue accused Manila of breaking its commitments by conducting an unapproved mission. Philippine officials, however, maintained that the bilateral provisional understanding did not require Beijing’s prior consent.

In October 2024, Hanoi accused Chinese law enforcement personnel of assaulting Vietnamese fishers near the archipelago. China disputed the account and maintained that its authorities had taken lawful steps to stop Vietnamese boats from fishing illegally in waters claimed by Beijing.

China asserts sweeping claims across the South China Sea based on an 11-dash line drawn on a Chinese map in 1947, which it later reduced to a nine-dash line in the early 1950s.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled that Beijing had no legal basis to claim historic rights over resources within the nine-dash line, which exceeded its maritime entitlements under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

Beijing rejected the ruling, maintaining that the tribunal lacked jurisdiction over the dispute.

In July, China’s Foreign Ministry reiterated its opposition, insisting that the decision would not affect its territorial sovereignty or maritime rights in the South China Sea.

“The so-called ‘award’ is nothing but a worthless piece of paper that is illegal, null and void, and has no binding force,” China’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement in response to the 10th anniversary of the ruling.

Nazery said the stakes in the South China Sea were high because it sat astride one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and had become a focal point of great-power rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“The last thing we need in Asean is to be adversely affected by the so-called great-power rivalry,” he said, warning that Malaysia must navigate differences carefully while maintaining its long-standing policy of neutrality and non-alignment.

While the fundamental question for Putrajaya was whether parties would respect existing international law, particularly Unclos, it must also maintain sufficient naval and surveillance capabilities at sea to protect its EEZ, Nazery said.

“You can talk all you want about safeguarding your maritime sovereignty, but typically you need the assets to back it up.”

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines rejects China’s calls for direct contact amid ‘miscalculation’ warnings
item.description:
The Philippine military has rejected calls to restore direct communication channels with its Chinese counterpart, despite warnings from Beijing that their absence risks “miscalculation” during confrontations and could further escalate tensions in the South China Sea.

On Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said it would not communicate with its Chinese counterpart in advance of its maritime operations, arguing that such channels were ineffective without mutual respect for international law.

Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the military’s operations in waters the Philippines considered its territory, said the channels had failed to improve trust, accusing Beijing of using them as a “smokescreen” for what Manila regarded as coercive and aggressive conduct.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine military has rejected calls to restore direct communication channels with its Chinese counterpart, despite warnings from Beijing that their absence risks “miscalculation” during confrontations and could further escalate tensions in the South China Sea.

On Tuesday, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said it would not communicate with its Chinese counterpart in advance of its maritime operations, arguing that such channels were ineffective without mutual respect for international law.

Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the military’s operations in waters the Philippines considered its territory, said the channels had failed to improve trust, accusing Beijing of using them as a “smokescreen” for what Manila regarded as coercive and aggressive conduct.

He also said the Philippine military supported Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s decision to suspend direct communication channels with China.

The Chinese embassy in Manila had called for such channels to reopen in a Facebook post on Monday, arguing that communication was essential to prevent misunderstandings and keep tensions from escalating.

“Everyone knows that no matter how difficult bilateral relations become, communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating,” it said.

The embassy accused Teodoro of suspending military-to-military communication for what it called “political self-interest”, saying such a move “fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation”.

The Philippine Department of National Defence (DND) responded on Tuesday by reposting a 2024 statement from Teodoro, in which he said he had barred contact between the department and the Chinese embassy since July 2023.

The statement followed the embassy’s claim that the armed forces’ Western Command had agreed with China on a “new model” for managing the situation at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal, including arrangements for resupply missions. The embassy said Teodoro and other key Philippine officials had approved the arrangement.

Teodoro denied the DND was involved in any such deal, saying there was no discussion of a “gentleman’s agreement” or a “new model” during a courtesy call by then Chinese ambassador Huang Xilian shortly after Teodoro took office.

“I reiterate that I have disallowed any contact between the DND and the Chinese embassy since the courtesy call of Ambassador Huang Xilian, a few days after I assumed office in July of last year,” Teodoro said in the statement.

“During the said courtesy call, there was no discussion or briefing on any ‘gentleman’s agreement’ or ‘new model’, which is contrary to the Chinese embassy’s pronouncements.”

Trinidad said the military supported suspending direct communication channels because dialogue could not be effective without trust and respect for international law.

“Bilateral dialogue will be effective if the messages match the actions on sea, air, and ground. Unfortunately, this has not been the case,” he said.

He rejected the suggestion that the absence of direct communication could increase the risk of miscalculation and further escalate tensions.

“The miscalculations happen when you are not following international regulations and international law,” he said, referring to incidents involving Chinese vessels that the Philippines says have entered waters it claims and attempted to prevent resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre.

The ageing warship, grounded at Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, serves as a Philippine military outpost on the disputed maritime feature.

Trinidad said the Philippine navy and coastguard had the legal right to challenge the presence of Chinese vessels in waters claimed by Manila, arguing that such encounters served as warnings to the ships involved.

“So, don’t take it literally that they are not being warned, they are not being challenged,” he said.

He maintained that China’s “coercive and aggressive actions”, rather than the absence of a direct communication channel, were the main source of miscalculation.

The dispute over maritime activities in the South China Sea is rooted in competing claims and sharply different interpretations of international law.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled that China’s historic-rights claims within the nine-dash line had no legal basis insofar as they exceeded the maritime entitlements permitted under the convention.

Beijing rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction and that the award was null and void. The ruling did not determine sovereignty over all disputed islands and reefs.

Competing accounts

The evacuation of a Philippine marine from the BRP Sierra Madre on October 8, after he suffered a medical emergency involving a nearly ruptured appendix, became the latest flashpoint in the disputed waters, with Manila and Beijing offering different accounts of how the operation unfolded.

Navy Captain Marissa Andres-Martinez said the Philippines would not seek China’s permission to conduct maritime operations in waters it claimed.

“Nothing was communicated to the Chinese coastguard,” she said of Manila’s response to the emergency.

Andres-Martinez said the navy would continue operations to sustain the soldiers aboard the vessel without seeking China’s permission.

The armed forces’ public affairs chief Colonel Xerxes Trinidad said other seafarers should also recognise the urgency of medical evacuations.

“The moment you call for a medical evacuation, it is something of concern that all. I think, a proper Navy or any seafarer would do to give way to that.”

His remarks came amid Philippine Coast Guard accusations that Chinese vessels had used water cannons against Philippine ships responding to the medical emergency.

China offered a different account of the incident.

On Friday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the Philippine coastguard had “intruded the adjacent waters of Ren’ai Jiao, Nansha Qundao of China”, referring to Beijing’s names for Second Thomas Shoal and the Spratly Islands.

“The China Coast Guard took legitimate and reasonable measures to handle the situation in accordance with laws and regulations,” Mao said.

China had allowed the evacuation on humanitarian grounds after communication between the two sides but “individual Philippine officials have distorted facts and wrongfully accused China without showing the whole picture to the public”, Mao added.

The Chinese embassy in Manila on Monday urged the Philippines to tow away the “illegally grounded” warship and evacuate its personnel to end their exposure to risk.

On the same day as the medical evacuation, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr called for a binding code of conduct in the South China Sea during a speech at the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore.

Marcos said an agreement between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations was “absolutely necessary” to reduce the risk of further confrontations.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s ‘golden age’ push hands top science honours to big tech. Will it work?
item.description:
The White House’s bid for a US “golden age” of science should put China on alert, Chinese analysts have warned, but they remain sceptical as to whether President Donald Trump’s alliance with Silicon Valley billionaires can pull it off.

This comes as Trump, in another arguably unconventional move, handed the country’s highest science and engineering awards to top American tech bosses.

Elon Musk, head of electric-vehicle maker Tesla and aerospace manufacturer SpaceX, received the National Medal of Science, the US’ top scientific honour.
item.content:encoded:
The White House’s bid for a US “golden age” of science should put China on alert, Chinese analysts have warned, but they remain sceptical as to whether President Donald Trump’s alliance with Silicon Valley billionaires can pull it off.

This comes as Trump, in another arguably unconventional move, handed the country’s highest science and engineering awards to top American tech bosses.

Elon Musk, head of electric-vehicle maker Tesla and aerospace manufacturer SpaceX, received the National Medal of Science, the US’ top scientific honour.

Joining him in receiving the award at the “Science: A New Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday were leading chipmaking chiefs Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices, as well as Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

Personal computer tycoon Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the US’ most prestigious award for the category.

While entrepreneurs have previously won these awards, observers noted that it was unprecedented for tech executives to be honoured on such a scale – particularly given that the National Medal of Science had long prioritised scientists and researchers.

The award was established by Congress in 1959, while the technology medal was introduced in 1980.

All of this year’s recipients have close ties with the White House. Musk is widely considered a Trump ally despite their months-long public feud last year, while Huang, Su, Brin and Dell are all members of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology.

The companies they lead have also deepened their commercial ties with the Pentagon to varying degrees.

With artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as a major arena of the China-US tech rivalry, those enterprises are also critical players in the supply chain. At Trump’s state dinner last month for Chinese President Xi Jinping, Musk, Huang and Su were seated at the same table as the two leaders.

Sun Zhanqing, a special researcher at the South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy, said the line-up of awardees showed that a “new type of power relationship” was taking shape in the US.

“Tech entrepreneurs’ standing in [shaping] resource allocation, technological road maps and the national science narrative is rising,” Sun wrote in a note on the think tank’s social media channel on Friday.

Still, he cautioned against conflating US tech executives’ growing influence over scientific research with scientists’ actual “capacity to create knowledge”.

“The Trump administration’s science awards may create a cycle that warrants vigilance,” warned Sun, who is also deputy director of the government-affiliated Guangzhou Academy of Social Sciences’ Urban Culture Research Institute.

Tech bosses’ resource advantages yielded more visible results, he said, earning them higher honours that in turn could reinforce their policy influence and ability to secure more resources.

“Ultimately, people may attribute the advantages created by this cycle to the idea that a certain group of people is inherently more creative,” he warned.

“A golden age of science cannot be judged solely by how glamorous the people standing on the podium are.”
