An analysis by Xinzhi Observatory, a technology-focused channel owned by Shanghai-based news portal Guancha, also struck a sceptical note on last week’s US science summit.

Even as the Trump White House continued to cut routine federal funding for basic science, it was trying to tap the massive computing power and capital of private giants to rebuild US global leadership in research through so-called superintelligence, the piece noted, using Trump’s new preferred moniker for AI.

With entrepreneurs increasingly steering research, the purity of scientific inquiry and the public interest could face an “unprecedented test,” it cautioned. “Whether reliance on the patronage of tech oligarchs can truly open a new, enduring golden age of science remains a highly contested unknown.”

However, China could ill afford to let its guard down, the observers cautioned.

“The award ceremony was not merely a ‘symbolic arrangement’,” Sun said. “Big tech companies are taking part in national tech competition as technology developers.”

He cited the more than US$6 billion in science and technology investments announced by the Trump administration at Thursday’s event. This includes US$2.4 billion in contributions from 11 companies, including Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, to provide AI “science tools and compute credits” for researchers.

Xinzhi Observatory said the investment plans announced at the summit might reveal a blueprint for “stockpiling talent reserves for future industrial competition” – by pushing advanced computing capacity directly to the local level to spur broader basic innovation.

Thursday’s event built on “Science: A New Golden Age”, a report by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director Michael Kratsios released in July.

It outlines a major overhaul of the framework for American science, whose foundations were laid by the 1945 report “Science, the Endless Frontier”, written by Vannevar Bush, director of the US Office of Scientific Research and Development during the second world war, while positioning itself as the 21st century successor to it.

Kratsios’ report argues that the post-war “linear model” of technological progress – flowing in sequence from university-based basic research funded through slow, consensus-driven peer review, to applied research, then to technological development and industry – no longer held in many fields.

It said US private companies dominated research spending, bureaucratic and funding structures were burdening scientists, and the fruits of American science often ended up helping rivals build their advantage due to decades of industrial offshoring.

It proposed prioritising funding for risk-taking individual scientists over “legacy institutions” and expanding the Genesis Mission – launched by the Trump administration in November to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery.

However, Kratsios’ report has drawn criticism at home, including over its ostensible aim to shift vast resources away from traditional academia towards big tech, effectively turning national research into a venture-capital model.

But Chinese observers say it could pose a challenge to Beijing, by shifting the gravity of US-China tech competition away from individual breakthroughs to how well each side governs its innovation system.

The report identified China as the first “peer-level competitor” to the US in research and development spending – driven by Beijing’s “all-of-society approach” to partnerships across sectors.

Strategically, the White House report was a “direct response” to China’s whole-of-nation approach to scientific research, said Zhu Yanmei, dean’s adviser at the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute.

She warned in a July post that regardless of future administrative shifts, its core propositions – that science must serve national competitiveness, that federal funding must pursue quantifiable gains in technological sovereignty, and that AI must be treated as national infrastructure – had probably become consensus in US strategic circles.

She also cautioned that the problems highlighted in the US report – bureaucracy, conservatism and inefficiency – mirrored chronic flaws in China’s own research system.

“What China needs is not simple benchmarking or a reflexive response but a profound reflection on its innovation paradigm. In criticising America’s own ailments, the report has inadvertently held up a mirror for China,” she wrote.

“For China, the report’s biggest takeaway may be this: a true science and innovation power is measured not by the number of papers or the scale of funding but by whether its institutions can keep generating ‘crazy ideas’ and turn them into ‘world-changing forces’.”

Beijing is also moving to streamline its research system.

Guidelines issued last Friday on developing new productive forces called for boosting the role of companies as the main force in scientific and technological innovation, and for supporting capable private firms to lead major national technology projects.

In April, Xi called for an open, inclusive innovation environment that tolerated failure and placed greater weight on AI-enabled basic research.

item.title: [SCMP] Is this the best time for US strategists to push for abandoning ambiguity on Taiwan?
item.description:
For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict.

This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise.

A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy.
item.content:encoded:
For nearly five decades, the United States’ Taiwan policy has centred on strategic ambiguity by not declaring whether it would intervene militarily in a potential Taiwan conflict.

This policy – designed to deter Beijing from using force while preventing Taipei from formally declaring independence – is being challenged by realist US strategists amid a broader debate over America’s role in the world, growing constraints on US military might and a shifting regional balance of power driven by China’s military rise.

A small group of realist US strategists is pushing for the US to rule out military intervention over Taiwan to avoid the possibility of a catastrophic war between mainland China and the US. Experts said this idea, despite still being a minority view, was at least opening debate on the long-standing one-sided policy.

“When US officials first adopted strategic ambiguity over Taiwan, China’s military was no match for that of the US. This is no longer the case,” wrote Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, in an opinion piece late last month.

“At the same time, the American military suddenly seems fragile, lacking the advanced munitions and naval forces it would need for a major power conflict and facing serious vulnerabilities in its basing infrastructure.

“Simply put, the US military remains the strongest in the world, but its ability to outlast China in a war over Taiwan is now in question.”

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not formally recognise the island as independent, although Washington is committed to supplying it with defensive weapons and opposes any forcible takeover.

Kavanagh told the South China Morning Post on October 8 that of her many modelling efforts looking at what would be required to break through a blockade of Taiwan, the bottom line was that neither Beijing nor Washington could defeat the other side.

“The conflict would start with some kind of intense war. [In the modelling, the] US typically runs out of air-defence missiles and offensive missiles before China does, even if China depletes stockpiles,” she said.

“My assumption is that China blockades Taiwan and just bleeds it out. And there’s not so much the US can do.”

In a research report published on September 10, Kavanagh not only proposed ending strategic ambiguity over Taiwan but also argued for replacing US mutual defence treaties with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia with narrower security partnerships.

The report also said the US should move most forces away from positions near mainland China in the first island chain – a string of US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines – towards a smaller presence centred farther east around the second island chain, stretching from Japan through Guam to Papua New Guinea.

Her proposal drew strong pushback within US national security circles, was called a “bombshell” and “radical”, and was deemed to be Communist Party “talking points”.

“When I started arguing this, I was trying to be careful how I phrased what I was saying in the way that would make it clear that I was arguing for something that I thought was in US interests,” said Kavanagh, explaining how her position had become more direct since she first made the argument earlier last year.

“The US foreign policy is in a period of flux. And people are debating what the US role in the world should be.

“Being clear and direct about alternatives and options that the US has, and making a strong case for why this is in the US’ interest contributes to the debate.”

Kavanagh belongs to a school of foreign policy that rejects military interventionism in favour of military restraint, narrow national interests and a focus on domestic strength. Since last year, she has written several reports and published opinion pieces proposing a Taiwan non-intervention policy.

From the late 1990s until recently, a group of US foreign policy scholars and analysts has advocated restraint and argued that Taiwan’s importance does not justify risking a war with Beijing.

In 1998, Ted Galen Carpenter, now a senior fellow at the Randolph Bourne Institute and the Libertarian Institute, advocated continued arms sales but explicitly ruled out military intervention in a policy paper he wrote while at the Cato Institute, a Washington-based libertarian think tank. Doug Bandow, a Cato senior fellow, made a similar case in 2024.

In a 2015 paper, Charles L. Glaser, now a senior fellow at MIT’s security studies programme, proposed that Washington end its commitment to defend Taiwan in exchange for Beijing peacefully settling its maritime disputes and accepting a continued US military role in East Asia.

More recently, Kavanagh and Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow in the Carnegie Endowment’s American statecraft programme, argued in Foreign Affairs in February 2025 that Washington should prepare to stay out of a Taiwan conflict if the People’s Liberation Army did not attack US bases or warships.

In September 2025, Michael Swaine, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute, proposed a gradual transition to explicit non-intervention, emphasising the reassurance of allies and Beijing.

Swaine said that maintaining the possibility of the US intervening militarily would become increasingly dangerous and would risk a major war with China under a worsening strategic rivalry between the two powers.

He said there was an increasing tendency in Washington to regard Taiwan as a vital strategic location that, by implication, must be kept from Beijing. Alongside this, Beijing was steadily increasing its military capabilities regarding Taiwan.

“These two trends are increasing the likelihood of one or both sides taking what they view as deterrent actions that cross red lines, leading to a major crisis and possible conflict,” Swaine said.

“If these trends do not change, the US must consider just how vital Taiwan is to the US. Since I believe that it is in fact not a vital enough interest to justify risking a major war with China.”

Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said the basis of strategic ambiguity stemmed from the extremely strong US military capability and its deterrent power, but the policy had become meaningless with the rise of Chinese military power.

But he said it would be difficult for this argument, which was still proposed by a minority voice, to become a mainstream view due to policy inertia.

“They’re actively debating it and it’s no longer just a one-sided policy position that leaves no room for discussion. The fact that this is happening is a good thing in itself, regardless of whether it will ultimately succeed,” Xin said.

The argument for policy change comes as US foreign policy is in a period of flux, with US President Donald Trump’s administration pushing the boundaries of what has long been status quo foreign policy.

Taiwan was among the most closely watched issues at the two summits between presidents Trump and Xi Jinping this year. While former US president Joe Biden repeatedly said the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a potential conflict, Trump has declined to say whether he would do so.

After the first summit in May, the US paused a US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, which is still on hold. And the US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, the SCMP reported last month.

While he was silent on the Taiwan issue during the second summit last month, Trump raised the question after the meeting in Beijing in May of whether it would make sense for US forces to travel 9,500 miles (15,300km) to fight a war.

.

item.title: [SCMP] Plan to live-stream US execution tests Southeast Asia’s content curbs
item.description:
The US government’s plan to live-stream the execution of a former Army member convicted in a deadly 2009 mass shooting is raising questions about how effectively Southeast Asian governments can restrict graphic online content.

Analysts say while authorities may have powers to restrict access to the live stream, containing clips and altered copies of the killing posted to social media could prove far more difficult.

The issue gained fresh urgency on Tuesday, after Australia’s Environment Minister Murray Watts condemned the proposed broadcast as “disgusting”.
item.content:encoded:
The US government’s plan to live-stream the execution of a former Army member convicted in a deadly 2009 mass shooting is raising questions about how effectively Southeast Asian governments can restrict graphic online content.

Analysts say while authorities may have powers to restrict access to the live stream, containing clips and altered copies of the killing posted to social media could prove far more difficult.

The issue gained fresh urgency on Tuesday, after Australia’s Environment Minister Murray Watts condemned the proposed broadcast as “disgusting”.

Australia’s online regulator, eSafety, told Agence France Presse it lacked the power to prevent the live stream, but stressed that online services had a responsibility to protect users from harmful content.

New Zealand’s Classification Office had earlier said it could not classify a live stream while it was taking place and lacked the authority to block access to such an event.

Nidal Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be live-streamed, and the Pentagon subsequently confirmed the plan.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not made a final decision on whether the execution would be live-streamed, despite his comments a day earlier approving the broadcast, leaving the plan’s current status uncertain.

Details of how the broadcast will be distributed also remain unclear.

In Southeast Asia, existing rules provide potential avenues for restricting access, but analysts say whether authorities invoke them depends on their assessment of the broadcast, how it is presented and where it appears.

Benjamin Ang, head of the Centre of Excellence for National Security at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said regulators would first need to determine whether the broadcast warranted restrictions.

“Regulators and platforms would then need to coordinate to pre-identify when and where the live stream will take place so they can effectively detect the live stream and block access to it in their countries,” he said.

Powers to restrict

In Singapore, the Internet Code of Practice requires licensed providers to comply with rules on prohibited material. For websites, internet access providers meet their obligations by denying access to sites notified by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) as containing such material.

The code considers whether content depicts “detailed or relished acts of extreme violence or cruelty”, alongside any intrinsic medical, scientific, artistic or educational value. These are assessment criteria, rather than an automatic requirement for blocking an execution broadcast.

Malaysia’s Online Safety Act provides for the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) to order licensed platforms or network providers to restrict access. This follows MCMC’s assessing a user report and determining on reasonable grounds that the content is harmful.

The law covers material that may incite violence or terrorism, promote public hostility or disturb public tranquillity, but does not specifically list execution live streams.

Indonesia’s Ministerial Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic-System Operators, amended in 2021, requires operators to prevent the distribution of prohibited material, including content that relevant authorities classify as unsettling the public and disrupting public order.

Operators must comply with takedown orders within 24 hours of receipt. In urgent cases, they must act without delay, and no later than four hours after receiving a warning. Failure to comply can lead to access blocking, including through internet service providers.

These deadlines, however, do not shield viewers from a short live event. This Week In Asia has reached out to IMDA, MCMC and Indonesia’s Communications and Digital Ministry for comment.

Beyond the original stream

Even if access to the original broadcast were restricted, recordings and excerpts could spread elsewhere, creating a separate challenge for regulators and platforms.

Drawing on lessons from Islamic State beheadings and the Christchurch terrorist massacre, Ang said regulators should work across platforms to limit resharing, while services should use machine learning to detect altered copies of the footage.

Platforms must also “downgrade related search terms, and de-monetise and disable offending accounts”, he said.

Benjamin Y.H. Loh, a communications and media scholar at Monash University Malaysia, said containing reposted footage could become “a cat-and-mouse game”, with social media users uploading clips of the event to spoof platforms’ detection efforts.

He also pointed to the Christchurch attack, where redistribution of footage on the massacre became a major content-moderation challenge. Clips were altered with music, sped up or mirrored before being uploaded in attempts to evade platform moderators and automated detection tools.

However, advance notice would allow platforms to prepare for the broadcast, Loh said. “You need to have a lot of human moderators on standby to handle the incoming reports.”

He said moderators could also monitor retransmission of footage, citing how illegal live streams of World Cup matches in June and July were quickly discovered and blocked or banned.

“It’s not going to be instantaneous, of course,” he said. “There will definitely be a few that will go through the cracks.”

Loh also cautioned that a broadcast showing the execution directly versus an indirect account of proceedings would raise different questions.

“The platforms’ decisions really depend on the material and how they apply their own Terms of Service,” he said.

Propaganda tool

The risks of broadcasting or live-streaming Hasan’s execution could extend beyond exposure to graphic imagery, as experts warn the footage could also be used to promote extremist narratives.

“Some of the accounts that clip or repost the original live stream may do so to advocate violence or incite hate against certain races or religions,” Ang said, adding that community and religious leaders and educators could help raise public awareness of the dangers of such content.

But for political scientist Bilveer Singh, live-streaming the execution would simply reinforce anti-West or anti-American views among extremist actors and susceptible audiences in Southeast Asia.

“It will also complicate ongoing deradicalisation efforts that Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have been pursuing, because if this execution goes through, it provides extremists with material to exploit,” he said.

Analysts warn that extremist sympathisers could also portray Hasan as a martyr, regardless of his crimes.

“Therein lies a radicalisation toolkit for these people,” Bilveer said.

For Ang, the practical objective is reducing harm rather than promising complete containment.

“It may be impossible to stop every instance of the livestream, but countries can do as much as they can to reduce the harm to their populations,” Ang said.

item.title: [SCMP] Systems to counter missiles and drones take centre stage at US defence expo
item.description:
As missiles and drones take a bigger role in modern warfare, major defence contractors gathered in Washington this week to showcase their latest advances in the technologies – and systems to counter them.

The three-day Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition, which opened on Monday, is one of the largest ground-based weapons shows in the US.

This year there was a strong emphasis on air and missile defence systems, reflecting growing concern about how to counter aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East rage on, and following reports that the US military’s missile stockpiles have been badly depleted by its war on Iran.
item.content:encoded:
As missiles and drones take a bigger role in modern warfare, major defence contractors gathered in Washington this week to showcase their latest advances in the technologies – and systems to counter them.

The three-day Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition, which opened on Monday, is one of the largest ground-based weapons shows in the US.

This year there was a strong emphasis on air and missile defence systems, reflecting growing concern about how to counter aerial threats as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East rage on, and following reports that the US military’s missile stockpiles have been badly depleted by its war on Iran.

Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest defence contractors, had its latest advanced missile systems on show – the Extended-Range Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), launched from its High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), a light multiple rocket launcher.

But the main focus was its air and missile defence systems, with the latest PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) on show – used for short- and long-range air defence, respectively.

The company also had its new PAC-3 Edge next-generation missile interceptor on show for the first time after it unveiled the programme on Friday.

The PAC-3 Edge is an upgrade of the PAC-3 MSE currently in operation in Ukraine, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific region.

It incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, which Lockheed Martin says enhance the interceptor’s ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, ‌at ⁠longer ranges and higher altitudes.

During the ceremony at the AUSA expo on Monday, Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control for Lockheed Martin, said the PAC-3 Edge would “fly further, faster and higher” than its predecessor, with more manoeuvrability, thrust and sensitivity. It is expected to begin testing by 2027 to be ready for deployment in 2031.

“We’re looking forward. We’re asking ourselves, what are our adversaries going to be doing in three or four or five or 10 years from now? And we’re preparing for that,” Cahill said.

“We’re going to make sure that the adversaries have nowhere to hide. It doesn’t matter what they do. It doesn’t matter what they try. This missile is going to take them out.”

It comes as the ongoing war in Iran has exposed the importance of munitions stockpiles and defence against low-cost drone swarms in modern warfare.

According to an April report by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, the US military may have used more than half of its pre-war inventory for four key munitions – PrSM, SM-3, THAAD and Patriot missiles – and more than 1,000 rounds of Tomahawk and Joint Air-to-Surface Stand-off missiles during the first 39 days of its war with Iran, which began on February 28.

That situation could be “critical” for a potential western Pacific conflict, the report said, as it would take up to four years to return stockpiles to pre-war levels, which were already deemed insufficient for a war against a peer. “Building stockpiles to levels adequate for a war with China will take additional time,” it added.

In contrast, Iran has heavily relied on its low-cost, one-way attack drones – such as the Shahed-136 “kamikaze” drone – that were used to swarm and overwhelm the air defences of US military bases in the region.

The US and Gulf states have consumed and depleted multimillion-dollar air and missile defence rounds to combat the cheap drones, prompting calls for more efficient solutions.

These drone warfare tactics are also projected to be critical in the Indo-Pacific flashpoints – particularly the Taiwan Strait, where both the US and China have been building up their drone fleets in preparation for a potential armed conflict.

A satellite imagery analysis suggests that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stationed over 200 obsolete 1960s-era J-6 supersonic fighter jets – converted into attack and cruise-missile-like drones – across six airbases near the Taiwan Strait.

In response, the US has introduced the “hellscape” concept into its Taiwan Strait strategy, aimed at deploying a massive fleet of autonomous drone swarms, loitering munition systems and marine drones to disrupt PLA amphibious invasion forces in any contingencies. It also requested US$54 billion for “autonomous and remotely operated systems across air, land, and above and below the sea” in the 2027 budget request, according to the Pentagon’s budget overview book.

To counter short-range drone swarms and incoming missiles, General Dynamics, one of the largest American land-based arms contractors, showcased its two latest air defence systems – the Leonidas Ground Vehicle (GV) and the Manoeuvre-Short Range Air Defence (M-SHORAD) Increment 4.

The Leonidas GV is a mobile high-power microwave counter-drone defence system developed as a collaborative initiative by the defence tech company Epirus and General Dynamics.

Scott Taylor, director of US growth at General Dynamics, said the Leonidas GV was developed with “drone swarm defeat” in mind and aimed to solve the “prolific problem” of being unable to use electronic warfare interruption against fibre-optically controlled drones by using weaponised electromagnetic interference technology.

In this way, the Leonidas GV could overload the internal electronics, navigation and communication systems of multiple hostile drones at once, causing them to drop from the sky simultaneously.

“One of the things that’s been very clear in a lot of the studies that are publicly discussed out there, particularly in Southwest Asia, is that the enemy can start flying enough drones at you that it overwhelms an electronic warfare or a kinetic machine gun capability,” Taylor said.

“So the Epirus-based vehicle – the Leonidas over there – that one uses electromagnetic interference to weaponise, and it can drop 50 drones at one time, single pulse, no bullets, no fratricide risk.”

Also on display, the M-SHORAD anti-aircraft weapon system uses a self-loading equipment dock mounted on light, tactical and utility vehicles to provide air defence against short-range drone and missile threats for light infantry brigades.

Taylor said it had “powerful short-range air defence and counter-drone capability integrated in one”. It is equipped with Iron Wasp suicide drones that intercept incoming enemy drone attacks, as well as a 30-calibre machine gun.

“With what’s going on in Ukraine, what’s happening in the Persian Gulf in the Strait of Hormuz, there’s a lot of people talking about the challenges with drone defeat,” he said.

“Now they’re having US$30,000 drones destroying multimillion-dollar vehicles, and so trust me, we’re being approached all of the time by our allied nations as well.”

The need to counter drone attacks – and a desire to reduce American casualties on the battlefield – has accelerated the integration of autonomous systems into US Army operations.

At the expo, GM Defence showcased its prototype of a “commercially derived” Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) concept, with a design based on Chevrolet’s Silverado to demonstrate potential future drive-by-wire controls, camera-based sensing and modular payload capabilities for support missions like logistics and casualty evacuation.

Pete Johnson, vice-president of integrated vehicle solutions at GM Defence, said the UGV was a “direct reflection” of how his company listened to the US Army and paid attention to the changing character of warfare.

“We’re watching closely the developments in Ukraine and the Middle East, and how the army is organising the campaign in the Indo-Pacific,” Johnson said. “And all of those observations are pointing to a very clear need: more robotic and autonomous capability to deliver operational effect and to reduce risk for our soldiers.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Singapore engineer love on dating apps? From public service to private romance
item.description:
For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it.

“It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said.

Singapore launched dating platform FirstDate last month, as the city state grapples with a record-low fertility rate. While the platform has drawn some criticism online for its limited range of eligibility, observers also say it is a good way to encourage first meetings for potential couples.
item.content:encoded:
For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it.

“It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said.

Singapore launched dating platform FirstDate last month, as the city state grapples with a record-low fertility rate. While the platform has drawn some criticism online for its limited range of eligibility, observers also say it is a good way to encourage first meetings for potential couples.

FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 by GovTech, which told local media there was no decision yet to expand the initiative beyond the public sector. The government agency has not provided figures on how many users in the sector meet its present criteria for the app.

Singapore’s public service workforce is about 158,000-strong as of March this year, according to the government job portal.

App users answer a survey about their interests and values, and the platform uses a Nobel Prize-winning algorithm to generate recommended pairings based on participants’ preferences and compatibility.

The first round of sign-ups closed on October 5 after emails on the platform were sent to public officers a week before. A matching cycle lasts about a month, according to local media reports.

Public reaction to the app has been mixed, with some online commentators arguing that limiting it to civil servants is elitist and that having an age limit implies an expiration date for relationships.

Many also pointed out that dating was not a top priority for young Singaporeans facing rising living costs.

If life was cheaper, people would “go out more often, go dating and have kids”, one social media user wrote.

The FirstDate platform, which matches participants to one partner at a time, can still be effective for those who are serious about finding love, according to Norman Li, a psychology professor at the Singapore Management University.

“Today, people are overwhelmed with perceived choices, many of which are not even real choices, which makes it psychologically hard to settle down and stay with any one person,” he said.

But he noted that the agency faced the challenge of getting enough sign-ups to broaden the dating pool and increase users’ chances of perceiving potential matches as suitable and attractive partners.

“A major problem today is that people’s standards are too high for the market to clear, due to constant exposure to celebrities, internet and movie stars and dating app choices,” Li said.

For Jean Liu, an associate professor of psychology at the Singapore Institute of Technology, restricting matches is a positive as it helps prevent dating fatigue and being overwhelmed by choices.

“You won’t have a few highly popular individuals flooded with attention, as you might on a typical app,” she said.

The platform launch comes amid the city state’s battle to raise its fertility rate, which sank to a low of 0.87 last year. The government has rolled out new measures, including increasing childcare leave and lowering childcare fees, and set up an inter-agency work group to tackle the trend.

Li said that FirstDate likely had similar goals of boosting marriage and fertility.

The platform – powered by an algorithm that earned one of its creators a Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences in 2012 – is the latest in a series of Singaporean initiatives aimed at matching singles.

In 1984, the government launched the Social Development Unit (SDU), which organised events for university graduates to meet up. In a speech a year earlier, Singapore’s founding father Lee Kuan Yew had warned that graduates were marrying late and having fewer children than the less educated.

A separate body, the Social Development Section (SDN), was created in 1985 for those with only secondary school qualifications. In 2009, both units were merged and renamed the Social Development Network to widen the dating pool and create more opportunities for singles to meet and eventually marry.

Li predicted FirstDate would be more successful than its predecessors. “The goals are the same as before, but SDU and SDN were event-based, which apparently didn’t attract too many people,” he said. “This time, a systematic dating app has been thoughtfully designed to create matches.”

Liu, however, said the initiatives were fundamentally different. FirstDate sprouted from a GovTech “hackathon”, she said, and should be best viewed as a government product trial that borrowed the agile and experimental approach of private tech.

She urged users to refrain from dismissing the platform because it was a government project.

“When others step in, whether the government or our own family members, it can feel orchestrated and ‘unromantic’,” she said. “However, if we look across history and in many parts of the world, relationships have often been arranged or brokered by families or communities.”

Daniel Goh, an associate professor of sociology at the National University of Singapore, agreed that it was premature to pass judgment on the platform since it was still in its pilot phase.

“I would be shocked if the government does not open the platform to citizens if it is proven successful,” he said. “The question is: what is the threshold for success?”

Other Asian countries, faced with a similarly dipping birth rate, have also tried to play Cupid. In 2024, Japan launched a government-backed dating app that required users to prove they were committed to marriage, verify their income and undergo an interview with the app operator.

As of June this year, 16,000 people had registered on the app, 760 couples were in “serious relationships” and 265 couples had tied the knot, according to Japanese government data.

Also in 2024, authorities in South Korea launched a dating programme for participants in Seoul to mingle through curated activities, such as outdoor dining by the Han River.

Some 126 couples were matched during that event, prompting the city government to roll-out the second edition last month, which was heavily oversubscribed with more than 2,300 singles aged 25 to 45 registering for just 100 slots.

According to a survey by pollster YouGov, one in four Singaporeans used dating apps in 2024, with Gen Zs and millennials more likely than older generations to have done so.

Out of those who have swiped for love online, 59 per cent used Tinder – making it the most popular platform – and 46 per cent took to Coffee Meets Bagel.

Civil servant Clare, meanwhile, is keeping her hopes up despite not finding a match after the first round of pairings concluded on FirstDate.

“I’m slightly bummed, but I’ll wait for the next cycle to start to try again.”

*Full name withheld at interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] China agrees to slash EU hybrid car exports in half, putting brake on trade war
item.description:
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.

Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.

“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.
item.content:encoded:
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.

Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.

“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.

The sides also agreed to expedite EU applications for rare earth mineral export licences and improve market access for goods including car parts, olive oil and textiles, which Sefcovic said could be worth “almost €4 billion” (US$4.5 billion) in current export value.

Beijing said it had received assurances that the EU and its members would “facilitate specific priority licences to China among dual-use sectors”, without naming the industries in question.

The parties agreed to give advance warning of export controls, “improve the transparency of listing and delisting procedures” and work towards delisting companies that have been named.

The latter is significant as powerful EU members are considering a new weapon that could instantly exclude firms from the single market.

Brussels said its incoming inverter ban was not aimed at any particular country, despite EU officials confirming it was intended to wind down a heavy dependence on China.

The Chinese commerce ministry described the talks as “equal, professional and constructive”, but Commerce Minister Wang Wentao made it clear that he was not happy with the EU’s newly assertive stance, expressing “concern over the recent trade and economic restrictions imposed by the EU”.

He added that “China is not the root cause of the EU’s problems, but rather a partner in resolving them”.

The ministry added that Wang had “urged the EU to work with China to properly handle frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation”.

For Beijing, however, the big prize could be preserving the status quo as far as possible, given the economic importance of exports and the closure of the US market to many Chinese goods.

“Judging from the details released by the EU, China appears to have made significant concessions on several issues. Whether these concessions will lead to corresponding adjustments by the EU on trade restrictions and market access remains to be seen over the coming months,” a commentary published by Geopolitechs, a website specialising in Chinese policymaking, said.

Sefcovic, meanwhile, said EU national leaders would decide next week whether China’s concessions were enough, but downplayed the likelihood of an all-out tariff war.

“It’s very easy to declare a trade war or any war, but it’s very difficult to stop it,” he said. “So therefore, I put so much emphasis on negotiations, and I’m glad that today I can present to you the outcome.”

Sefcovic declined to share further detail on the arrangement on hybrid cars – shipments of which have ballooned in recent months – but hinted that it could follow a recent import curb the bloc placed on Chinese steel.

“There are different techniques,” he said. “If you look in recent couple of months, I think you would find the answer.”

A source briefed on the talks suggested that it would be a safeguard measure, by which the EU is able to place quotas and tariffs to urgently curb import surges.

This is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing

Maros Sefcovic, European commissioner for trade

Earlier in the week, EU sources had explained that the bloc was seeking a “proof of concept” deal in a single sector – hybrid cars – which would be seen as a test of whether Beijing was negotiating in good faith.

A joint statement by the two sides, published following two days of negotiations, said that talks would continue over reducing tariffs and creating minimum price deals that would allow Chinese electric vehicles to enter the EU market at a lower duty rate.

The 16-point agreement listed a series of deliverables from the latest round of talks, with the two sides set to meet for further discussions in March next year. Most of these centred on further talks over long-standing trade disputes, including over medical equipment and power inverters.

Sefcovic – who met with Wang and Vice-Premier He Lifeng – had been pressing Beijing to cap exports of hybrid vehicles, as a recent surge in shipments to Europe had led to fears within the bloc that its car industry could be hollowed out.

“We never had the level of intensity of our exchanges and contacts as we have [had] over the last three to four months with our Chinese counterparts,” Sefcovic said. “I want to say that this was done in good faith, and this is the result of very intense work.”

But he cautioned that the outcomes laid out in the joint statement would not be enough by themselves to reduce tensions between the two sides.

“I often say that genuine negotiations deserve a real try. Therefore, I appreciate my counterparts’ engagement. Having said that, this is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing,” Sefcovic said.

“As President von der Leyen has said, dialogue needs results, and where the dialogue cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to ensure rebalancing.”

The latest talks came amid rising tensions between China and the EU over a range of trade issues, with calls growing in Europe for Brussels to take firmer action to curtail a surge in Chinese exports to the bloc.

Next week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will brief EU national leaders on the results of the talks with Beijing, as the European Commission seeks instruction on how to respond to what is now widely described in Europe as a “China shock 2.0”.

Member states have been coalescing around a tougher approach, shown by a joint paper from the governments of France and Germany – leaked on Monday – which called for a weapon to cut countries or firms perceived to be cheating on trade out of the EU market almost instantly.

The commission is then likely to present a series of new trade tools before the end of the year. It was also expected to launch a flurry of investigations aimed at quickly curbing Chinese imports in sectors including chemicals, plastics and automotive, though it remained unclear on Friday whether the progress in Beijing would alter those plans.

Businesses responded positively to the Beijing talks.

The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) welcomed the “pragmatic outcomes”, saying they showed both sides’ “willingness to handle trade frictions and stabilise bilateral trade relations through dialogue”.

The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association said “this announcement is a positive step in easing trade tensions between the two” sides.

Pascal Canfin, a lawmaker who manages the China file in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told the South China Morning Post that the hybrid deal was “a very first step towards rebalancing our trade relationship”.

“But while dialogue has delivered a first result today, we are under no illusion: the imbalance is systemic,” Canfin said. “We will therefore have to go further, and we must of course not give up on using our trade defence instruments to safeguard our economic security.”

item.title: [SCMP] This womb for rent: why are some Chinese cities hubs for illegal surrogacy services?
item.description:
It was like something out of a movie: blindfolded, her cellphone confiscated, Miranda was being driven in a van carrying only other women. When she attempted to strike up a conversation with the passenger next to her, the driver made her move to another seat.

The silence stretched for 45 minutes before the blindfolds were removed and the vehicle pulled up at what appeared to be a resort-style compound.

“I only knew the site lay on the city’s outskirts, nothing more,” said Miranda, who declined to give her full name. “They did not want me to learn the precise location. That was standard procedure every single time I was taken there.”
item.content:encoded:
It was like something out of a movie: blindfolded, her cellphone confiscated, Miranda was being driven in a van carrying only other women. When she attempted to strike up a conversation with the passenger next to her, the driver made her move to another seat.

The silence stretched for 45 minutes before the blindfolds were removed and the vehicle pulled up at what appeared to be a resort-style compound.

“I only knew the site lay on the city’s outskirts, nothing more,” said Miranda, who declined to give her full name. “They did not want me to learn the precise location. That was standard procedure every single time I was taken there.”

The facility was a surrogacy house in Wuhan, capital of central China’s Hubei province and Miranda’s hometown.

Chinese law says assisted reproductive technologies can only be performed by permitted medical institutions for married couples dealing with infertility, and only for medical purposes. Those using such technologies for surrogacy can be fined or face criminal charges.

‘Professional’ services

“I knew it was illegal, of course, but surrogacy was a forced choice for me, and it was my last hope of having my own baby,” Miranda said. She opted for it following two second-trimester miscarriages caused by moderate intrauterine adhesions, which complicate pregnancy by damaging the uterine lining and shrinking the space required for a fertilised egg to develop.

About five years ago, she learned about the Wuhan surrogacy agency from a friend in Shenzhen.

Her first impression was that the facility was clean and well-equipped. She described the agency as “professional”, while noting the irony of applying that term to an illegal operation.

“The doctors they arranged came from top local hospitals,” Miranda said. “For egg retrieval, a doctor and anaesthetist would come to the house, and nurses would make home visits for the ovulation-induction injections. But for key examinations, they would drive me to hospitals.”

Two years later, her son was born in a Wuhan hospital. The baby’s birth certificate listed the names of her husband and the surrogate mother. After obtaining her son’s household registration document, Miranda asked the surrogate mother to sign a contract waiving her parental rights.

She paid more than 600,000 yuan (US$89,454) to the Wuhan facility, with roughly a third going to the surrogate mother.

Miranda said the agency told her that most of its clients turned to surrogacy for the same reason: their uteruses were no longer medically viable to carry a pregnancy. Others were seeking to avoid exhausting rounds of hospital treatment.

China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists

Olivia Ngan, University of Hong Kong

Government concerns

An analysis released in March by Frost & Sullivan, a consultancy firm, said the number of infertile couples in China had risen from 54.8 million in 2020 to 60.6 million last year, and was projected to climb to 74.4 million by 2035.

While surrogacy may appear to be the solution for women like Miranda, Chinese policymakers consider it a practice carrying far more risks than benefits, and the authorities are adamant that surrogacy activities – in any form – are prohibited.

In 2021, when deputies to the National People’s Congress – the country’s top legislature – suggested allowing legal surrogacy to prevent repeated illegal operations, the National Health Commission replied that “surrogacy severely harms women’s health rights and interests”.

The practice “objectifies women and gives rise to a string of grave social problems, including human trafficking, and can cause ethical crises within the family and society”, it said.

The authorities renewed a clampdown on underground surrogacy networks last month.

Two laboratories, one in Wuhan and the other in Changsha, the capital of neighbouring Hunan province, were shut down for offering surrogacy services. Wuhan’s municipal health commission said eight people had been detained, police were investigating and “any illegal activities” would be severely punished.

This month, the health commission in Taicang, part of Suzhou bordering Shanghai, said it had carried out inspections together with police at an alleged surrogacy facility following online tip‑offs. It has yet to release its findings.

They were not the first crackdowns by national and local regulators targeting surrogacy operators.

In the second half of 2023, a 14-department task force headed by the National Health Commission rolled out a targeted nationwide campaign. It sought to root out crimes stemming from the unauthorised use of assisted reproductive technology, including commercial surrogacy and illegal egg harvesting.

“China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists,” said Olivia Ngan, research assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s school of clinical medicine. “The central ethical concern is that commercial surrogacy may lead to the commodification of women, reproduction and children.”

She said critics argued that “when pregnancy becomes a paid service, there is a risk that economically vulnerable women may be pressured into acting as surrogates, raising concerns about exploitation, coercion and unequal power relationships”.

‘One-stop service’

“Demand for surrogacy does not arise in a vacuum,” Ngan said, noting that those who had experienced infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss or related medical conditions could have a profound desire for genetically related children.

Propelled by such desires, China’s underground surrogacy industry now provided “one-stop service”, said Karen, a Shanghai resident who also declined to give her full name.

She married late and struggled with infertility for over five years. By the time she turned 45, her diminished egg quality meant scant prospects for wholly natural conception.

That was when Karen began exploring alternative options outside hospital care and was surprised to discover that the underground industry offered everything she needed. She opted for the same agency used by Miranda.

“The eggs I bought were relatively affordable,” she said. “I paid around 10,000 yuan because the donor – a woman in her twenties – did not have a top-tier educational background.

“The surrogate mothers were typically in their thirties. The agency told me that all of them had previously given birth, and it only recruited women from southwestern China’s Yunnan or Guizhou provinces because they tended to come from relatively low-income backgrounds.”

After the eggs were successfully fertilised with her husband’s sperm, the agency matched Karen with a surrogate mother.

Industry insiders said Wuhan and Guangzhou, the capital of southern China’s Guangdong province, were the two major Chinese hubs for surrogacy agencies, drawn by convenient transport links and relatively lower living costs, which helped keep overall expenses down.

China recorded a crude birth rate of 5.63 per thousand people last year, less than half the 12.95 per thousand in 2016, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Block or channel?

Ngan said that as China’s population aged and fertility rates remained low, “reproductive aspirations and reproductive health needs may become even more prominent social issues”.

To address infertility, China provides assisted reproductive technology services, with more than 600 medical institutions having been approved to deliver them or serve as human sperm banks by June last year.

At a news conference in June this year, the National Health Commission said the success rates for assisted reproductive technology services in China had reached internationally advanced levels. “Following comprehensive interventions, 80 per cent to 90 per cent of couples experiencing fertility difficulties are able to conceive naturally,” a commission official said.

However, that means multiple fertility treatments fail for 10 per cent to 20 per cent of women who are unable to carry a pregnancy.

Professor Kirsty Horsey, from the school of social sciences and humanities at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom, said: “Prohibition [of surrogacy] tends to make people seek alternatives, like going overseas or entering into more dangerous clandestine and potentially unethical arrangements. It is not unknown for trafficking and surrogacy to be connected, but ‘feeding’ this market by prohibitions really does not help.”

Chinese media have reported that because legal surrogacy services were unavailable, some people had sought them out overseas, with the US serving as one of the top destinations. Several high-profile Chinese actresses have been caught up in overseas surrogacy controversies in recent years, leading to some of them being effectively banned from the entertainment industry.

Beyond the United States, the UK, Canada and New Zealand also permit altruistic surrogacy, while banning the commercial arrangements allowed in America. Australia is conducting a review of its laws related to surrogacy.

Ngan said many countries that permitted surrogacy only allowed altruistic arrangements, where surrogates were reimbursed for expenses but received no payment for carrying a pregnancy. “This approach seeks to reduce commercial incentives and the risk of exploitation,” she said.

Horsey said overseas experience in jurisdictions with regulated surrogacy showed that “having a regulated and safe form of surrogacy available to infertile couples – with involvement of legitimate clinics, counsellors, lawyers, et cetera to give their respective advice and guidance – would legitimise a particular form of or route through surrogacy, meaning people would not have to resort to dangerous underground arrangements which are also likely to be less ethical”.

Miranda said that without surrogacy, “women like me” who were basically incapable of conceiving babies, even with modern medical help, “might never have children”.

“So I don’t believe this government-led clampdown will fully stamp out the business,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond the summit: how US-China relations could still unravel
item.description:
This year’s Chinese National Day reception in Washington felt noticeably jollier than those I have attended in recent years. The mood was more relaxed and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng’s opening speech was upbeat. He even joked about the panda ambassadors at his own expense.

The cheerful tone followed President Xi Jinping’s short but successful state visit to the US, during which his counterpart, President Donald Trump, gave him an unprecedented high-level reception that would have flattered even the most fastidious of guests.

Yet the mood outside the embassy was decidedly different. The opposition Democrats criticised Trump’s cosying up to “communist” China as another example of his misguided foreign policy, a betrayal of American allies and even a sell-out of national interests.
item.content:encoded:
This year’s Chinese National Day reception in Washington felt noticeably jollier than those I have attended in recent years. The mood was more relaxed and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng’s opening speech was upbeat. He even joked about the panda ambassadors at his own expense.

The cheerful tone followed President Xi Jinping’s short but successful state visit to the US, during which his counterpart, President Donald Trump, gave him an unprecedented high-level reception that would have flattered even the most fastidious of guests.

Yet the mood outside the embassy was decidedly different. The opposition Democrats criticised Trump’s cosying up to “communist” China as another example of his misguided foreign policy, a betrayal of American allies and even a sell-out of national interests.

The mainstream media, locked in a feud with Trump over his ban on media access to the White House, either downplayed the visit or focused on its lack of tangible progress. Even the president’s allies admitted in private that the timing “was not right” to expect a major breakthrough.

With the midterm elections just weeks away, the polarisation of American politics can only deepen. Even among Trump’s supporters and the business community, there is little agreement on what deals to seek with Beijing. Americans certainly want China to lift its rare earth export controls, but there is no consensus on what to offer in return.

Relaxing the US ban on advanced chips to China meets strong opposition. At the risk of oversimplification, there are two camps. One argues that the restrictions will only push Beijing to accelerate its own chip development, and that it is in American interests to allow a controlled flow of advanced chips to China to maintain its “chip dependency”.

The other believes that China will pursue an alternative chip industry regardless, and that selling advanced chips would merely buy Beijing time. This camp holds that the US should double down on the restrictions, particularly as nobody can be sure whether China, or any other country, can really build an alternative system independent of American-controlled components.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su sat at the head table at the state dinner Trump hosted for Xi, but the South China Morning Post was told that chip controls were never on the negotiating table. That suggests the hawks on this issue are in the driver’s seat.

There is similarly no consensus among Americans on regulating artificial intelligence, or “superintelligence” as the White House calls it. Some see regulation as a power grab by a handful of tech giants. Advocates of the open-source approach want to know how standards would be set, who would be responsible for verification, and how, even if a common set of standards could be agreed. The Chinese proposal to include chip controls in the bilateral AI dialogue only complicates matters.

The same is true of allowing more Chinese investment, or Chinese-owned electric vehicle and battery factories, in the United States. As the SCMP reported, some Chinese company executives travelled to Washington in the hope of a last-minute agreement that might open the door to US investment, but it proved futile.

It is telling that just a few days after Xi’s visit, Ford CEO Jim Farley warned that the US must carefully consider whether to admit Chinese carmakers to the American market, lest it become another Europe – a reference to the explosive growth of Chinese cars there. Farley wants to work with the Chinese only in areas where America can acquire technologies it lacks, which is hardly something Beijing will be excited about.

Beyond business, matters are even more complicated. It is widely known that Taiwan is Beijing’s absolute red line. Trump showed remarkable restraint on this sensitive issue throughout Xi’s visit, but even for him, the Chinese request that he openly oppose Taiwan independence was a bridge too far.

There is considerable pushback on the issue, even among Trump’s supporters. The president has delayed the latest round of arms sales to Taiwan, partly helped by supply shortages for more urgent needs elsewhere, but how long the administration can keep the lid on is an open question.

In his speech, Ambassador Xie highlighted the good rapport between Xi and Trump, which has become the most critical ballast stabilising the bilateral relationship. Western media wrote about how Trump caged the China hawks. Yet it is always risky to predict the American president’s behaviour.

He has been careful to maintain his relationship with Xi, but his China policy can change course drastically at any time. Those who accuse Trump of going soft on China would do well to remember that he launched an unprecedented trade war against Beijing just 18 months ago.

Trump has still to make a historic trip to Shenzhen, home of Huawei, BYD and DJI, and Xi will visit Miami. But the focus of these meetings will be more on international affairs, compared with their summit in September. The whispers in Washington are that, besides the lack of American consensus, US allies alarmed at the unprecedented reception Xi received are also working hard to lobby Washington to push back.

Japan is the most obvious example, but it is hardly the only country that feels this way. If there is no significant progress between Beijing and Washington by the time of the G20 summit, it will give the US, the European Union, Japan and others an opportunity to press China on issues such as the trade imbalance and rare earth controls.

Added to this is uncertainty over the impact of the midterm elections, which many predict will go badly for Trump. How will the president react? Will he shift his focus to domestic issues, take a more conciliatory approach, or double down? Dabbling in the arcane art of Trumpology is a career hazard.

None of this is to gainsay the positive results of Xi’s state visit, about which Beijing has plenty of reasons to feel pleased. But it would be dangerous to assume smooth sailing for China-US ties from here on. The next three months will determine whether strategic stability can truly emerge, or the relationship could go off the rails again.

item.title: [SCMP] 80 years on from WWII, China’s interests lie in peaceful Asia-Pacific: Rana Mitter
item.description:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?
item.content:encoded:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?

World War II is one of the most important factors in the shaping of modern China, but it’s often underestimated, both in China and the West.

This was the greatest political and economic trauma of the 20th century. The invasion of China by Japan led to many millions of deaths. Many Chinese became refugees within their own country.

The infrastructure and the communications built in the 1920s and 1930s were largely smashed into pieces, so that was a huge influence in terms of having to start again after the war.

The war made it more likely that China would have a revolution rather than just reform after it ended, because economic and social conditions became so devastatingly bad that it opened up space for the Chinese Communist Party to really develop the revolution in the countryside.

Beyond that, many aspects of modern China that we think of as part of the revolution actually emerged during the war – such as the system of work units for example, that existed for a long time in socialist China under Mao Zedong and even beyond.

The role of women became more prominent in Chinese life during the war years. Many younger women also became involved in national defence, health and nutrition, trying to make society after the war better for families and more stable.

During the 1920s and 1930s, China was heavily split between rival military leaders. At the end of the war, China was much closer to becoming unified as a country, as many of those warlords were eliminated during the wartime period.

Although it would finally be the 1949 revolution under Mao that provided a solid unification of the country, the process began in the wartime years.

World War II continues to be very important in terms of remembering a time when different factions and parties, nationalists, communists and others came together against an outside enemy and were able to find a sense of national purpose.

How could Beijing use the 80th World War II anniversary commemoration as an opportunity to improve people-to-people exchanges with the West?

The problem is that China still isn’t very good at seizing diplomatic opportunities because it tends to fall back on language that is mainly about China’s complaints, rather than about opportunities that could really open up.

The opportunities tend to be expressed in very broad, positive but vague terms, and the complaints tend to be very specific. And the problem is, it’s quite hard to get people on your side if you don’t actually engage in a dialogue that seems as if both sides are genuinely talking to each other.

An example is cutting down the EU-China summit from two days to one. Beijing also insisted that the Europeans should come to Beijing, when actually it was China’s turn to come to Europe.

So Europeans have done these things – they’re diplomatic people. They say OK, but it’s not the easiest start in terms of suggesting that China is opening up a new conversation, where China is willing to actually be expansive and creative in its thinking.

So maybe a sort of reset of Chinese diplomacy is an opportunity to do that. So far, there aren’t many signs of that. China has, in the past couple of years, withdrawn from the famous Wolf Warrior diplomacy, but it hasn’t yet worked out what sits in its place.

Do you think Chinese officials understand how their diplomacy is viewed from an outside perspective?

Very smart Chinese diplomats are aware that China has a PR problem. Just because people now find the US much less predictable doesn’t mean that they think China is a safe bet.

So, finding ways to essentially define China – not just in words, but in actions and in patterns of behaviour – as a reliable partner, that’s the really key challenge for Chinese diplomacy in the next few years.

The language is sometimes there – not always, but sometimes – but the actions involve a lot of quite difficult and long-term effort. And so far, if that’s happening, it’s only at a very early stage of that process.

A lot of Chinese diplomats, publicly and privately, have said they thought the previous Wolf Warrior effort was a mistake, asking what comes next and how China actually takes advantage of the changing world order.

That will involve more than just hoping that people will feel alienated from America and automatically seek out China. They won’t. Well, that will not be enough on its own.

World War II ended in the Pacific theatre with two atomic bombs dropped on Japan. Now, 80 years later, Britain and France have announced joint cooperation on nuclear weapons and the US has once again deployed nuclear forces in the UK. What does this say about the future of nuclear weapons?

Nuclear non-proliferation is definitely much weaker than it has been. Many of the Cold War-era treaties between the Soviet Union and the US seem to be essentially falling away. Britain and France are primarily concerned with their own major security vulnerability as the future American position on Russia remains uncertain.

A lot of different actors are looking at new threats in the world and trying to work out whether their current nuclear stance is sustainable. Ukraine gave up nuclear weapons in 1994, which made it vulnerable to the Russian invasion. Many countries will be looking at Ukraine’s experience and trying to avoid that.

The US has engaged directly with Russia to end the Ukraine war but those warmer ties now seem to have cooled off. What is your view of the changing dynamic between them?

Right now, the person who is probably having to think most carefully about changing the US position is Russian President Vladimir Putin.

For much of the first part of the year, the Donald Trump administration tried to find ways to bring Moscow back into the negotiations about Ukraine.

But in the past few weeks, it’s become clear that President Trump thinks Putin has no intention of coming to a peace agreement. It’s possible that he may take a much more confrontational attitude with Russia.

The world was very surprised when Trump actually made the decision to bomb Iran. His general doctrine is that getting into wars is a bad idea, but when he considers it necessary he is prepared to use force – and that’s something Putin might now have to think about.

How could this changing dynamic in Russia-US ties affect China?

Maybe several months ago, there were some people in Washington who thought that it might be possible to detach Russia from China in a “reverse Nixon”, or “reverse Kissinger” play, but that is not a very widely held idea any more, for two reasons.

First, people realise that there is a very close relationship between Russia and China. This was made clear by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when meeting his European Union counterparts. For the first time, it was much more explicit that China would not wish to see Russia lose.

The other factor is the American idea that they could detach Russia from China and bring it close to the US has fallen away. People have seen that Putin has not changed his policy towards Ukraine at all and is bombing it more fiercely than before.

We’re likely to see a scenario in which the US tries to neutralise Russia as much as possible while still looking for a negotiation on Ukraine, but essentially there probably will be more concentration on pushing back against China alone.

What conditions could bring about the end of the war?

We don’t know what conditions it will take to come to an end, but we do know that, at least in the past few weeks, President Trump has reauthorised the supply of weaponry to Ukraine to fight back against Russia, which at one point he was holding back on.

Now it’s clear that weaponry is going to Ukraine and the war may last longer than would have seemed the case just a few weeks ago, when it seemed Ukraine might run out of ammunition.

The question becomes whether Russia can maintain its all-out war-based economy and conscription of soldiers, while keeping inflation – which is very, very high – under control.

The longer the Ukraine war continues, the less likely it is that Russia can do that, and the more weapons that are supplied by the Americans, along with the Europeans, the longer the Ukrainians can keep fighting.

Under former president Joe Biden, Washington and other Western capitals formed a united stance on a wide range of China-related issues. How will Trump’s presidency change that alliance on China?

Europeans are looking to negotiate on their own issues with the US, such as tariffs. The question of China has been put a bit on the back shelf but essentially, the issue is that China provides useful supply chains.

There is also a problem, in particular for Europe, of whether it can draw on China’s markets but not be overwhelmed by Chinese exports, particularly in areas like autos and electric batteries. Those problems are not really changed by the relationship with the US.

The EU has a whole variety of fundamental issues it needs to solve – about how it creates a new industrial model, where it cooperates with China and where it needs to restrict its market.

And in some ways, it’s learning from China, because China has heavily restricted its own market in some areas, such as online service provision. So the Europeans will also pick and choose where they feel vulnerable, opening up in certain areas and closing in others.

The Trump administration is still figuring out its policy on China. There are different strands of thinking that you can see from the outside, but how important they are in relation to each other, and how they will balance out in the end, is still unclear.

For instance, there are some traditional hawks, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others, who take a view on China that in some ways would not have been that different from Republicans seven or 10 years ago.

But you also have the whole technology world – Silicon Valley and beyond. A lot of them are still very interested in making sure that the relationship with China is smooth.

Apple is one of the most profitable and innovative companies in the United States, but huge amounts of its production and connection still take place in China. Of course, some production has moved to India, but China is still really important to a company like Apple.

There has been a growing interest in moving more production and intellectual property back to the US but there’s no sense yet that this is a complete disconnection from China, and that points in a different direction from the hawks.

Then there is the question of what Trump himself thinks. It’s interesting to look at the tariff policy, because tariffs have been put on China but also on other countries, including traditional US allies.

Also, when Trump says “I like to talk to my good friend Xi Jinping. We can talk about things” – what does he want to talk about? Not clear.

Compared with other presidents, Trump seems to really like personal diplomacy. In other words, he believes that his personal relationships with leaders are the important thing.

Speaking of leadership diplomacy, what conditions do you think will be needed for Trump and Xi to meet?

I think a meeting between the two leaders is quite likely. Trump is announcing that the deal has been done with China. He would only want to go to China if the deal is kind of there, so he can mark it in a big ceremony and have a prominent meeting with Xi.

I don’t think he would want to go to China to negotiate. We’re moving into a phase where the US wants to get most of its tariff deals done within the next couple of months.

During his first term, Trump had a very grand welcoming ceremony provided by Xi in Beijing. I think he would like to do that again – a big, grand meeting that Trump will think of as a historic event, that showcases he’s able to do negotiations and deals with China in a way that other presidents haven’t been able to do. I think he would want to push quite hard in that direction. That’s my guess.

Are the two presidents likely to get along?

I think that’s perfectly possible. You might remember that when Trump invited Xi to Mar-a-Lago, he said that he gave Xi a big piece of chocolate cake. He never talked about giving chocolate cake to German chancellor Angela Merkel.

That’s a sign that he feels there’s some sort of ability to speak leader to leader in that sense. Xi has said less about Trump, but he hasn’t said any very publicly hostile things personally about him.

Will it stop competition? No. Will it stop conflict? Maybe. In some areas – I would single out technology – I think the US and China are going to be increasingly in competition and there will be less sharing of intellectual property or scientific development.

That would mean other countries could benefit from both, or they may have to choose a side. This will not change because of a meeting.

But can the two leaders talk about lowering the temperature and avoiding misunderstandings that could lead to military confrontation? That might be more possible.

Turning to China’s security environment, how might Beijing’s relations with its neighbours change, given the uncertainties of Washington’s policies during the Trump administration?
