While Dedi has earned a reputation as an on-the-spot problem solver, venturing beyond his provincial boundaries risks overstepping his mandate, said Aditya Perdana, a political science lecturer at Universitas Indonesia.

By attempting to intervene in crises outside West Java, Aditya argued, the governor was increasingly playing “offside” in the eyes of party elites by projecting influence where he had no jurisdiction.

His widening ground engagement has likely not gone unnoticed inside Prabowo’s party, which Dedi joined only in 2023 after decamping from Golkar, according to analysts.

“The potential main friction lies in Prabowo’s inner circle in Gerindra, who may perceive Dedi’s activities outside of West Java as his political warm-up agenda for the 2029 election,” said Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political researcher at the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN).

Gerindra’s bind

Publicly, Gerindra has dismissed the polling disparity between the two men. After the release of the SMRC report, the party’s daily executive chairman, Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, brushed off pollster’s figures, saying surveys could “fluctuate” from one cycle to the next.

Djayadi has noted Dedi’s “strategic ambiguity” by routinely deflecting questions about his national ambitions and insisting he remains focused on his present position.

“I am currently just thinking about how to be a successful governor,” Dedi told reporters last month when pressed on his 2029 prospects. “Now is not the time for that.”

As for Prabowo, while Gerindra elites have already publicly pushed him to run for a second term, the 75-year-old incumbent has so far refused to commit, stating repeatedly earlier this year that he would not run in 2029 if he felt his administration had underperformed.

Should Prabowo decide to run, Dedi has been touted by some observers as the president’s running mate. But Burhannudin said voter data suggested that such an alliance could fail.

“One complication is the emerging ‘anyone but Prabowo’ sentiment,” Burhanuddin explained.

“If Dedi becomes the running mate of an incumbent whose popularity has been declining significantly ... some voters who currently support Dedi could instead move towards Anies or Gibran,” he added, referring to former Jakarta governor Anies Baswedan and Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, both of whom are also seen as potential 2029 contenders.

“We should not assume that all Dedi supporters would automatically follow him into a Prabowo-Dedi ticket. Some may prefer Dedi precisely because they see him as an alternative to the incumbent.”

Nor can Gerindra sideline Dedi and order him to remain an obedient campaigner on Prabowo’s behalf without consequence, Burhanuddin said.

“The publicly available survey data suggest that, if Dedi is removed from the presidential-choice simulation, Anies and Gibran benefit more than Prabowo,” he added.

Another possibility is that Dedi could leave Gerindra to seek a ticket elsewhere.

This prospect has become plausible following a landmark Constitutional Court ruling last year that abolished the minimum requirement of 20 per cent of the vote for a political party before it could nominate a presidential candidate, which has opened a back door for popular independents to contest in an election for the top job.

“This significantly changes the strategic environment,” Burhanuddin said. “Other parties that lack a sufficiently popular presidential figure of their own may be interested in nominating Dedi for president.”

Long road to 2029

Dedi, however, faces the daunting task of sustaining his populist aura given the relentless public scrutiny. While his personal approval rating remains sky-high, his governance record is not without blemishes.

In June, the turbulent rollout of West Java’s public school admissions system left thousands of parents frustrated after their children failed to secure places at state schools, prompting Dedi to issue a public apology.

With West Java facing a projected 3.4-trillion-rupiah deficit, Dedi announced last month that he was halting all new provincial projects to avoid taking on massive debt.

The polling landscape, however, remains far from uniform. A nationwide survey conducted in late August by pollster Median offered a counterweight to earlier findings, placing Prabowo in the lead with 32.4 per cent support, followed by Dedi at 20.6 per cent and Anies at 20.5 per cent.

Three years is a long time in Indonesian politics, Burhanuddin warned, and early regional momentum can easily evaporate as the stakes rise.

“His current popularity is real, but sustaining it until 2029 will depend on whether his personal appeal can survive the much harder tests of governing performance, greater national scrutiny and the changing political environment.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia urged to police its firms in Indonesia as haze shuts schools
item.description:
Malaysia is facing renewed pressure to clamp down on its companies over their alleged links to forest fires abroad, as recurring haze from Indonesia continues to disrupt schools and daily life despite years of regional efforts to tackle the problem.

On Thursday, Malaysia ordered schools to close across several states, including Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and the Rompin district in Pahang, while sporting events scheduled for the weekend were cancelled.

The latest closures follow findings by environmental watchdogs Greenpeace and Pantau Gambut alleging links between Malaysian and Singaporean corporate interests and fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Kalimantan. The findings have intensified calls for Putrajaya to take action on companies linked to fires abroad, rather than rely on regional cooperation that has yet to prevent recurring haze crises.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia is facing renewed pressure to clamp down on its companies over their alleged links to forest fires abroad, as recurring haze from Indonesia continues to disrupt schools and daily life despite years of regional efforts to tackle the problem.

On Thursday, Malaysia ordered schools to close across several states, including Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and the Rompin district in Pahang, while sporting events scheduled for the weekend were cancelled.

The latest closures follow findings by environmental watchdogs Greenpeace and Pantau Gambut alleging links between Malaysian and Singaporean corporate interests and fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Kalimantan. The findings have intensified calls for Putrajaya to take action on companies linked to fires abroad, rather than rely on regional cooperation that has yet to prevent recurring haze crises.

On Wednesday, Greenpeace Malaysia and civil society groups marched to parliament, demanding stronger legislation to investigate companies linked to fires that have contributed to the ongoing haze crisis.

“Malaysia must have the legal power to investigate and hold companies accountable where credible evidence links them to environmental harm beyond our borders,” Greenpeace Malaysia campaign manager Heng Kiah Chun said in a statement.

“A transboundary haze law cannot remain on the drawing board while communities continue to bear the health consequences of haze year after year.”

Members of parliament received the memorandum from Greenpeace on Wednesday, with Bandar Kuching MP Kelvin Yii saying authorities had struggled to gather evidence, investigate and enforce laws against entities outside the country’s jurisdiction.

Bukit Bendera MP Syerleena Abdul Rashid said the recurring impact on schools, air quality and public health demanded stronger regional action.

“We already know the cause. Now we need action,” she said, according to local news outlets.

Malaysia has sought to draft a transboundary haze law since 2019, with the previous Pakatan Harapan government agreeing in principle in February 2020 to develop a framework that would give authorities powers to pursue companies over activities abroad. The proposal was championed by former environment minister Yeo Bee Yin after the severe haze crisis in 2019.

But the proposal was not advanced after a change of government. The new administration argued that its ability to pursue companies for activities in foreign jurisdictions was limited, particularly without cooperation from foreign authorities.

As civil society groups press for the law to be revived, Malaysia faces the challenge of holding its companies accountable for environmental damage beyond its borders. Experts say targeted legislation and continued cooperation with Indonesia would be needed.

Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of environmental politics and governance at the University of Malaya, said the country had a responsibility to ensure its companies operated responsibly abroad but currently lacked the jurisdiction to take action against them for misconduct in Indonesia.

“If the Malaysian law is revived and passed according to this ‘Malaysian entities only’ format, it should be quite effective,” Varkkey said.

She said a revived law should focus on Malaysian entities operating overseas whose activities had caused haze at home, rather than adopting Singapore’s broader approach of pursuing companies regardless of nationality.

Such a focus could deter Malaysian companies while signalling to Indonesia that Malaysia was also overseeing its own entities.

Singapore enacted its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014, allowing authorities to pursue Singaporean and foreign entities whose conduct abroad causes or contributes to unhealthy haze in Singapore.

Under the law, perpetrators can face criminal or civil liability for activities such as land clearing by fire, with companies facing fines of S$100,000 (US$78,000) per day of haze pollution, capped at S$2 million.

Varkkey said Malaysia’s proposed legislation could also ease diplomatic tensions following Singapore’s adoption of its haze legislation, which Indonesia has viewed as interference.

“Limiting the legislation to Malaysian entities could give Indonesia diplomatic space to deal with other companies while avoiding diplomatic sensitivities of an extraterritorial law,” she said.

However, other experts said giving Malaysian authorities powers to pursue companies abroad would not solve the enforcement problem that derailed the legislation six years ago.

Renard Siew, climate adviser at the Malaysia-based Centre for Governance and Political Studies, said any transboundary haze law would need clear standards of liability, credible evidence, meaningful penalties and due process if it was to become more than a symbolic deterrent.

“A company’s responsibility should not stop at Malaysia’s borders simply because its operations are offshore,” Siew said, but cautioned that detecting fires alone did not establish who started them or prove corporate wrongdoing.

Greenpeace Malaysia, Greenpeace Indonesia and Pantau Gambut identified Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong (KLK), through its reported ties to Indonesian entity Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana, among the top 20 entities linked to findings on fires in Indonesia in 2026, according to a report released on Monday. The analysis drew on data tracking haze sources from August to October 1, the groups said.

Greenpeace said Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana had also been identified as having fires on its land in a separate 2019 report. The findings do not, by themselves, establish that KLK or the Indonesian entity started the fires or was legally responsible for them.

“Forest and peatland fires that continue to persist are not part of a natural cycle but a reflection that economic expansion based on global commodities is valued more highly than the lives of citizens,” Greenpeace said in a statement.

Separately, Greenpeace Indonesia said its analysis identified 5,540 smoke-source points across Indonesia between August 8 and September 20. Of these, 774 were within 210 oil-palm plantation concessions and 859 within 115 licensed forestry concessions. The figures indicate the locations of detected smoke sources, not proof that concession holders caused the fires.

KLK rejected suggestions that Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana was responsible for the fires, saying most had originated outside its concession area and had since been extinguished.

“As a Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil member, we uphold our zero burning policy aligned with its principles and criteria,” KLK said in a statement on Tuesday. “We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations.”

Experts say the dispute shows why legislation alone may not be enough, as Malaysia’s ability to pursue companies beyond its borders ultimately depends on obtaining evidence, establishing liability and enforcing it against those found responsible.

While Asean cooperation matters, cooperation without enforceable obligations risks becoming a cycle of statements followed by the same crisis.

“The biggest failure is not a lack of regional commitments; it is the gap between commitments and consequences,” Siew said.

He said the fundamental problem was no longer the lack of regional commitments but the failure to translate those promises into consequences.

“When schools close, the costs are borne by the public, while those responsible may face limited consequences. This is fundamentally an accountability failure.”

item.title: [SCMP] The hidden heartbreak of losing a pet in Singapore and Malaysia
item.description:
Growing up in a Malay family in Singapore, Hafeez Hassan feared dogs. He never expected to mourn one like a sibling.

“Maybe that is what I have been grieving all along … The experience of loving something that I was taught I was not supposed to love,” he said.

Even as an adult, walking his former partner’s husky Pieces in public made Hafeez anxious that a relative might see him, or that he might be judged for being close to an animal whose saliva and waste are regarded as ritually impure by many Muslims in the region.
item.content:encoded:
Growing up in a Malay family in Singapore, Hafeez Hassan feared dogs. He never expected to mourn one like a sibling.

“Maybe that is what I have been grieving all along … The experience of loving something that I was taught I was not supposed to love,” he said.

Even as an adult, walking his former partner’s husky Pieces in public made Hafeez anxious that a relative might see him, or that he might be judged for being close to an animal whose saliva and waste are regarded as ritually impure by many Muslims in the region.

Touching or holding a dog is not sinful, according to the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore. Though it did note in a 2014 advisory that other schools of Islamic jurisprudence had different views on dogs.

Hafeez, who is a dance choreographer and movement coach, did not immediately seek counselling when Pieces died.

Years passed before he started to talk openly about what the loss meant to him with George Chan, a loss and grief counsellor in the city state whom Hafeez knew from their work together on dance productions and musicals.

Disenfranchised grief

Hafeez’s experience is one that counsellors in Singapore and Malaysia say they recognise all too well.

Those in the profession call “disenfranchised grief”, a term for a loss that is not openly acknowledged or socially supported, and that others may not readily understand or accept.

A dead pet can bring on such a feeling when owners sense the bond they had with an animal is being minimised or dismissed.

“The moment they feel like they have to defend their grief, it becomes a very lonely thing,” Chan said.

What is lost is often more than just an animal, according to grief counsellors. It can be the routines that were built around the pet, or the absence of a steady companion that helped an owner through upheavals and challenging times.

Some clients come to Chan specifically because their pets have died. For others, the grief only surfaces while they are working through other issues such as a divorce or the death of a parent.

Chan’s sessions often begin with the pet’s name and what kind of companion it was.

“I’m not trying to understand death,” he said. “I’m trying to understand the relationship.”

For owners who had to decide whether to euthanise their pet, guilt over acting too soon or waiting too long was often part of the grieving process, Chan said.

“Sometimes it is easier to hold on to a guilt story than to accept that you were completely helpless … with guilt, you can still blame yourself, the vet or someone else,” he said, adding that the alternative was to admit there was nothing more the owner could have done.

He sets no fixed number of sessions for his clients and does not regard grief as a problem to be solved.

“My job is not to fix a five-week-old grief, you grieve because you loved,” Chan said.

Lifelines after loss

In Malaysia, PiePie Pet Memorial has made follow-up care part of its services, rather than treating the farewell ceremony as the end of its role.

Manager Tan Chien Yung said the company began formally tracking counsellor follow-ups in 2022, with more than 4,000 bereaved pet owners receiving such support in the years since.

Last year, the pet funeral and cremation services provider recorded around 1,250 follow-ups with grieving owners, up from 1,030 the year before. So far in 2026, some 850 owners have been contacted.

Not all follow-ups result in a dedicated grief support session. In fact, only 21 owners had booked a complimentary session since 2022, Tan said.

“The purpose of the service is not to encourage more people to attend counselling,” he said. “It is to make sure that no pet owner feels they have to navigate their grief alone.”

Tan Su Wen, a licensed counsellor who works part-time with PiePie on its follow-ups, usually calls about a week after the final farewell, or sooner if funeral staff report that an owner appeared particularly distressed during the ceremony.

“Some owners feel a degree of closure after a formal send-off,” she said, adding that guilt was a common concern among those owners who sought help after euthanising a pet or losing one to an unforeseen accident.

Like Chan, she finds that many owners struggle with the shock of a sudden death or the loss of an animal companion that had become part of the family.

For Adam Ishak, her help really mattered. Samuel, his orange Persian-Maine Coon mix, died in late February at the age of 12, after a year-long battle with feline chronic kidney disease.

As the cat’s condition worsened, Ishak and his wife opted for euthanasia to spare it further suffering. Their advice to other owners is to look out for possible signs of the disease and seek veterinary advice early.

Ishak, who has lived with cats all his life, said Samuel “left a mark on my life like no other”.

The PiePie team’s support had been invaluable, he said, especially the “certificate of life … which is hanging above his ashes in our home”.

Every day, the couple light a candle and say Samuel’s name, based on a traditional Central American belief “that a life dies three times: when the body dies, when it is interred and when its name is spoken for the last time”.

“Because of the last ‘death’, I believe Samuel is still alive for as long as we remember him,” Ishak said.

Enduring taboos

While losing a dog or cat is the most common reason people see a pet bereavement counsellor, grief is not necessarily dictated by the pet’s species or size.

Chan noted a tendency for society to create a hierarchy even within pet loss, assuming the death of a dog carried more emotional weight than that of a bird, fish or reptile.

Most of his clients were dog owners, but he said he had also counselled someone grieving a bird.

At PiePie, grief-support appointments have mainly involved dogs and cats, but also rabbits and hamsters. The company has even held a farewell for a pet fish.

Hafeez got another dog after Pieces’ passing. Ali, a shih-tzu, has been with him for six years. But there are still family gatherings at which Ali is not welcome.

“There is something painful about loving an animal deeply while knowing that a relationship is considered forbidden or unacceptable by parts of your own community,” Hafeez said.

“And the more I think about it, the more that hurts, not because I need everyone to relate to dogs the way I do, but because I would genuinely love for my family to meet someone who has become part of my family too.”

item.title: [SCMP] After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
item.description:
As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets.

Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.

Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.

Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific.

Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade.

“Unlike tariffs, which can be set out as part of a policy framework, sovereign debt management involves actual capital allocation and is highly sensitive, making it unlikely to be formally addressed in official statements,” Chang noted.

“However, from a strategic perspective, Beijing’s ongoing reserve diversification does serve as an important piece of leverage in these high-stakes bilateral negotiations.”

These moves, together with Beijing’s push to internationalise its currency and develop alternative payment infrastructure, are viewed by some analysts as largely defensive measures rather than an attempt to displace the US dollar.

But they cautioned that any efforts to protect China against potential US financial pressure could themselves become a long-term source of friction between the two countries, particularly if Washington sees them as weakening its currency’s international role.

Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well

Matteo Giovannini, Centre for China and Globalisation

The Treasury retreat

Long regarded as one of the safest assets in global markets, US Treasuries have come under increasing pressure as investors grapple with the more than US$40 trillion federal debt burden and the prospect of interest rates continuing to remain high amid stubborn inflation.

A global sell-off in government bonds in recent months has pushed long-term Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, with both the 10-year and 30-year yields recently rising to their highest levels since 2002. Underscoring this retreat, Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages Norway’s US$2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, recently proposed a significant reduction in its exposure to US government bonds.

Short-term market factors have played a role, but the latest unease about American government debt has also fed into a broader debate over “de-dollarisation”.

Barry Eichengreen, a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, described this latest wave as different from previous episodes, as questions mount over the strength of American political institutions and the durability of its geopolitical alliances.

Japan, one of Washington’s long-standing allies, cut its US Treasury holdings for three consecutive months to US$1.1 trillion in July, according to the latest data from the US Treasury Department.

Once Washington’s largest foreign creditor, China continues to diversify its foreign reserves away from US Treasuries as uncertainties in the bilateral relationship persist. The shift has also coincided with growing concern among Chinese officials and academics over the risks of relying too heavily on the American currency.

China dropped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year, and its holdings fell to an 18-year low of US$618 billion this July, according to the US Treasury Department – though questions remain over whether headline figures tell the full story.

Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last month that China’s state-owned banks held substantial dollar assets offshore that were not included in the country’s official reserves.

At the same time, Chang said China’s massive US Treasury holdings might give Beijing some potential leverage because a deliberate sell-off could destabilise markets.

“Beijing can also use modest, short-term increases in its holdings to send a friendly signal, particularly when the Treasury market is under pressure,” Chang said. “It is a reciprocal diplomatic dynamic – if China shows goodwill, it would naturally expect certain concessions from the US in exchange.”

Some analysts argued that China also had an interest in preventing a disorderly crisis in the US Treasury market, even as it continued to gradually reduce its stockpiles.

“Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “I would therefore distinguish between gradual diversification and actively destabilising the market.”

China’s continued trimming of Treasury holdings was nevertheless part of a broader shift in the market’s investor base, Giovannini noted, making it “more sensitive to supply-demand pressures.”

Wiring a safety net

Alongside China’s diversification away from US dollar-denominated assets, Beijing is building financial infrastructure that could give it more options for cross-border payments and trade. That includes efforts to expand the international use of the yuan and systems such as the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) and Project mBridge.

CIPS provides an alternative channel for cross-border payments to Western-dominated networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly known as Swift. Project mBridge, meanwhile, is a multilateral platform designed to ease direct settlements using digital currencies issued by central banks.

Both initiatives have made headway, though the pace of growth has varied. The value of transactions processed through CIPS grew at a double-digit pace for several years before rising by just 2.7 per cent last year, official data showed. Transaction value then rose 11.9 per cent year on year to 100.9 trillion yuan (US$14.9 trillion) in the first half of this year, according to the People’s Bank of China’s annual yuan internationalisation report released last month.

By the end of June, CIPS had 210 direct participants and 1,619 indirect participants, with services reaching 192 countries and regions, the report said.

Analysts said Beijing’s main objective was to make China’s financial system more resilient and reduce its vulnerability to potential sanctions or other restrictions.

“I would see this as building a safety net, consolidating global financial influence and even laying the groundwork for the future – but not as an effort to replace the US dollar, which is not something that could be achieved in the foreseeable future,” said Chang of Fudan University.

He added that meaningfully challenging the US dollar would require China to fully open its capital account – the rules governing how freely money can move in and out of the country. Any such move would require Beijing to surrender greater control over the exchange rate and could undermine its export-driven economic model, he said.

Data also underscores how far the yuan remains behind the US dollar as a reserve currency. The yuan accounted for 2.11 per cent of global central bank reserves in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 56.7 per cent for the US dollar, according to the International Monetary Fund.

The purpose of projects such as mBridge, Chang argued, should be understood primarily in terms of making cross-border trade and payments easier in regions that had often been underserved by the US financial system.

“Once you establish payment infrastructure, you can build trust and facilitate capital flows, which also opens the door to broader financial services,” Chang said.

Project mBridge has brought together the central banks of mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Macau, which joined in June. Saudi Arabia joined the project in 2024 but ceased taking part in May of last year.

Even if replacing the US dollar is not Beijing’s intention, analysts cautioned that a larger global role for the yuan could still be viewed in Washington as a challenge to the dollar-based financial system.

“Parts of Washington will treat even a regional yuan system as a strategic threat, because payments infrastructure is dual-use: trade convenience plus sanctions resilience,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

These concerns could lead to greater scrutiny of CIPS links and correspondent banks, she added.

Washington has also shown sensitivity to potential challenges to the US dollar’s dominant role, including Trump threatening to impose 100 per cent tariffs on Brics countries if they move to create a new currency or replace the dollar.

Brics, a grouping of major emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members.

Garcia-Herrero forecast a future of “managed coexistence”, with the US dollar retaining its role as the global reserve and invoicing currency while the yuan expands across Asia, energy markets and China-centric trade. She also expected “occasional political flare-ups when either side talks [about] ‘weaponisation.’”

Giovannini, also an AsiaGlobal Fellow at the University of Hong Kong, expressed a similar view, saying concerns in Washington could become more pronounced if the yuan expands its role in trade and financial infrastructure across the Global South.

“This could also create a feedback loop, with US financial leverage encouraging China to build alternatives, and those alternatives in turn increasing US concerns about dollar primacy,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing’s policy advisers map out how post-reunification Taiwan could be governed
item.description:
In 2019, President Xi Jinping became the first Chinese leader to publicly call for the exploration of detailed proposals for governing Taiwan after reunification.

Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance.
item.content:encoded:
In 2019, President Xi Jinping became the first Chinese leader to publicly call for the exploration of detailed proposals for governing Taiwan after reunification.

Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance.

“The earlier Taiwan engages in talks with the mainland, the more bargaining power it would have, and therefore the greater the space it would have to shape the terms. That is almost inevitable,” said Chen Xiancai, a Taiwan affairs professor at Xiamen University.

Chen said that, given the state of cross-strait relations, one scenario he considered “highly viable” would be forcing Taiwan into reunification talks by applying pressure across the political, military and international arenas.

While this does not represent Beijing’s official policy, Chen said he believed some of the measures had already been employed in recent years, and that a blockade of the island could not be ruled out if deemed necessary in the future.

The sooner they talk, the better the terms

The study led by Chen, the director of the university’s Centre for Taiwan Studies, is among the research projects undertaken by mainland Chinese scholars since Xi’s landmark speech to explore a “two systems” Taiwan.

These projects have not yet been published.

Xi’s call built on the “one country, two systems” model, which was first formulated by former Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s as a possible solution to the Taiwan question. It has already been implemented in Hong Kong and Macau.

Under the formula, which holds that there is only one China, the island could retain its existing economic and social systems and enjoy a high degree of autonomy after reunification.

In that 2019 speech, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-standing position that peaceful reunification remained “the best approach”, saying the “one country, two systems” formula was designed “precisely to accommodate Taiwan’s actual conditions”.

Seven years after the speech, Beijing has said little publicly about how it would seek to govern Taiwan following reunification.

However, Tsinghua University and Xiamen University have finalised their studies on the subject this year, with another one conducted by Peking University close to completion, according to academic sources.

The studies do not represent Beijing’s official policy, but serve as a reference for policymaking and offer a rare glimpse into academic discussions about the possible terms of a future settlement across the Taiwan Strait.

A recurring theme discussed by scholars involved in the studies is that the circumstances under which reunification took place would determine the extent of autonomy granted to Taiwan.

“If reunification were achieved entirely through peaceful means, with the two sides negotiating now, Taiwan’s room to manoeuvre – or the powers and status it might retain – could potentially be greater than those of Hong Kong and Macau,” Chen said.

But if reunification were achieved through what Chen described as “compelled reunification”, Taiwan could be offered a Hong Kong- or Macau-style model, or possibly “even less autonomy” than the two special administrative regions, he said.

“Compelled reunification” – or bitong – is a term coined by mainland scholars to describe an approach between complete peaceful reunification and a full-scale attack.

This approach, they argue, means reunification is compelled after Beijing deploys a range of political, economic, military and diplomatic measures.

“However, if Taiwan does not accept the goodwill offered by the mainland or its policy of peaceful reunification, and instead forces the mainland to resort to military means, Taiwan will have fewer bargaining chips, and its room to manoeuvre will be severely curtailed,” Chen said.

Other heavyweight policy advisers have echoed this point, including Li Yihu, a lawmaker and Taiwan specialist at Peking University, who warned last year that if Taiwan left Beijing no choice but to reunify by force, the island’s autonomy would be the same as an average province.

Discussions among scholars about a detailed plan for Beijing to govern Taiwan have grown in the past month. On September 12, more than 20 mainland scholars, led by Wang Jianmin of Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, reached a 12-point consensus on a plan for Taiwan at a seminar in Beijing.

Their proposal included maintaining a People’s Liberation Army presence on the island and introducing patriotic education.

However, another scholar, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Taiwan-related academic research on the mainland was far more diverse than the 12-point proposal, which did not represent the full range of views among mainland academics.

The discussion was joined by Li Ci-ze, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education. In a proposal published in August, Li argued that after peaceful reunification, Taiwan should be able to retain its direct elections for the island’s top executive official and legislature while “fully retaining” its opposition parties.

Beijing said it was pleased to see the proposal, without hinting at whether it agreed with the details.

Chang Ya-chung, head of the Taiwan-based Sun Yat-sen School advocacy group, said the two sides should take gradual steps towards signing a peace deal before discussing the details of post-reunification governance.

He made the comments during his trip to Beijing to attend last month’s Xiangshan Forum security conference, and later elaborated on them in an article.

When asked about Chang’s remarks, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office said it welcomed suggestions from Taiwan’s people, and “the sooner and more extensively” the Taiwanese held such discussions, the more benefits they would see.

‘Compelled reunification’

The strategy of “compelled reunification” is highly feasible under current cross-strait conditions, according to Chen, though Beijing authorities have never publicly acknowledged the idea.

“What we mean by ‘compelled reunification’ is essentially the use of certain measures to shape, guide or pressure the Taiwan authorities towards reunification,” Chen said.

He argued that this was a special form of “peaceful reunification”.

“It is carried out within the broader policy of peaceful reunification, but its distinctive feature is the use of pressure,” he said, adding that it could encompass military, diplomatic, economic and legal measures.

“Compelled reunification does not necessarily mean a military conflict. It would not necessarily be like the Russia-Ukraine war, where the PLA would have to enter Taiwan or launch a landing operation on the island.”

A blockade could also be one possible form of pressure under such a scenario, he added.

In recent years, Beijing has conducted large-scale military exercises around Taiwan, including drills that have simulated elements of a blockade and involved coordination between the PLA and mainland China’s coastguard.

Chen said the approach also had historical precedents in the Communist Party’s handling of the civil war against the Nationalists before 1949. He cited the case of the “Beiping model”, referring to the peaceful takeover of Beiping, now Beijing, by the Communist Party in 1949.

The Communist forces’ military advantage in north China, including the seizure of Tianjin and the siege of Beijing, forced the Nationalist defenders to agree to a peaceful takeover by the PLA in Beijing.

Although Chen said the approach did not represent an official policy of Beijing, he believed that elements of such a strategy had already been put into practice, with pressure extended across military and international arenas.

In the military domain, PLA exercises in recent years have pushed beyond the Taiwan Strait median line, an unofficial boundary that has long served as a de facto buffer between the two sides.

After then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022, Beijing intensified military exercises around the island, and PLA aircraft have increasingly crossed the median line.

Diplomatically, Beijing has stepped up efforts to restrict Taiwan’s international space. A total of 10 countries have cut off diplomatic ties with Taipei since 2016, when the island’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party came to power.

In April, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te was forced to postpone his visit to eSwatini, the island’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa, because three countries along the flight route – Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar – revoked flight permits for Lai’s aircraft, according to Taipei.

Integration push

The idea of “one country, two systems” appears to be highly unpopular in Taiwan. More than 80 per cent of people in Taiwan oppose the “one country, two systems” formula, according to a poll in August conducted by Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council.

However, mainland scholar Chen argued that peaceful reunification remained possible, saying Beijing was seeking to integrate Taiwan with the mainland and gradually shape public opinion in favour of reunification.

“It’s not that the prospect of peaceful reunification has disappeared. That’s why both the government and academia are still discussing it – the prospects for peaceful reunification remain strong,” he said.

He argued that Beijing’s growing power was one factor, and “internationally, the situation is also moving in the mainland’s favour”.

He added that the stability of Sino-American relations as well as Washington’s stance on Taiwan were things Beijing could work on to create a more favourable environment for its reunification goals.

It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee?

Chen Xiancai, Taiwan affairs expert

After meeting Xi in May, US President Donald Trump said of Taiwan: “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent.” The American leader also described a US$14 billion arms sale to the island as “a good negotiation chip”.

Chen said Beijing could not rely on any single political party in Taiwan to support reunification, and that Beijing sought to work with pro-reunification forces across the island and use cross-strait integration to influence public opinion.

“Our approach to reunification is to win people’s support. We are not simply trying to work through individual political parties,” he said.

He added that public opinion in Taiwan could ultimately change policy, though it would take time.

Wang Huning, Beijing’s fourth-ranked official and its top official overseeing Taiwan affairs, last year outlined what he described as “seven betters” that Taiwan could enjoy through reunification, covering areas including infrastructure, the economy, energy and disaster relief.

The remarks marked a rare effort by a senior Chinese leader to explicitly spell out the potential benefits of reunification for people in Taiwan.

Beijing has in recent years promoted greater cross-strait “integration”, particularly through pilot projects in the coastal province of Fujian.

These initiatives have been presented as potential models for future cross-strait arrangements while also serving as a means of increasing pressure on Taipei, according to Chen.

For example, construction of the mainland section of a bridge between the Fujian city of Xiamen and the Taiwan-controlled island of Quemoy is nearing completion. The necessary connecting infrastructure is already in place for it to eventually link up with Quemoy, also known as Kinmen.

Chen said Beijing had taken the initiative in showing the potential benefits of reunification while maintaining pressure on Taiwan’s authorities.

“It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee?” he said.

“We have the financial resources and the machinery. We can get these projects built, continually putting pressure on Taiwan while making people in Kinmen feel that they stand to benefit.”

item.title: [SCMP] Antwerp: a well-seasoned melting pot of Rubens, diamonds and Belgium’s only Chinatown
item.description:
Tourists visiting the Belgian city of Antwerp are usually drawn by its reputation as the cradle of Flemish culture.

This was home to the Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), whose masterpieces decorate churches across the city, including St Charles Borromeo Church and the soaring Cathedral of Our Lady. Grand squares and marketplaces are lined with flamboyant Renaissance guild-houses and palatial merchants’ mansions dating back to a golden age, at the beginning of the 16th century, when Antwerp’s port was the undisputed capital of world trade. And then there is the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which showcases an unparalleled collection of Low Countries old masters, from Rubens, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625) and Jan van Eyck (1390-1441) to modern artists such as René Magritte (1898-1967), Rik Wouters (1882-1916) and James Ensor (1860-1949). But Flemish heritage is just one face of this city of 568,000 people.

On closer inspection, the city reveals itself to be a colourful melting pot of cultures, cuisines and religions, those of generations of immigrants who have chosen to make their home in Antwerp.
item.content:encoded:
Tourists visiting the Belgian city of Antwerp are usually drawn by its reputation as the cradle of Flemish culture.

This was home to the Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), whose masterpieces decorate churches across the city, including St Charles Borromeo Church and the soaring Cathedral of Our Lady. Grand squares and marketplaces are lined with flamboyant Renaissance guild-houses and palatial merchants’ mansions dating back to a golden age, at the beginning of the 16th century, when Antwerp’s port was the undisputed capital of world trade. And then there is the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which showcases an unparalleled collection of Low Countries old masters, from Rubens, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625) and Jan van Eyck (1390-1441) to modern artists such as René Magritte (1898-1967), Rik Wouters (1882-1916) and James Ensor (1860-1949). But Flemish heritage is just one face of this city of 568,000 people.

On closer inspection, the city reveals itself to be a colourful melting pot of cultures, cuisines and religions, those of generations of immigrants who have chosen to make their home in Antwerp.

Jews began to settle in the city after their expulsion from Spain in the late 15th century, and their descendants transformed it into a global centre of the diamond trade. Belgium’s 19th century empire resulted in immigration from the Maghreb and Central Africa, and after World War II, a wave of settlers from Hong Kong and mainland China arrived, creating what is today the only official Chinatown in the country. The latest additions to the city’s cosmopolitan character have been refugees fleeing conflict in countries such as Afghanistan, Syria, Iraq, Somalia and Ukraine.

Just 40 minutes north by train from the Belgian capital, Brussels, Antwerp’s late-19th century Central Station has a lavish dome, a sweeping marble staircase, frescoes and stained-glass windows that periodically win the building awards for “World’s Most Beautiful Station” in travel magazines.

Walk out of what locals call their “railway cathedral” and you plunge into a harmonious clash of cultures: on one side, the ornamental pagoda gate at the entrance to Van Wesenbekestraat that marks the beginning of Chinatown; on the other, Pelikaanstraat, home to a tight-knit Orthodox Jewish community and its diamond stores.

One-hundred-and-twenty boutiques full of glittering, dazzling diamonds and gold jewellery are crammed into this single square mile, though it is a wonder how they all survive when they seem to be selling the same items.

“I came to Antwerp 35 years ago, from Israel, though my family is originally from Georgia,” says Yosef Degan, standing proudly next to a replica of a gold bullion bar in his temptingly named store, Be Very Rich. “I am one of the last authentic goldsmiths here, because apart from dealing diamonds, I specialise in buying old gold, melting it down and creating my own unique jewellery designs.”

Although Yiddish is the lingua franca for the hundreds of Jewish dealers, brokers, cutters and jewellers working here, and the kippah skullcap and tzitzit trouser tassels can be seen everywhere, Degan insists that his community remains discreet.

I take his recommendation to have lunch nearby, at Hoffy’s, a kosher diner filled with noisy diamond dealers, whose owners, three Hoffman brothers, explain their Hasidic Ashkenazi culture to customers through their unique cuisine: in my case, a slow-cooked cholent of baked beef and vegetables, kugel potato pancakes, veal schnitzel, poached gefilte fish and salt-beef pastrami.

Another world awaits through the jewel-toned archway that stands at the entrance of Van Wesenbekestraat, ablaze in radiant reds and brilliant golds and proudly flanked by two sculpted stone lions.

Attracted by the city’s port, Chinese sailors and dock workers began settling in Antwerp from the early 20th century. They were followed in the late 1940s by larger numbers of mainly Cantonese-speaking immigrants from Hong Kong (particularly the New Territories) and southern China, who were escaping political turmoil and a lack of jobs, and were drawn by a post-war European revival and what was known as the “chop-suey boom”.

As with all Chinatowns, the restaurant business was the obvious line of work for most of these new immigrants, and from the 70s, the closeness to Antwerp’s railway station helped solidify Van Wesenbekestraat and the surrounding area as a genuine community.

Recognised as Belgium’s sole official Chinatown in 2001, the neighbourhood’s culinary scene has mushroomed from the early Cantonese restaurants to an eclectic kaleidoscope of Thai, Philippine, Malaysian and Nepalese eateries. A dozen bustling Asian supermarkets rub shoulders with two martial-arts schools, traditional-medicine establishments, a lion-dance school and the Fo Guang Shan Belgique Temple, located not in an ornate pagoda but in a simple Flemish house on a terraced row, painted a distinctive yellow, with a wrought-iron-framed window in the front door.

Much of the fare on offer in Chinatown is cheap and cheerful street food – hand-pulled noodles, char siu pork, wonton soup, even the classic sweet and sour chicken – but two addresses stand out, both just off the main drag of Van Wesenbekestraat.

Fong Mei opened more than 30 years ago and its classic Cantonese cuisine – more than 50 handmade varieties of dim sum alongside steamed fish with ginger and coriander, lacquered roast duck, beef-tripe soup and duck tongue – has been recognised by Belgium’s Michelin Guide. The decor is delightfully kitsch, with red lanterns, giant photos of Hong Kong, even a poster depicting a dragon boat powering through a village scene and celebrating Chinese-Belgian friendship.

The proprietor at the hole-in-the-wall Ni Shifu Sichuan Cuisine & Fondue, “Master Ni”, as the chef-owner describes himself, came to Antwerp 25 years ago, from Chengdu, and still does not speak a word of Flemish or English, but he certainly cooks up a storm in his tiny kitchen, dressed in shorts and a T-shirt, bent over his smoky wok. His dan dan noodles are wickedly spicy, the best I have eaten outside Asia, with the small dining room packed with a mix of Flemish locals, Antwerp Chinese and savvy visiting foodies. Ni Shifu has been singled out for Michelin praise for its authentic Sichuan cuisine and booking in advance is recommended.

Antwerp’s crucial bridge to the world, the docks – alongside the Scheldt river – are still among the busiest in Europe, but much of the surrounding Het Eilandje neighbourhood has been redeveloped. Its cutting-edge architecture includes the abstract pile of towering red-sandstone blocks that is the MAS maritime, history and cultural museum and Zaha Hadid’s metallic Port House, which resembles the shimmering prow of a floating ship.

Less conspicuous is the old red-brick warehouse that houses the Red Star Line Museum, a memorial to the millions of emigrants who passed through Antwerp on their way to a new life in North America. This intensely personal collection graphically illustrates the stories of some of the two million people who transited through Antwerp between 1873 and 1924, often after a long, tortuous journey from Central or Eastern Europe. Here, they endured medical examinations, disinfection and exhaustive immigration checks before finally being allowed to board a Red Star Line ship bound, in most cases, for New York. Most were fleeing poverty and persecution, little different from today’s migrants, and the anonymous tales are just as moving as those of the more famous émigrés who set sail on the Red Star Line: theoretical physicist Albert Einstein, composer Irving Berlin and future Israeli prime minister Golda Meir.

Just around the corner, in the Montevideo area – Antwerp’s quays are named after the exotic ports that produce was exported to and imported from – celebrity chef Nick Bril has just relocated his two-Michelin-star restaurant, The Jane, into a minimalist dining room, a striking departure from its original location, in a deconsecrated chapel downtown.

“Choosing Het Eilandje felt like a very logical step,” explains Bril, who has appeared on television in Belgian reality show Special Forces: Who Dares Wins, has served as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef Vlaanderen and is a renowned DJ. “It is an area where Antwerp’s history and future come together in a very natural way. The city has always drawn its strength from its openness to the world, and though our cuisine is firmly rooted in Belgium and in the products that surround us, it has always been influenced by experiences beyond our own borders.”

Gert de Mangeleer is present for every service in his kitchen at the two-Michelin-star Hertog Jan at Botanic, overseeing a tasting menu that is his own interpretation of a Japanese omakase experience.

“When I decided to open my restaurant in Antwerp, it was the perfect inspiration for my cuisine: this cosmopolitan harbour city that is an entrepôt for spices and exotic produce from around the globe,” says de Mangeleer, who gained prominence as part of the Flanders Kitchen Rebels campaign, a movement of young, talented chefs who brought a modern, rebellious attitude to traditional Belgian gastronomy.

His diners are tempted with dishes such as Japanese binchotan-grilled Wagyu beef served with locally smoked eel sauce, crispy veal sweetbreads, steamed dumplings of spinach dim sum and a sauce of Zeeland oysters.

One of Belgium’s two three-Michelin-star restaurants, Zilte, stands in the old docks area of Antwerp, but a favourite haunt of local chefs and sommeliers – evidenced by the fact that it’s open on Mondays, a traditional day off for restaurant staff – is the casual bistro Invincible. Here, animatedly supervising a brigade of cooks, Kenny Burssens interprets traditional Flemish cuisine, sautéing crunchy Brussels sprouts with bone marrow, and pairing tiny girolle mushrooms with tender chunks of milky cows’ udder, or line-caught cod with the salty sea-vegetable salicorne. The wine list includes vintages from little-known Belgian vineyards.

A little different is a meal at Samenloop, a restaurant that occupies the ground floor and cobbled courtyard of the Maagdenhuis, which was opened in 1552 as an orphanage for girls and also houses a museum and a chapel. The recently opened Samenloop is a social project for refugees: its waiters from Afghanistan and Palestine, and kitchen staff from Eritrea, the Maldives and Colombia are offered hospitality training so they can better integrate into society. One of a changing cast of celebrated chefs (for two months from November, it will be Karen Shu, an American-Filipino chef with a restaurant near Antwerp who is known for vegan and plant-based cuisine) collaborates by selecting recipes from the homelands of the refugees and adapting them into a tasting menu: crispy Nepalese pani puri surprisingly stuffed with chopped local asparagus; traditional Syrian falafel with fresh green peas; a light Ukrainian strawberry sernik cheesecake.

Another string to Antwerp’s bow is its reputation as a cutting-edge capital of European fashion. The Fashion Museum, known as MoMu, is a hotbed of creation, its studios and ateliers training the next generation of designers.

The city broke onto the international fashion scene in the 80s, with the rise of the Antwerp Six: revolutionary stylists who all graduated from the city’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts and colonised the pages of Vogue, Elle and Harper’s Bazaar.

“[Antwerp] is the perfect place to work,” one of the six, designer Walter Van Beirendonck, told Surface Magazine in 2016. “It’s not expensive, it’s quiet and it’s close to Paris, Milan and London. The art is great, the food is good, you can live well. There’s a real sense of possibility here.”

The visionary designs and eye-catching fashion shows of the likes of Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester and Van Beirendonck can now be seen at the MoMu exhibition “Antwerp Six”, which runs until January 17, 2027.

Another innovative temporary show can be found at the monumental Royal Museum of Fine Arts, with its colonnaded facade, neoclassical architecture, marble staircase and huge exhibition rooms. “KMSKA x Young Fashion Designers” (until November 8) gives free rein to 10 young graduates from the Antwerp Fashion Academy to create fashion sculptures influenced by pieces in the museum’s collection, inspiration having come from the dramatic flowing robes with cascading folds of fabric often depicted by Rubens and the revolutionary slashed canvases of Lucio Fontana (1899-1968).

A fitting way to end an exploration of eclectic, multi-ethnic Antwerp is to head for the Theaterplein square on a Saturday, the venue for the Exotic Market.

As Chinese immigrants were arriving after the end of World War II, migrants from countries such as Spain, Greece, Turkey and Morocco settled here, too, bringing the spices and ingredients of their native cuisines. They started selling their wares at the Theaterplein every Saturday, at what was first termed the Foreigners’ Market.

Teeming with locals and tourists from 8am to 4pm, this is more a multicultural, all-day party than a commercial centre, where the cava flows and food trucks serve customers sitting on temporary terraces a kaleidoscope of global cuisine: cheesy Turkish börek; plump Tibetan momo dumplings; Pakistani palak paneer; Peruvian panini; North African couscous and tagines; Vietnamese glass noodles. And to remind you that this is still Antwerp, there are also Flemish specialities, such as matjes (herrings), local oysters and bowls of karakol, a tasty soup of whelks and celery.

item.title: [SCMP] Taiwanese leader welcomes talks between Washington and Beijing ‘to reduce risk of war’
item.description:
Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has welcomed talks between Washington and Beijing aimed at reducing the risk of conflict.

Lai’s annual Double Tenth address on Saturday, marking the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name, also called for democracies to work together to safeguard regional peace and for the Taiwanese people’s right to exist to be respected.

He also warned that mainland China was trying to put pressure on the island to change the status quo, but Beijing accused him of “stirring up confrontation across the Taiwan Strait”.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has welcomed talks between Washington and Beijing aimed at reducing the risk of conflict.

Lai’s annual Double Tenth address on Saturday, marking the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name, also called for democracies to work together to safeguard regional peace and for the Taiwanese people’s right to exist to be respected.

He also warned that mainland China was trying to put pressure on the island to change the status quo, but Beijing accused him of “stirring up confrontation across the Taiwan Strait”.

“Lai Ching-te’s speech disregarded facts … misled the public and revealed sinister motives, constituting a performance true to form by a ‘pragmatic worker for Taiwan independence’,” said Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office, using a label Lai had previously attached to himself.

Zhang also accused him of “stubbornly clinging” to a “separatist mindset” and playing up the alleged “mainland threat”.

She said Beijing would resolutely crack down on separatist forces, oppose interference by external forces and safeguard peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.

She also said Beijing would promote “peaceful and integrated” cross-strait relations and “advance the great cause of national reunification”, but did not address his comments about the talks with Washington.

On Saturday, Lai said: “We welcome the US and China managing their competition through dialogue to reduce the risk of conflict and war.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump met last month in Washington, where Xi urged Trump to handle the Taiwan question prudently and oppose independence.

Lai added that maintaining regional peace and stability required rejecting “distortions of World War II history”, respecting the Taiwanese people’s right to exist and joint efforts by democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to preserve the status quo.

During their meeting, Trump and Xi highlighted their countries’ alliance during World War II, prompting criticism from Taipei, which says it was the Republic of China government, rather than the People’s Republic of China – established only in 1949 – that fought alongside the Allies.

Beijing has described such arguments as “a betrayal of history”.

Saturday’s address was Lai’s third Double Tenth speech since taking office in May 2024. The annual address has traditionally served as a platform for the government in Taipei to outline its policies, and is closely watched by Beijing and the international community for signals about cross-strait relations.

Speaking outside the Presidential Office Building in Taipei, Lai said: “China continues to exert pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.”

Faced with the “expansion of authoritarianism”, Lai said Taiwan’s resolve was not only about its own survival but also about “whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules and that powerful countries cannot deprive people of the right to determine their own future”.

Lai also warned of the challenges posed by “red supply chains”, a term commonly used in Taiwan to refer to supply chains centred on mainland China.

“Peace cannot rely solely on wishes,” he said, adding that Taiwan would continue to strengthen its defences and use its strengths in sectors such as semiconductors to develop a more self-reliant defence system.

In last year’s address, Lai outlined plans for a missile shield dubbed the “T-Dome” to counter growing military pressure from Beijing. He also said Taiwan’s defence spending would pass 3 per cent of gross domestic product this year and reach 5 per cent by 2030.

On Saturday, Lai said the increase in defence spending was not intended to provoke, but to deter war. He also said Taiwan was willing to engage in dialogue with the mainland, but insisted that it must take place on an equal and dignified footing.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification.

It has stepped up its pressure on the island since Lai, whom it views as a “separatist”, took office and has since conducted several large-scale military exercises around the island, including one that came days after his first Double Tenth speech in October 2024.

Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main arms supplier and international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. Washington, however, is bound by law to arm Taiwan for self-defence and opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force.

On Saturday, Lai avoided repeating some of his more contentious remarks from earlier addresses, including the assertion two years ago that Taiwan and the mainland “are not subordinate to each other”.

Zhu Songling, a professor at the Institute of Taiwan Studies at Beijing Union University, said Lai’s speech was largely in line with expectations, noting that he did not use other provocative phrases.

His welcome for the dialogue between Washington and Beijing reflected Lai’s “awareness of new developments in US-China relations and the situation across the Taiwan Strait”, Zhu said.

“The broader US-China relationship clearly has a significant impact on the Taiwan issue,” he added.

However, Zhu said Lai’s pro-independence position remained unchanged, and he was increasingly framing Taiwan’s security in international terms and linking it to democratic values.

“The speech placed greater emphasis on repackaging the separatist narrative around Taiwan independence in terms of democracy and international engagement,” he said.

Wang Kun-yi, head of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, said Lai had maintained a hard line with his comments accusing the mainland of pressurising Taiwan.

While the speech broke little new ground on cross-strait policy, it suggested that improving US-China relations could make Lai more cautious, Wang said.

He said Lai had shown “greater strategic flexibility” than in previous speeches, indicating that “Taipei must take into account the impact of US-China interactions on the situation across the Taiwan Strait.”

“The Lai administration supports efforts by Washington and Beijing to reduce tensions, while stressing that Taiwan’s interests must not be sacrificed in negotiations between major powers,” he said.

Wang Jianmin, a cross-strait specialist from Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, also said Lai’s most significant comments were those about the talks between Washington and Beijing.

“To some extent, he is endorsing the idea of the US and China jointly managing regional stability,” Wang said, adding that they should be understood in the context of Taiwan’s pro-US stance rather than a shift in his view of Beijing.

Wang added that Lai had not mentioned cross-strait exchanges, which had become constrained under his ruling Democratic Progressive Party.

“He is not a pragmatic Taiwan independence advocate, but a radical one,” Wang said.

Tang Shao-cheng, a research fellow at the Institute of International Relations at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University, said there was “no sting” in Lai’s comments, but they still fell far short of what Beijing wanted to see.

“The new international environment shaped by Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States is highly unfavourable to Taiwan independence forces, prompting Lai to make some adjustments to his rhetoric,” Tang said.

He said Lai appeared to be adapting to this environment, describing it as a “positive development, but it is far from enough”.

Tang added that Beijing would look at Lai’s actions, such as his policy on cross-strait tourism, rather than his words.

During Saturday’s speech, Lai also highlighted Taiwan’s economic performance, saying the island’s annual economic growth was expected to exceed 11 per cent, its highest rate in 39 years.

He also pledged to make Taiwan a “city upon a hill” – invoking a biblical metaphor widely used in the United States to invoke a model for others to follow.

Lai also outlined a range of policy priorities, including expanding social benefits, tackling drugs and strengthening Taiwan’s advanced technology industries.

item.title: [SCMP] Elon Musk’s Starlink row in India exposes Asia’s deeper battle over satellite power
item.description:
Elon Musk’s accusation that powerful Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into India has sparked a political row, but analysts say the dispute also highlights security concerns, regulatory hurdles and strategic calculations shaping the satellite service’s expansion across Asia.

In a post on social media, Musk said Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian laws and regulations.

“So why still no licence? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he wrote, suggesting Reliance Group chairman Mukesh Ambani – one of India’s wealthiest tycoons whose sprawling conglomerate has a major footprint across the economy – might wield undue influence over the licensing process.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk’s accusation that powerful Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into India has sparked a political row, but analysts say the dispute also highlights security concerns, regulatory hurdles and strategic calculations shaping the satellite service’s expansion across Asia.

In a post on social media, Musk said Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian laws and regulations.

“So why still no licence? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he wrote, suggesting Reliance Group chairman Mukesh Ambani – one of India’s wealthiest tycoons whose sprawling conglomerate has a major footprint across the economy – might wield undue influence over the licensing process.

The post drew a sharp response from Rahul Gandhi, leader of India’s main opposition party. “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy,” Gandhi said, apparently referring to Gautam Adani, another prominent Indian billionaire whose infrastructure and energy empire has expanded rapidly in recent years.

Gandhi has frequently accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and its ruling Bharatiya Janata Party of favouring Ambani and Adani.

The Indian government said its regulatory framework for satellite communication services was fair and non-discriminatory.

Raj Kapoor, president of the India Blockchain Alliance, said Musk’s accusation overlooked the intense scrutiny Starlink was likely to face from security regulators across Asia.

“It is a foreign-controlled satellite network with the ability to provide connectivity across political borders and potentially bypass conventional terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure,” Kapoor said, adding that Indian security agencies had been scrutinising infrastructure localisation and whether user traffic could be routed outside domestic jurisdiction.

“Calling this an oligarch conspiracy is good politics on X but a poor reading of what is actually happening,” Kapoor said, pointing to past seizures of Starlink terminals from separatist militants in India’s Manipur state and from a drug-smuggling vessel off the coast. “That tells a security agency that the network can be reached by people the state cannot see.”

Starlink’s regional expansion has run into regulatory hurdles, security concerns and geopolitical resistance in several Asian countries, including Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Nepal.

Kapoor said the regulatory concerns differed across jurisdictions and should not be generalised.

Starlink’s launch in Sri Lanka faced delays over regulatory assessments, data monitoring processes and national security vetting before receiving approval in mid-2025. In Vietnam, it launched nationwide operations in August under a tightly controlled five-year pilot programme.

Globally, Starlink has expanded rapidly across more than 160 countries, serving millions of customers.

“One of the reasons for the rapid expansion of Starlink has been how quickly countries have licensed it,” said Simon Baker, a UK-based senior research director for satellite and non-terrestrial connectivity at market research firm IDC.

“The service offers productivity gains to many services with poor telecoms infrastructure and this has encouraged them to overlook security issues for the time being. However, as Starlink use grows, the conditions imposed on it could increase in many places,” Baker added.

Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based technology policy adviser to governments, said security concerns among Asian countries were “entirely genuine” because satellite networks bypass land-based infrastructure, raising questions over data sovereignty, surveillance and national defence.

“States require concrete guarantees that domestic user data remains localised and that authorities retain crisis management capabilities,” Lian said. “These regional delays are not anti-innovation roadblocks; they are standard sovereign prerogatives. India’s methodical approach reflects a sovereign state establishing equitable telecommunications rules.”

The delays facing Starlink’s application in India stemmed mainly from complex regulatory requirements, Lian added.

India’s telecommunications market is currently dominated by Reliance Jio Infocomm and Bharti Airtel, which together control more than 80 per cent of the market. Reliance is expanding its own satellite ambitions through Jio Satellite Communications and a joint venture with Luxembourg-based satellite operator SES.

While OneWeb and Starlink are among the providers granted preliminary satellite communications licences in India, none has yet received spectrum allocation or launched full commercial services.

The government said that all applicants must undergo mandatory security assessments before spectrum allocation.

An uneven landscape

Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said that India’s market structure was heavily concentrated among a small group of large companies.

“Under such an industrial organisation, it is not unusual for foreign entrants to find the competitive conditions less than ideal,” Lim said, noting that entering a market dominated by established players was always difficult, regardless of an entrant’s technological advantage.

The dispute between Musk and New Delhi also reflects growing geopolitical overlay in economic policymaking.

“It does not help that the Indian government has had its own share of friction with the United States,” Lim said.

India has indicated that trade negotiations with the United States have largely stalled, with its willingness to make further concessions to Washington reaching a limit. US lawmakers have also enacted sanctions legislation authorising discretionary tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil, a move aimed partly at India’s continued energy trade with Moscow.

Lim noted that while Musk’s companies had “deep pockets” they should “expect no favours from Indian policymakers”.

Despite regulatory hurdles, proponents argue that Starlink offers significant benefits to Asian economies by delivering high-speed digital connectivity to remote and disaster-prone regions.

But Lian said that Starlink’s Asia-wide roll-out “will be a marathon, not a sprint”.

Kapoor predicted a segmented roll-out across the region: while some Asian countries would adopt Starlink rapidly, others would impose strict localisation rules, and a third group would pursue domestic or allied satellite alternatives.

“India does not want to exchange dependence on one set of telecoms gatekeepers for dependence on a foreign satellite network,” Kapoor said. “It wants the benefits of Starlink without surrendering strategic autonomy.”

Satya Gupta, president of the VLSI Society of India and a veteran telecoms industry executive, said the controversy highlighted the need for India to develop its own satellite service.

“We should aim to have this over the next five to seven years. This is the future of the internet for a range of services,” Gupta said. “We have all the ingredients and we need to put it together.”

India has already emerged as a major global hub for low-cost small satellite manufacturing and cost-effective space projects. Gupta said India could develop its own satellite services and offer them to regional neighbours, including Sri Lanka and Nepal.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Asian parents are trapped in a private tuition arms race
item.description:
Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school.

She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue.

“Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency.
item.content:encoded:
Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school.

She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue.

“Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency.

Her dilemma reflects a wider tension across Asia, where parents continue to invest in private tuition to give their children an academic edge, despite growing concerns over the stress placed on young learners and the widening gap between families who can afford extra classes and those who cannot.

In Singapore, a recent survey found that parents were spending more on tuition and enrichment classes than ever before, despite widespread concerns that children are already devoting too much time to them.

The survey of 1,500 primary school parents by the Institute of Policy Studies found that nearly nine in 10 agreed children in the city state were spending too much time on private classes, even as overall expenditure on extracurricular activities had increased.

Seven in 10 parents said they would spend more on such classes if they had the resources, while around half admitted feeling pressure because other parents did so.

The report, published last month, noted that parents were increasingly seeking both academic success and holistic development for their children, creating tension when one was perceived to come at the expense of the other.

“Concerns about school placement, future pathways, wider social comparisons and their own desire to safeguard their children’s opportunities can make it difficult for parents to act fully on their holistic preferences,” the report stated.

The dilemma is not unique to Singapore. Across Asia, in education systems where families compete for limited opportunities, parents can find themselves paying for tuition even when they believe the collective pressure damages children’s well-being.
