Ong Ee Cheng, an associate professor of economics at the National University of Singapore, described the situation as a “thorny” paradox as everyone would be “better off” if no one sent their children to private tuition.

“But if I send my kid to tuition and you don’t, my kid will do better than yours, and vice versa,” she said. “Ironically, when we both send our kids to tuition, we’re worse off than if neither of us had done so.”

The competition has fuelled demand for private education in Singapore, where parents spent an average of S$677 (US$529) a month on tuition this year – an increase from S$318 a decade ago.

House of Hows, a tuition centre offering classes for primary, secondary and junior college students, has more than 1,000 prospective students on its waiting list.

Founder and lead tutor Laura Oh warned against viewing all tuition spending simply as a fear of missing out. While some parents viewed extra classes as a way to secure an advantage, she said many were increasingly prioritising stress management and helping children find enjoyment in learning.

Other than Chinese lessons, Grace has enrolled her children in swimming, netball and art classes to develop their interests outside the classroom.

“It’s important for parents like us to recognise their interests early in life and provide them with as much help as possible early on,” she said.

Educational arms race

Across the region, the private tuition industry continues to expand as parents try to give their children a head start. But observers warn that these advantages extend beyond the classroom, reinforcing socio-economic divides as academic perks translate into better access to further education and, potentially, the job market.

Students whose parents can afford private classes are more likely to do well in entrance examinations, experts say, with those advantages potentially creating inequalities that continue into employment.

Nathan Peng, an assistant professor of political science at Singapore Management University, said countries that sorted students through high-stakes national examinations at a young age were particularly vulnerable to widening social divides.

“Even if all schools were equally good, the earlier you test a child, the more the results reflect family background rather than schooling, because the child has spent less time in the formal education system,” he said.

“And the more a society believes credentials reflect someone’s ‘true’ potential, the less likely it is to ask how much adversity different candidates overcame to reach the same point.”

The pressure to secure an advantage can begin long before formal schooling starts. Ong said well-off parents in Singapore, China and South Korea often engaged in what she termed an educational arms race well before primary school.

The effects of private tuition on social mobility could be more pronounced in countries with high levels of inequality, she added. “Unfortunately, many countries in Southeast Asia and Asia fit the bill.”

In Malaysia, gaps in the quality of public education could leave children reliant on extra help to keep up, said M Niaz Asadullah, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka.

Learning gaps caused by under-resourced public schools disproportionately affected poorer families, who were less able to pay for private lessons, he said.

“Tuition markets can expand both because schools leave learning gaps and because families compete for limited opportunities,” Asadullah said. “The risk of widening inequality depends on how unequally families can participate in that competition.”

Can policy curb the trend?

The challenge for governments across the region is addressing both sides of the problem: fixing shortfalls in public education while curbing intense competition for scarce educational opportunities.

In South Korea, households spent about 29.2 trillion won (US$21.8 billion) on private education in 2024 – a 60 per cent increase from a decade earlier. In April, authorities announced measures banning private tutoring academies or cram schools, known locally as hagwons, for children under three and capping preschoolers’ time spent in such lessons at three hours a day.

Singapore has also attempted to reduce academic pressures. In 2021, the government replaced aggregate scoring for the Primary School Leaving Examination with wider scoring bands, allowing students to be graded on their individual learning mastery rather than relative to their peers. In 2024, full subject-based banding replaced streaming scores to reduce academic labelling.

Asadullah urged regional governments to provide free, targeted tutoring through state schools, prioritising disadvantaged students, while ensuring classroom instruction was good enough to make private tutoring unnecessary.

Peng said early support was crucial as children often started school from very different academic baselines.

“Governments should help narrow gaps in family resources from pregnancy through early childhood, including nutrition, learning materials and parents’ knowledge of child development,” he said.

Other observers acknowledged that policy fixes alone could not dismantle the culture of tutoring without a wider shift in how families and societies defined success.

“If there were more emphasis on overall well-being – including mental and emotional – and less on material wealth, perspectives may start to shift to ensuring children are happy, resilient and confident,” Ong said.

“But of course, that’s more likely if parents know that even if their children fall, there’s only so far that they can fall.”

item.title: [SCMP] Russia lifts plague lab-related measures. Should China – and the world – be relieved?
item.description:
While Russian authorities have denied the death of a woman who worked in a laboratory at an anti-plague institute in Siberia was connected with the pathogen, the incident has sparked global concern – including in China – over a potential spread of the disease and a lack of transparency.

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he planned to speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin after it emerged late last week that the 28-year-old female lab technician had been admitted to hospital with severe pneumonia and died.

Initial unconfirmed reports linked the death to pneumonic plague – a severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis – following a laboratory exposure at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
item.content:encoded:
While Russian authorities have denied the death of a woman who worked in a laboratory at an anti-plague institute in Siberia was connected with the pathogen, the incident has sparked global concern – including in China – over a potential spread of the disease and a lack of transparency.

US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he planned to speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin after it emerged late last week that the 28-year-old female lab technician had been admitted to hospital with severe pneumonia and died.

Initial unconfirmed reports linked the death to pneumonic plague – a severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis – following a laboratory exposure at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

On Thursday, Igor Kobzev, the governor of Irkutsk, said the region had completed quarantine measures and monitoring of close contacts of the technician, who had a case of “community-acquired pneumonia”.

“No health issues related to infectious disease were detected. Laboratory analysis of nearly 5,000 samples revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms,” Kobzev added. He did not indicate the cause of the lab worker’s pneumonia.

Experts stressed that even if plague had been involved as initially suspected, the risk of a broader outbreak would have remained low.

However, suspicions about the incident have continued to be aired across social media platforms, including in China, even after Russian authorities denied the pathogen’s involvement.

Russian consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said over the weekend that the worker died of a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, according to Russian state news agency Tass.

The watchdog said samples taken from the patient found no microorganisms associated with the technician’s professional activities. It has yet to confirm the causative agent behind the pneumonia.

Kobzev said the employee “had been vaccinated and possessed immunity against the dangerous pathogens she worked with”.

Rospotrebnadzor also said no emergency incidents involving pathogenic microorganisms were identified at the institute, which was founded in 1934 to study the plague and now also works with anthrax and other infectious diseases.

Yuen Kwok-Yung, chairman of infectious diseases at the University of Hong Kong’s department of microbiology, noted that there was still little microbiological, epidemiological or clinical information available regarding the incident.

Based on a general understanding of infectious diseases, Yuen assessed that as long as the bacterial strain involved was not “bioengineered” to possess multidrug resistance or increased transmissibility, there should be no concerns about any effect on Hong Kong.

If the pneumonia was caused by the “natural” Yersinia pestis bacterium – denied by Russian authorities, Yuen noted – the outbreak would be contained if all lab, family and hospital contacts were properly quarantined and given antibiotics, he stressed.

“If the contact tracing, isolation of cases and quarantine of contacts are correctly done in this Siberian incident, there should not be any crossover into the Chinese mainland,” Yuen told the South China Morning Post in an email on Thursday.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said on Wednesday that the agency had been in touch with Russia, which responded that no case of plague had been reported in the Irkutsk region.

According to the WHO chief, the Russian authorities also said they had placed about 200 contacts of the woman in quarantine.

Tedros said the agency had requested further information and more detail on what prompted the public health measures as well as the health status of the contacts.

“As we don’t yet have the full picture of this event, we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” he added.

Trump told US broadcaster NBC that he did not believe the incident was the result of biological weapons research.

According to several popular bloggers in China, suspicions over the incident and the official narrative may not be unfounded.

The concerns over bioweapons stem in part from a Telegram post by Siberian journalist and blogger Pavel Stepanov on October 2, which alleged that the infection potentially involved “military-grade strains”.

Stepanov’s post also speculated that the cause of the infection was the pneumonic plague and that the incident had occurred in a laboratory.

When asked about the outbreak on Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said “China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation on the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague”.

Animals frequently move across the border between Russia and China, with the two countries establishing wildlife corridors to help the movement of species such as the endangered Siberian tiger.

According to the WHO, Yersinia pestis – the bacterium behind the infamous Black Death that swept through Europe in the 14th century – naturally occurs in wild animals, typically small mammals like rats, as well as their fleas, in Siberia and much of the world.

The form that began the outbreak that caused more than 50 million deaths in Europe was bubonic plague, which came about when the pathogen was transmitted from animals and fleas to humans.

Pneumonic plague is an especially contagious form that occurs when the bacteria infect the lungs. This can spread from human to human through respiratory droplets or contact with infected materials and is often fatal if left untreated.

However, pneumonic plague can be easily treated using antibiotics if administered early, according to the WHO.

Yuen said that since the advent of effective antibiotics along with improved hygiene and sanitation measures against rats and rat fleas, the risk of a plague epidemic or pandemic was “rather low”.

Brendan Wren, a professor with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told the Science Media Centre that while Yersinia pestis was “fairly transmissible”, it was not as transmissible as Covid-19.

In a statement posted by the centre on Monday, Wren said the plague remained endemic across the world. There were around 2,000 cases per year that could be treated with standard antibiotics, he added.

Tedros said the Russian side had confirmed that an epidemiological investigation was conducted following the incident.

“However, [the] WHO has requested further information on the laboratory tests conducted on the individual who died and the contacts, more detail on what prompted the public health measures, and details about the health status of the contacts,” he said.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”

According to Tass, monitoring of the close contacts of the deceased researcher identified two cases of Covid-19 and two of rhinovirus, which causes the common cold.

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi called ex-father-in-law ‘old crook’ amid HK$72m flat row, court hears
item.description:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her former father-in-law an “old crook” as she accused her ex-relatives of turning her children against her when she tried sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat, a court has heard.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023.

Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her former father-in-law an “old crook” as she accused her ex-relatives of turning her children against her when she tried sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat, a court has heard.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023.

Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial.

“My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her heart to the wrong people. This family, this family really bit the hand that fed them.”

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial at the High Court after pleading not guilty to murdering the model on February 21, 2023.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial.

The killing allegedly stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so he could keep it for himself.

Cheung said on Monday that her daughter had bought the property in 2019 for her children and partly as a personal investment, but she registered it in her former father-in-law’s name to avoid double stamp duty. She stressed that Choi had never intended to give the flat to her former in-laws.

Giving evidence for a second day, Cheung said Kwong Kau became furious when her daughter first told him in June 2022 that she intended to sell the flat. He threatened to kill her entire family if she went ahead, Cheung said.

The elder Kwong signed a power of attorney authorising Choi to negotiate the sale only five months later, after Cheung threatened to sue him.

Choi aired her grievances in a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, saying her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years.

“She does not cherish her blessings at all,” Choi said in an apparent reference to Li, who is not a defendant in the case. “[They are] not grateful to me even while leading such a lifestyle.”

The influencer also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in Kwong Kau’s name.

Cheung said Kwong Kau and his wife also disparaged her daughter in front of the two children she had with Alex Kwong and told them not to listen to their mother.

The court heard that Choi and her mother had further discussions in November 2022 about how to get Kwong Kau to sign legal documents authorising her to negotiate the sale.

Choi suggested that the elder Kwong, whom she called an “old crook”, “scum” and a “stinking bastard”, was deliberately delaying the process and would play tricks on them unless the matter was settled quickly, the court heard

Cheung said her daughter wanted to sell the property as soon as possible and was willing to lower her asking price by a few million dollars because Kwong Kau could revoke the power of attorney at any time.

The model also complained that the Kwong family had prevented her from speaking to her two children by phone while she was attending a fashion event in France during the Lunar New Year holiday in January 2023.

Cheung told the court she received her final message from her daughter at around 2pm on February 21, saying she would pick up her daughter from school.

Fear for the model’s safety grew that night when Choi’s husband, Chris Tam Fong-chun, informed Cheung that she had gone missing.

Cheung said she called Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s temporary chauffeur at the time, but he appeared impatient and insisted the influencer had got out of her car after an argument over the phone.

She said her former relative gave conflicting answers when pressed to explain Choi’s whereabouts. He also allegedly suggested that she might have got drunk and become lost, even though she normally avoided alcohol.

Cheung said she and Tam reported the case to police shortly before midnight, much to Alex Kwong’s dismay.

“He said: ‘Damn you! Why didn’t you alert me when you called police?’” she said.

“I said to him: “Damn you! I reported my daughter’s disappearance to police. What does it have to do with you?”

When Cheung suggested that Alex Kwong and his father must have taken Choi somewhere, her former son-in-law replied with a question: “Why did you say so?”

“I called the whole [Kwong] family but nobody cared,” the witness added.

Defence counsel Trevor Beel, representing Anthony Kwong, argued the elder Kwong was reluctant to sell the flat during the economic slump linked to the Covid-19 pandemic.

“I suggest, madam, that it would be understandable that Kwong Kau would not be keen to sell the property at that time, because the property price was low,” he said in cross-examination.

Cheung disagreed.

“The money wasn’t his. What did he stand to gain? We were entitled to reclaim [the flat]. He had no say on it,” she said.

Some members of the public burst into laughter when Cheung recalled her exchange with Alex Kwong, drawing a stern warning from lead prosecutor Charlotte Draycott SC.

“It’s important for the public to remember that this is a woman who has lost her daughter,” she said. “If you want to laugh, you go outside.”

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
item.description:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.
item.content:encoded:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.

That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data.

The platform’s breakneck rise continued to gain momentum from there, bringing Chinese-style e-commerce to markets around the world.

However, three years on, Temu’s initial business proposition is being rewritten amid a wave of global regulation, with rising customs barriers eroding some of the advantages that made its cut-to-the-bone prices possible.

At the heart of the change is a simple issue: shipping a dress directly from a warehouse in China to doorsteps in America or Europe is no longer as simple – or cheap – as it was a couple of years ago.

Temu’s ability to offer such ultra-low prices was built on two main factors: its vast, well-oiled Chinese supply chain and a clever distribution strategy that allowed the firm to avoid paying hefty import tariffs.

[PDD] has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature ... and reusable supply chain system

Chen Tao, Analysys International

On the supply side, Temu could draw on parent company PDD Holdings’ years of expertise operating Pinduoduo – one of China’s largest e-commerce platforms, which has built a sprawling supply chain with deep roots in the Chinese manufacturing sector.

PDD “has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature … and reusable supply chain system”, said Chen Tao, an e-commerce analyst at consultancy Analysys International.

Temu had effectively copied Pinduoduo’s business model and rolled it out globally, Chen added.

The model allows Temu to draw on China’s sprawling network of factories, suppliers and cross-border merchants, which is able to produce and ship goods at a scale and cost unmatched anywhere else in the world.

Since China began opening its economy in the late 1970s, specialised clusters for producing particular products have formed across the country, concentrating factories, suppliers, logistics firms and skilled workers into dense, tightly woven ecosystems.

In southern China’s Guangdong province, for example, the city of Dongguan is known for electronics and toys, while Shenzhen is a hub for electronics. Foshan specialises in furniture, and Zhongshan is a major centre for lighting products.

Vast trading and logistics networks have formed alongside these manufacturing clusters, helping factories reach buyers around the world.

Yiwu, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, has developed a gargantuan wholesale market where hundreds of thousands of vendors sell almost any small product imaginable to overseas buyers – from toy cars to Christmas decorations.

The city is home to well over 260,000 cross-border e-commerce businesses, according to non-exhaustive local government data. Temu estimates that about 40 per cent of its merchants are based in the city.

Another critical piece that made the economics work for Temu was the once-permissive trade policy in some of its largest overseas markets including the US, according to Chen.

In the US, the long-standing “de minimis” exemption allowed individual shipments worth less than US$800 to enter the country without the duties normally imposed on larger commercial imports, helping make it economical for Temu to ship low-cost goods directly from Chinese suppliers to American doorsteps.

It had become a major conduit for Chinese cross-border commercial parcels entering the US. About 60 per cent of the more than 1 billion packages that entered the US under the de minimis exemption in fiscal 2023 came from China, according to US Customs and Border Protection data.

Temu paired that trade advantage with its fully managed model, under which Chinese merchants supplied the goods while the platform handled much of the overseas sales process, from pricing and marketing to cross-border logistics.

“For a small merchant, the cost of shipping a small batch is very high,” Chen said. “But with a platform like Temu, many small batches of goods can be consolidated,” significantly reducing logistics costs.

At Temu’s scale, analysts said, orders from different merchants could be gathered in China and transported together across the Pacific, spreading freight costs across huge volumes of parcels while retaining their identities as individual consumer shipments for US customs and qualifying separately for de minimis treatment.

China’s low-cost supply base, Temu’s fully managed model and duty-free treatment of small parcels allowed the platform to sell to consumers an ocean away while keeping inventory in China until they ordered.

However, that formula was attracting scrutiny almost as quickly as Temu was attracting shoppers.

In April 2023, just two months after Temu’s first Super Bowl appearance, research staff at the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a congressional advisory body, identified the de minimis exemption as one of the regulatory advantages helping Chinese e-commerce platforms expand in the US.

The report said the huge volume of low-value packages made it harder for US authorities to inspect shipments and enforce trade rules, while also pointing to accusations against Temu over product quality and copyright infringement.

The commission said Chinese e-commerce platforms were particularly well positioned to benefit from de minimis because their goods were typically shipped as individual low-value parcels.

Temu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The formula that once worked like magic began to quickly unravel in the US in May 2025 – four months after Trump was sworn into office – when the Trump administration ended de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from mainland China and Hong Kong. The exemption was later removed for shipments from all countries in August.

The change struck at one of the central advantages of Temu’s original model: goods could still be made cheaply in China, but getting them into the hands of American consumers suddenly became more expensive.

The impact was swift. Temu’s daily US users fell 48 per cent in May compared with March, according to Sensor Tower data cited by Reuters.

Analysts said the policy change threatened to weaken Temu’s low-price proposition by raising the cost of the direct-shipping model that had powered its expansion.

The new taxes would significantly increase the cost of shipping low-priced goods directly to overseas consumers and potentially push up retail prices, Chen said. That posed a particular challenge for Temu because many of its customers were price-sensitive, meaning higher prices risked driving some away, he added.

Zhang Zhouping, executive director at Ben Se Think Tank, a cross-border commerce consultancy, echoed Chen’s view.

“Taxes on small parcels erode the low-price advantage, while tax, logistics and compliance costs pile up,” Zhang said. “If those higher costs are reflected in final prices, price-sensitive consumers could be affected.”

In response, Temu began moving goods closer to American shoppers.

The company had already started recruiting US-based sellers and rolling out what it called a “semi-managed” model in 2024, under which merchants took greater responsibility for moving and stocking their goods overseas.

Under the semi-managed model, merchants take on more responsibility for overseas logistics and warehousing, shifting inventory closer to consumers and reducing reliance on individual parcels shipped directly from China.

The change makes Temu less dependent on the cross-border shipping model vulnerable to changing tariff rules, but introduces more inventory, warehousing and local fulfilment costs into the supply chain.

By early 2025, about 20 per cent of Temu’s US sales were being shipped by local sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse, cited by Reuters. The end of de minimis accelerated that transition.

The pressure is not confined to the US.

The European Union has also tightened rules on low-value e-commerce imports. Since July, goods worth less than €150 (US$177) entering the bloc have been subject to an interim €3 customs duty for each different category of goods contained in a parcel, ending the previous duty-free treatment ahead of a broader overhaul of the EU customs system.

The change has particular implications for Chinese e-commerce platforms, as some 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, with 91 per cent coming from China, according to the European Commission.

Other markets have moved in the same direction. Thailand began imposing a 10 per cent customs duty in January on imported goods worth 1,500 baht (US$46) or less, which had previously been exempt from customs duties. South Africa has also tightened tax treatment of low-value e-commerce parcels.

Together, the changes point to a broader erosion of the favourable treatment for low-value parcels that helped Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms expand internationally, increasing the pressure to rethink a model built heavily around shipping inexpensive goods directly from China to overseas consumers.

PDD has acknowledged the consequences.

At the company’s latest earnings call, Zhao Jiazhen, PDD’s co-chairman and co-chief executive, said cross-border orders in affected markets would face “lower fulfilment efficiency and higher costs”, which would have a “considerable impact” on parts of its business.

For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world … In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power

Wang Xin, Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association

In the longer term, Zhao said Temu would bring in more local merchants and accelerate investment in local warehousing and fulfilment infrastructure to “integrate more deeply into every market we serve”.

That marks a significant pivot for a platform whose original appeal rested partly on reaching overseas consumers without building out the extensive local infrastructure associated with established global e-commerce businesses such as Amazon.

Another response could be geographic diversification, with Chinese platforms accelerating expansion into markets beyond the US and Europe where regulatory conditions differ, Ben Se’s Zhang said.

Analysys International’s Chen said Temu was unlikely to abandon its original model altogether. Instead, he expected it to combine direct shipping where it remained economical with overseas warehouses and locally held inventory elsewhere.

But the transition may ultimately involve more than changing how Temu gets goods to consumers. It could also change what it sells.

If the low-price strategy becomes less effective, Temu could increasingly turn towards branded products carrying higher margins and more moderate prices, Chen said.

PDD has already taken a significant step in that direction.

In March, the group announced Xinpinmu, a strategic project to develop and operate its own brands by combining the supply chain resources accumulated by Pinduoduo in China with Temu’s overseas reach.

The group has injected 15 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion) into the project and plans to invest a total of 100 billion yuan over three years, with the venture developing brands across different product categories and markets for global consumers.

“Temu’s rapid growth over the past three years was a key leap made possible by the strength of China’s supply chain, and has also created a new opportunity to upgrade and reshape the domestic supply chain,” Zhao said when announcing the initiative.

Three years after Temu promised Americans they could “shop like a billionaire”, the factories capable of producing a US$8.99 dress cheaply have not disappeared, nor has the vast Chinese manufacturing ecosystem behind them.

What has changed is the economics of getting that dress from China to consumers thousands of kilometres away, and, increasingly, the kind of goods PDD wants those factories to sell.

Those economics could shift again as Washington and Beijing continue to negotiate the terms of their trading relationship.

During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month, tariffs and other trade issues were high on the agenda as the world’s two largest economies seek to manage a fragile detente.

For Temu and other Chinese cross-border e-commerce companies, the stakes of that meeting are high, as their low-price model is particularly sensitive to tariffs and trade rules that raise the cost of moving goods from Chinese factories to US consumers.

For some in the industry, however, the changing environment is accelerating a broader push to upgrade China’s cross-border e-commerce sector beyond its reliance on low prices.

“For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world,” said Wang Xin, president of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, in an interview with state broadcaster CCTV earlier this year.

“In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Jeffrey Sachs says US sabre-rattling at China can become self-fulfilling prophecy of war
item.description:
Jeffrey Sachs is an economics professor and director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at Columbia University. He is president of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. He was a special adviser to the UN Secretary General and has advised multiple governments on economic transition, debt crisis solutions and poverty alleviation policies. Part 1 of the Sachs interview, published in July last year, can be found here. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The tariff truce between China and the United States is set to end in August. What do you forecast will happen after that? And what will happen to trade relations between China and the US for the rest of US President Donald Trump’s second term?

The United States learned that it can’t impose its will on China. The rare earths threat by itself was enough to cause the US to reconsider. So, almost immediately after putting on the high tariffs, the US backed down. And both sides know that each has some chokeholds on the other. For that reason, we might expect the two sides to maintain certain limits on the trade frictions in the years ahead. There will be, therefore, some kind of agreement, but it won’t stick in the details, and frictions will continue to wax and wane, with neither side definitively imposing its will on the other. The basic reason is that both sides have a mutual gain from continued trade. I’m hopeful that a measure of rationality will therefore prevail.
item.content:encoded:
Jeffrey Sachs is an economics professor and director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at Columbia University. He is president of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. He was a special adviser to the UN Secretary General and has advised multiple governments on economic transition, debt crisis solutions and poverty alleviation policies. Part 1 of the Sachs interview, published in July last year, can be found here. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The tariff truce between China and the United States is set to end in August. What do you forecast will happen after that? And what will happen to trade relations between China and the US for the rest of US President Donald Trump’s second term?

The United States learned that it can’t impose its will on China. The rare earths threat by itself was enough to cause the US to reconsider. So, almost immediately after putting on the high tariffs, the US backed down. And both sides know that each has some chokeholds on the other. For that reason, we might expect the two sides to maintain certain limits on the trade frictions in the years ahead. There will be, therefore, some kind of agreement, but it won’t stick in the details, and frictions will continue to wax and wane, with neither side definitively imposing its will on the other. The basic reason is that both sides have a mutual gain from continued trade. I’m hopeful that a measure of rationality will therefore prevail.

The biggest challenge, of course, is the behaviour of the US. The US started this trade war. This is not two sides fighting each other, but rather the US fighting China. We should remember that. The US needs to show some prudence at this point. I do suspect that there is a chastened view among many senior US officials. Trump himself is unpredictable. He has a very short attention span. Agreements with Trump don’t stick. So, I don’t foresee a quiet period, but I do foresee some limits to the competition because each side can do damage to the other and both sides have a strong reason to achieve some cooperation.

Let me add one more point. From a long-term point of view, China certainly should not regard the US as a growth market for its exports. The US is going to restrict China’s exports to the US one way or another. The relationship will not be harmonious. The US will not be friendly to China, or trustworthy. China should just take care that it’s expanding its exports to other markets, and should not be overly focused on trying to break through to the US market, or even to Europe for that matter. The rapid growth of China’s exports will be with Africa, Southeast Asia, South Asia, west Asia, Central Asia, Latin America – not with the US and western Europe.

What is your forecast for the US midterm elections, and will it be a tough battle for Trump? Can you comment on how divided the US is compared to before the election of Trump last year?

I think that the Democrats will likely regain control of one or both houses of Congress, because in midterm elections that is generally the pattern.

Even without getting deeply specific about the current context, the prevailing party that holds the White House almost always loses ground in the midterms, and the Republican majority in both houses of Congress is very small. Having said this, we should also understand that Trump is ruling mainly by executive decree, not by legislation. Even if the Democrats regain one or both houses of Congress, Trump will continue with his decrees.

The US currently does not have a functioning constitutional system in my view. It is one-person rule by declarations of emergencies by Trump. The orders generally start with the statement: “By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered”. This is a kind of soft dictatorship, not a constitutional system. The lower courts object, but the Supreme Court lets Trump have his way. The Congress is nearly moribund.

Even if the Democrats regain some control of the House or the Senate, it won’t stop a lot of what Trump is doing. I should also add that while Americans are polarised, they generally dislike both political parties. Most Americans are unhappy about the direction of the country. They’re distrustful of the politicians. Our political institutions are not functioning properly and that’s why there’s a high level of distrust.

I don’t think that China can, or should, base its policies on a return to normal trade with the US

Jeffrey Sachs

Another point that I think is important to understand is that the swings between the Democrats and the Republicans do not change US foreign policy. [Former president Barack] Obama started the anti-China policies in his term. Then came Trump’s tariffs in his first term. Biden kept those Trump tariffs and had a hostile policy towards China. Now Trump is picking up where Biden left off. The deep state drives foreign policy, not public opinion or presidents.

In sum, I don’t have much hope that some change in the midterm elections will change the direction of US politics very much. Even a change in the White House in four years is not likely to change US politics very much. Our problems are deep seated. Our institutional failings are deep. It’s going to take perhaps 20 years to work through this. This is not a Trump phenomenon by itself.

What effect will the One Big Beautiful Bill have on the US economy?

The One Big Beautiful Bill weakens the US in two ways. First, it adds to the already large budget deficits by making additional tax cuts that mainly benefit rich Americans and the corporate class. These tax cuts raise the budget deficit substantially and are partially offset by cuts in healthcare benefits for the poorest Americans. The bill, therefore, is dramatically unfair and unwise in its impacts on the deficit and inequality.

Second, the legislation phases out some of the modest earlier US efforts towards low-carbon energy and modernisation of infrastructure. So, the legislation marks a US retreat from leadership on 21st-century technologies. Basically, the Trump administration is a gift to China, with Trump’s policies saying to China, “China should lead the way on climate safety, low-carbon energy, electric vehicles and all of the green and digital technologies that the world needs, while the US will ignore the future”.

So, none of this is a big, beautiful bill. It is a mess that reflects the failures of the American political system.

What are the implications of the fallout between billionaire Elon Musk and Trump?

Trump doesn’t have long-term relations with any individual other than his immediate family. Trump falls out with everybody. Remember Steve Bannon? He was once Trump’s closest adviser. That came to an end quickly. Almost all Trump advisers get fired at one point or another. Trump is not a person with long-term loyalties to anybody.

The individual feuds don’t mean very much. Breaking with Musk does not mean breaking with Silicon Valley. Silicon Valley put Trump back into the White House with enormous financial backing for Trump’s campaign. There are still tens of billions of dollars of government contracts going also to Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and other Big Tech operators.

The basic relationship between Silicon Valley and Washington remains intact because the Pentagon believes that it needs AI and can’t pursue AI on its own. While Trump has cut support for EVs, including Tesla, the Pentagon will continue to rely on Musk’s SpaceX for many years to come. And the same is true of the Pentagon’s reliance on Big Tech’s AI capacities generally.

You have mentioned in other interviews that Trump lacked a coherent strategy in foreign policy, including his handling of China. Why do you think this? And what do you see ahead for China-US relations?

The most fundamental trend in the world economy is the rapid rise of the non-Western economies, led by China and including Russia, India, Southeast Asia and, in future decades, Africa. The US is flailing about trying to maintain its dominance in a world in which the emerging economies are rising rapidly. The US will not be able to prevent the emergence of multipolarity, but it will try. Trump will try one thing or another, but without success or coherence. Multipolarity has already arrived.

The broad pattern of economic convergence – in which the emerging economies narrow or close the income gap with the high-income countries of the West – means that Western hegemony is over. This is leading to deep frustration, not only in the US political class but in Europe as well.

China vastly outproduces the United States in advanced industrial goods, such as EVs, solar power, wind power, advanced nuclear power, batteries, low-cost 5G and many other key technologies. China incorporates AI into advanced manufacturing processes more than the US.

Many European leaders feel that if they stick with the US against China and Russia, then maybe the Western hegemony will continue. This is delusional in my view, but nonetheless creates a lot of noise, friction and risks of conflict. None of it is a coherent strategy, however.

The US has no strategy to stay ahead of China. In fact, the US can’t succeed in that. We hear a lot of US sabre-rattling against China, Russia and the Brics countries. This is all dangerous. I think the heated rhetoric by itself can become a self-fulfilling prophecy of war. There are a lot of ignorant people in the US political leadership, and I worry very much about their naivety and delusions.

This, in my view, is essentially the origin of the “trade war”. The US decided during 2010-2015 that China is now a threat to US primacy. The US has tried a lot of things to block China’s continued rise, including: a military build-up in East Asia; export restrictions on hi-tech goods, especially advanced chips; economic sanctions on key Chinese companies; investment restrictions by US companies, and ownership restrictions on Chinese companies in the US; high tariffs against China’s exports; and others. But none of this stops China’s rise. China’s development results from hard work, ingenuity, high rates of saving, high rates of investment, very effective long-term planning and a very skilled, very entrepreneurial generation of business leaders, especially young business leaders. Those fundamental strengths continue despite America’s anti-China policies.

Trump’s policies are accelerating the move of top scientists to China. My overall view is that Trump is creating a lot of noise and some real dangers, but with no real strategy and no likelihood of success in holding back China’s rise. That’s a good thing. The rest of the world benefits from China’s economic success, including the US.

In your last Open Questions interview, you talked about “the deep state”, a complex vested interest group in industry, the military and other spheres. Does the deep state want military conflict with China? And do foreign governments – such as China and Russia – believe in the existence of a deep state, which many dismiss as a conspiracy theory?

The deep state means the permanent security system of the United States and its partners in Europe and in East Asia, including Japan, Korea and other places where the US has military bases and other security institutions. It includes the military, the CIA, the military contractors and the politicians who serve the military-industrial complex.

Does such a deep state exist? Yes. The US has around 750 overseas military bases and many of them are in East Asia. The US has many major military contractors with hundreds of billions of dollars of annual business with the US government. The US fights overt and covert wars pretty much non-stop, some of which are proxy wars (in which the US arms and funds Ukraine to fight Russia), and sometimes open conflicts with heavy US involvement, as in Iraq and Afghanistan. The US has the extensive global networks of the CIA and other intelligence and covert institutions. All of this constitutes the deep state. Presidents come and go but the underlying foreign policy is consistent and set largely out of view of the public, and without any reference to public opinion.

When Obama replaced [US president George] Bush Jnr, and Trump replaced Obama, and Biden replaced Trump, and Trump replaced Biden, on the PR level there was alleged to be change, but in fact very little policy change occurred. For example, how much foreign policy change was there when Obama succeeded Bush Jnr? Very little. Obama launched many wars, just as Bush had done. Obama’s team actively participated in the coup in Ukraine in 2014 that set the path for the Ukraine war. Obama went to war against Libya. Obama gave the CIA the order to overthrow the Syrian government. All of this was a continuation of the policies of the Bush period.

Trump continued most of the same policies. Trump continued to build up the Ukraine military. The Trump administration dismissed the Minsk 2 agreement that could have prevented the escalation of the Ukraine war. There was not any major change between Obama and Trump.

When Biden came in, their claim again was that there would be a new foreign policy, but it didn’t happen. What did Biden do with China? He continued Trump’s tariffs. He continued Trump’s hardline rhetoric. Biden absurdly divided the world between the so-called democracies and autocracies, which was an incredibly naive approach, as I said from the beginning.

Biden escalated the Ukraine war. He rejected all attempts at peace negotiations, including the Istanbul process that could have ended the Ukraine war in 2022. When it came to the Middle East, Biden was complicit in Israel’s ongoing genocide. So, Biden did very little different from Bush Jnr, Obama and Trump before him.

Now, Trump has returned. What’s the real difference? Trump is different in style, in his unpredictability, nastiness, self-dealing and endless flip-flops. Yet, in terms of basic foreign policy, Trump is not very different from his predecessors.

This is the sense in which deep state means an ongoing consistency of the US security institutions that run American foreign policy. American foreign policy is not determined by public opinion, or Congress, or even the president in large part. Look instead to the CIA, the Pentagon and the other parts of the deep state.

The deep state also determines the politics of US vassal states. Many observers consider Japan to be a US-occupied country, with Japan’s foreign policy basically subservient to the US. One can say the same about many other countries. Where the US has military bases, the host countries tend to act like occupied countries, bending their own foreign policy to that of the US.

The US deep state is profoundly arrogant, thinking that it can have its way around the world. The US deep state thinks that it can dominate not only US allies, which is typically true, but also China, Russia, Iran, Brazil and others. When US arrogance becomes too strong, we face the danger of disaster. That’s what happened in Ukraine. The US thought that it could push Russia around to its will. It could not. The attempt to assert US power in Ukraine led to war.

US arrogance deeply worries me. Trump certainly is not a strategist. There’s no long-term plan. The US is playing poker, but not very well or wisely. It often bluffs. The whole approach can lead to war.

China is now drafting its economic policies for the next five years. You have advised many countries before. What is your advice to China in the face of this tension and the global tariff war?

My main advice to China is look to the non-Western world for the strongest partnerships in trade, investment and diplomacy, at least for a while. The US-led alliance (US, Canada, Britain, EU, Japan, Korea, Australia and New Zealand) is around 13 per cent of the world population. China is another 17 per cent. The remaining 70 per cent of the world – in Asia, Africa and Latin America – wants good and strong economic and diplomatic relations with China. That 70 per cent of the world population wants to modernise, and China provides the means for those countries to achieve rapid growth and modernisation. China is key to the global energy transition to zero-carbon energy, especially in the markets outside the US and Europe.

The emerging and developing economies of Asia, Africa and Latin America will be the markets for China’s rapid export growth in the years ahead. China will play a vital global role in these economies in building advanced green and digital economies, using Chinese cutting-edge technologies.

This will be a great win-win for the world because China will continue to grow rapidly while also empowering rapid growth throughout the emerging and developing nations. Sadly, in my view, the US will not play much of a role in that modernisation in the next generation. The US under Trump is withdrawing from green technologies, and from global responsibility.

The US cannot compete with China for the global renewable energy market. The US can’t compete with China for the global digital connectivity market. The US can’t compete with China in fast rail or low-carbon ocean shipping. In all these sectors, Trump is handing world trade and leadership over to China.

Regarding the US markets, China should certainly attempt to make a suitable trade deal with the US but China should not fret too much either way. The US is already a small part of China’s exports – perhaps around 10-12 per cent. That share of China’s exports will most likely decline further.

I hope that I’m wrong and that the US regains some sense and rejoins the global effort for green transformation and re-establishes normal trade with China. Yet, I don’t think that’s going to happen for many years, and I don’t think that China can, or should, base its policies on a return to normal trade with the US.

More specifically, I advocate expanding [China’s] Belt and Road Initiative. I advocate that China should deal with regional groups, including Asean, the African Union, the Arab League and the Community of Latin America and Caribbean States (CELAC). China’s relations with these regional groups can be very strategic, as the regional groups can, and should, spur the interconnectivity of infrastructure among all the members of the group. For China, it will be easier to interact with regional plans rather than one country at a time.

In fact, no individual state in Asean, or the Middle East, or Latin America can modernise on its own without strong links with its neighbours through trade, finance and infrastructure. With Asean, for example, there really is the need for an Asean-wide energy system, not separate energy systems for Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia etc. These countries need an interconnected power grid, and China will play a key role in achieving an Asean-wide grid. Therefore, China-Asean diplomacy is strongly win-win.

I also believe that Hong Kong will have a huge and indeed unique leadership role in the global transformation. Hong Kong is vital for China’s growing links with Asean, the African Union, and beyond. The Greater Bay Area (GBA) combines Hong Kong’s world-class leadership in international finance, higher education and global management, with Shenzhen’s leadership in cutting-edge technologies, and the advanced manufacturing of Dongguan, Guangzhou and other GBA cities.

Put these strengths together, and the GBA becomes the beating heart of the global green transformation, in zero-carbon energy, robotics, AI-based manufacturing, digital connectivity and much more. All of this will help to fuel China’s – and Hong Kong’s – rapid growth for the next generation.

This year marks the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. How is the post-war world order changing and what will the new world order look like?

There are three scenarios.

One is that we create a truly multilateral world. For that, we need a United Nations 2.0. We need an upgraded international system in which all the major powers agree to invest in the international rule of law and peaceful resolution of conflicts. This will require an upgrade of the UN Security Council, and UN institutions more generally.

I’d love to see a major UN campus in China, to help lead the green and digital transformation worldwide. I’d love to see China and India working together closely at the UN, including towards India’s seat in the UN Security Council. I’d like China to support the African Union to play a much larger role in global governance. I’d like to see China, Japan and Korea end the geopolitical divisions and form a strong alliance in northeast Asia. Most importantly in this scenario, the US and Europe accept the rising role of China, India and the rest of the non-Western world.

A second scenario is that the Western world hunkers down. It goes protectionist and the US tries to divide the world into camps. This is perhaps the likely US strategy, but I think it is significantly worse for the US and the rest of the world than the first scenario. I think the US absolutely should abandon the idea of building competing camps.

The third scenario is that we don’t have a global system at all, but rather increasing chaos from climate change, wars and geopolitical conflicts. This dire scenario is a real possibility.

Any of these three trajectories is possible. We should be aiming for the first. The United States and Europe should take a deep breath, sigh and welcome the non-Western world into a shared global leadership. The major powers – the US, Europe, Russia, China, India – should agree to prevent confrontations.

The US should stop Nato enlargement and should stop providing armaments to Taiwan. Such actions are provocative and lead to great-power conflicts that threaten the safety and security of the whole world.

In short, the West should stop asking “Who is Number One?” and instead ask, “How can the whole world work together for the global common good?” In my experience, China, Russia and other nations would enthusiastically back such a global, cooperative effort that is based on mutual respect and mutual security.
